title: vector bundles over real and complex manifolds
text:
\(\newcommand{\k}{\mathbb{K}}\) \(\newcommand{\r}{\mathbb{R}}\) \(\newcommand{\c}{\mathbb{C}}\)
All manifolds considered here are aasumed to be Hausdorff. Let \(\k\) be the field \(\r\) or \(\c\).

Definition 1
A smooth \(\k\)-vector bundle of rank \(r\) is a triple \((E,M,\pi)\) of smooth manifolds \(E\) and \(M\), and a smooth surjective map \(\pi:E\rightarrow M\) such that:

for every point \(x \in M\), the set \(E_x = \pi^{-1} (x)\) is a vector space over the field \(\k\).
for every point \(x\in M\), there is an open neighborhood \(U\) of the point \(x\) and a diffeomorphism \[
\varphi_U: \pi^{-1}(U) \rightarrow U \times \k^r\,,
\] whose restriction to every vector space \(E_y, y\in U\), is an isomorphism onto the vector space \(\{y\}\times \k^r\).

title: Fiber Spaces
text:
Let \(E,X\) be two topological spaces and let \(p:E \rightarrow X\) be a continuous map.

Definition 1
The triple \((E,X,p)\) is called a fiber space, \(E\) is called the total space, \(X\) is called the base space, and \(p\) is called the projection. If \(x \in X\), the set \(E_{x}= p^{- 1}( x)\) is called the fiber over \(x\).


A fiber space \((E,X,p)\) will be denoted simply by \(E\) when no confusion is possible. We shall also say that \(E\) is a fiber space over \(X\).
Let \(E=(E,X,p)\) be a fiber space and let \(Y\) be a subset of \(X.\) The restriction of \(E\) to \(Y\) is the fiber space \(E\mid Y=(p^{-1}(Y),Y,p\mid p^{-1}(Y)).\) We shall also write \(E\mid Y=(E\mid Y,Y,p)\).
Let \(E= ( E, X, p)\) be a fiber space and let \(F\) be a subspace of \(E.\) The fiber space \(F=(F,X,p\mid F)\) is called a subfiber space of \(E\).

Definition 2
Let \(E\) be a fiber space over \(X\) and let \(Y \subset X\). A continuous map \[
\sigma:Y \rightarrow E
\] such that, for every \(x\in Y,p\circ\sigma(x)=x\), is called a cross-section of \(E\) over \(Y\).


If \(Y=X\),the cross-section \(\sigma\) is called a global cross-section of \(E\). A cross section \(\sigma\) of \(E\) over \(Y\) is a global cross-section of \(E\mid Y\). By cross-section of \(E\) we shall always mean global cross-section.
Let \(E\) be a fiber space over \(X\), let \(Y\) be a subset of \(X\) and let \(W\) be a subset of \(Y\). If \(\sigma\) is a cross-section of \(E\) over \(Y\),we shall denote by \(\sigma|W\) the restriction of \(\sigma\) to \(W\).
Let \(F\) be a subfiber space of a fiber space \(E\) over \(X\) and let \(\sigma\) be a cross section of \(E\). Then \(\sigma\) is a cross-section of \(F\) if and only if \(\sigma(x)\in F\) for every \(x\in X\).
Let \(E= ( E, X, p)\) be a fiber space. If \(Y\in X\), we shall denote by \(\Gamma(Y,E)\) the set of all cross-sections of \(E\) over \(Y\). If \(W\in Y\), the inclusion \(W\to Y\) induces a restriction map:
\[
\varrho_{W}^{Y}:\Gamma(Y,E)\rightarrow\Gamma(W,E)
\]
It is easy to check that, if \(V\subset W\subset Y\), the restriction maps satisfy the property: \(\varrho_{V}^{W}\circ\varrho_{W}^{Y}=\varrho_{V}^{Y}\), and, for every \(Y\subset X\), \(\varrho_{Y}^{Y}=\operatorname{id}\).
Let \(E=(E,X,p)\) and \(F=(F,Y,q)\) be two fiber spaces. A pair \((\phi,\psi)\) of continuous maps \(\phi:E \rightarrow F, \psi: X \rightarrow Y\) such that the following diagram



commutes is called a morphism of a fiber map and is denoted by \((\phi,\psi):E\rightarrow F\). It’s clear that a morphism maps fibers of \(E\) into fibers of \(F\).
A particular case occurs when \(E,F\) are two fiber spaces over the same base space \(X\) and the map \(\psi\) is the identity. A fiber map \(E\to F\) is given now by a single continuous map \(\phi:E\to F\) such that the diagram



commutes. In this case, \(\phi\) is called an \(X\)-morphism. For every \(x\in X\) we now have \(\phi(E_x)\subset F_x\).
Let \((\phi,\psi){:}E\to F\) be a fiber map and let \(\sigma\) be a global cross-section of \(E\). If the map \(\psi{:}X\to Y\) is a homeomorphism, then, \[
\sigma^{\prime}=\phi\circ\sigma\circ\psi^{-1}:Y\rightarrow F
\] is a global cross-section of \(F\) called the cross-section of \(F\) induced by \((\phi,\psi)\).



If \(E\) and \(F\) are two fiber spaces over the same base space \(X\) and \(\phi: E \rightarrow F\) is a fiber map, to every cross-section \(\sigma\) of \(E\) over \(X\) there is always an induced cross-section \(\sigma^{\prime}\) of \(F\) over \(X\) given by \(\sigma^\prime=\phi \circ \sigma\).

Remark. Let \(X=(X,X,i)\) be the fiber space defined by the identity \(i:X \rightarrow X.\) Then, if \(E=(E,X,p)\) is any fiber space over \(X\), every cross-section \(\sigma\) of \(E\) can be defined as an \(X\)-morphism \(\sigma{:}X\rightarrow E\).

Let \(E=(E,X,p)\) ånd \(F=(F,Y,q)\) be two fiber spaces. A fiber map \((\phi,\psi){:}E\to F\) is said to be an isomorphism if both \(\phi\) and \(\psi\) are homeomorphisms. If \((\phi,\psi)\) is an isomorphism, then \((\phi^{-1},\psi^{-1})\) is a fiber map \(F\to E\) and \((\phi\circ\phi^{-1},\psi\circ\psi^{-1}),(\phi^{-1}\circ\phi,\psi^{-1}\circ\psi)\) are identities.
If \(E\) and \(F\) are two fiber spaces over the same base space \(X\) and \(\phi{:}E\to F\) is a homeomorphism, then \(\phi\) is called an \(X\)-isomorphism.
Two fiber spaces \(E,F\) over \(X\) are said to be locally isomorphic if to every point \(x\in X\) there is a neighborhood \(U_{x}\) of \(x\) and an \(U_{x}\)-isomorphism between \(E\mid U_{x}\) and \(F\mid U_{x}\).
Let \(p{:}E\to X\) be a fiber space over \(X;\) let \(Y\) be a topological space, and let \(f{: }Y\to X\) be a continuous map. The induced fiber space \(f^*E\) is a fiber space \(\pi{:}f^*E\to Y\) where the total space \(f^*E\) is the subspace of the product space \(Y\times E\) consisting of those points \((y,e),y\in Y,e\in E\) such that \(f(y)=p(e).\) The projection \(\pi\) is given by \(\pi(y,e)=y\).
The restriction of a fiber space \(E\) over \(X\) to a subset \(Y\subset X\) is a particular case of induced fiber space. In fact, if \(i{:}Y\to X\) is the inclusion map, clearly \(i^{*}E\) is Y-isomorphic to \(E\mid Y\).
The notion of a fiber space, as we defined it, is nothing more than the notion of a continuous function. We shall obtain a less trivial and rather useful obiect by requiring many additional structures.

title: regular space and other spaces
text:
Base and subbase
A topological space \(X\) is called a regular space if \(X\) is a \(T_1\)-space1 and for every \(x\in X\) and every closed set \(F\subset X\) such that \(x\notin F\) there exist open sets \(U_1,U_2\) such that \(x\in U_1,F\subset U_2\) and \(U_1\cap U_2=\emptyset\).
Clearly the separation condition is equivalent to the following Characterization:

Characterization 1: \((\mathbf{O}_{\rm{III}})\)
Each point \(x\in X\) has a closed neighborhood basis.



Proposition 1
A \(T_1\)-space \(X\) is a regular space if and only if for every \(x\in X\) and every neighborhood \(V\) of \(x\) in a fixed subbase \(\mathscr{P}\) there exists a neighborhood \(U\) of \(x\) such that \(\overline{U}\subset V\).
In particular, a \(T_1\)-space \(X\) is a regular space if and only if for every \(x\in X\) and every neighborhood \(V\) of \(x\) there exists a neighborhood \(U\) of \(x\) such that \(\overline{U}\subset V\).



Proof. Suppose that \(X\) is a regular space and \(\mathscr{P}\) a subbase for \(X\); take an \(x\in X\) and a neighborhood \(V\in \mathscr{P}\) of \(x\). By the definition of a regular space, there exist open sets \(U_1,U_2\) such that \(x\in U_1\) and \(X\setminus V \subset U_2\) and \(U_1\cap U_2=\emptyset\). We then have \(U_1\subset X\setminus U_2 \subset V\) which implies that \(\overline{U_1}\subset V\), since \(X\setminus U_2\) is closed.
Suppose now that the condition is satisfied. Take an \(x\in X\) and a closed set \(F\) such that \(x\notin F\). By the definiton of a subbase there exist \(V_1,\dots,V_k\in \mathscr{P}\) satisfying \(x\in \bigcap_{i=1}^{k} V_i \subset X\setminus F\). For \(i=1,\dots,k\) take a neighborhood \(W_i\) of \(x\) such that \(\overline{W_i}\subset V_i\). The open sets \(U_1=\bigcap_{i=1}^{k}W_i\) and \(U_2=X\setminus \bigcap_{i=1}^{k} \overline{W_i}\) are disjoint, \(x\in U_1\) and \[
F \subset X\setminus \bigcap_{i=1}^{k}V_i \subset X\setminus \bigcap_{i=1}^{k} \overline{W_i}=U_2\,.
\]

We shall now give an example of a Hausdorff space that is not regular.

Example 2: T_2 but not T_3
Let \(X\) be the set of real numbers and \(Z\subset X\) the set of reciprocals of all integers different from zero. For every \(x\in X\) let \(U_i(x)=(x-1/i,x+1/i)\) and \[
B(x)=
\begin{cases}
\{U_i(x)\}_{i=1}^{\infty} \quad \text{if } x\neq 0\,,\\
\{U_i(x) \setminus Z\}_{i=1}^{\infty} \quad \text{if }x=0\,.
\end{cases}
\]



Proposition 2

Any subsapce of a regular topological space \(X\) is regular.
If for any point \(x\in X\) there exists a regular closed neighborhood of \(x\), then \(X\) is regular.




Example 3: T_1 but not T_2
Suppose that \(X\) is the interval \([-1,+1]\) of \(\mathbf{R}\). We consider the equivalence relation \(S\) on \(X\): if \(x\neq \pm 1\), the equivalence class of \(x\) is \(\{x,-x\}\); the equivalence class of \(1\) and \(-1\) are each reduced to that point. Show that the relation \(S\) is open and that the quotient space \(X/S\) is accessible (\(T_1\)) but not separated (\(T_2\)). Furthermore, every point of \(X/S\) possesses a neighborhood in \(X/S\) which is a regular subspace.



Exercise 1

In a topological space \(X\), an open set \(U\) is said to be regular if we have \(U=\operatorname{int}(\overline{U})\). It is equivalent to saying that \(U\) is the interior of some closed set. \(X\) is semi-regular (the topology \(\mathscr{T}\) on it is then called semi-regular) if the regular open sets in \(X\) form a base of \(X\). Prove that if \(\mathscr{T}\) satisfies \((\mathbf{O}_{\rm{III}})\), then \(\mathscr{T}\) is semi-regular.

title: regular space and other spaces
text:
Footnotes


Clearly, every regular space is a Hausdorff space. It is in order to guarantee this implication that we assume - besides the possibility of separation of points and closed sets - that a regular space is a \(T_1\)-space. The anti-discrete space has the required property of separation but it is not a \(T_1\)-space.↩︎

title: locally finite family
text:
We shall now define an important class of families of sets for which the closure operator is additive.

Definition 1
A family \(\{A_s\}_{s\in S}\) of subsets of a topological space \(X\) is locally finite if for every point \(x\in X\) there exists a neighborhood \(U\) such that the set \(\{s\in S:U\cap A_s \neq \emptyset\}\) is finite. If every point \(x\in X\) has a neighborhood that intersects at most one set of a given family, then we say that the family is discrete. Clearly, any discrete family, as well as any finite family, is locally finite.


It is clear that if \(\{A_s\}_{s\in S}\) is a locally finite family and \(B_s \subseteq A_s\), then \(\{B_s\}_{s\in S}\) is locally finite.
It follows that the union of a family of closed sets is closed.

Theorem 1
For every locally finite family \(\{A_s\}_{s\in S}\) we have the equality \(\overline{\bigcup_{s\in S}A_s}=\bigcup_{s\in S}\overline{A_s}\).



Proof. It follows that \(\overline{A_s}\subset \overline{\bigcup_{s\in S}A_s}\) for every \(s\in S\); therefore we have \(\bigcup_{s\in S}\overline{A_s}\subset \overline{\bigcup_{s\in S}A_s}\). To prove the reverse inclusion, let us note that, by local finiteness of \(\{A_s\}_{s\in S}\), for every \(x\in\overline{\bigcup_{s\in S}A_s}\), there exists a neighborhood \(U\) such that the set \(S_0=\{s\in S:A_s\cap U \neq \emptyset\}\) is finite. It follows from the definition of closure that \(x \notin \overline{\bigcup_{s\in S\setminus S_0}A_s}\); since \[
x \in \overline{\bigcup_{s\in S}A_s}=\overline{\bigcup_{s\in S_0}A_s} \cup \overline{\bigcup_{s\in S\setminus S_0}A_s}\,,
\] we have \(x\in \overline{\bigcup_{s\in S_0}A_s}=\bigcup_{s\in S_0}\overline{A_s}\subset \bigcup_{s\in S}\overline{A_s}\).


Proposition 2
If \(\{A_s\}_{s\in S}\) is a locally finite (discrete) family, then the family \(\{\overline{A_s}\}_{s\in S}\) also is locally finite (discrete).



Proof. It follows readily from the fact that if a neighborhood \(V\) of \(x\) intersects \(\overline{A}\) then \(V\) intersects \(A\).

title: base and subbase
text:
Definition 1

In a topological space \(X\), a neighborhood of a subset \(A\subset X\) is a set containing an open set containing \(A\).
Let \(x\in X\) and suppose that there exists an open set \(U\) which contains \(x\). Then \(U\) is called an open neighborhood of \(x\).




Remark. Henceforth, When we speak simply of a neighborhood, we will always mean an open one; otherwise, we will specify closed neighborhood or compact neighborhood, or others, in order to avoid any confusion in terminology.


Definition 2
A family \(\mathscr{B}\subset \mathscr{O}\) is called a base for a topological space \((X,\mathscr{O})\) if every non-empty open subset of \(X\) can be represented as the union of a subfamily of \(\mathscr{B}\).


One can easily check that a family \(\mathscr{B}\) is a base if and only if \(\mathscr{B}\subset \mathscr{O}\) and for every point \(x\in X\) and any neighborhood \(V\) of \(x\) there exists a \(U\in \mathscr{B}\) such that \(x\in U\subset V\). Any base \(\mathscr{B}\) has the following properties:

Proposition 1

For any \(U_1,U_2\in \mathscr{B}\) and every point \(x\in U_1\cap U_2\) there exists a \(U\in \mathscr{B}\) such that \(x\in U\subset U_1\cap U_2\).
For every \(x\in X\) there exists a \(U\in \mathscr{B}\) such that \(x\in U\).




Definition 3
A family \(\mathscr{P}\subset \mathscr{O}\) is called a subbase for a topological space \((X,\mathscr{O})\) if the family of all finite intersections \(U_1\cap U_2\cap\cdots\cap U_k\) where \(U_i\in \mathscr{P}\) is a base for \((X,\mathscr{O})\).

title: Inverse function theorem
text:
Theorem 1: Inverse function theorem
Let \(W\) be an open subset of \(\mathbf{R}^n\) and \(W\rightarrow \mathbf{R}^n\) a \(C^r\) mapping, \(r=1,2,\dots\) or \(\infty\). If \(a\in W\) and \((df)_a\) is nonsingular (has rank \(n\)), then there exists an open neighborhood \(U\) of \(a\) in \(W\) such that \(V:=f(U)\) is open and \(f:U\rightarrow V\) is a \(C^r\) diffeomorphism. If \(x\in U\) and \(y=f(x)\), then we have the following fomula for the derivatives (differential) of \(f^{-1}\) at \(y\): \[
(df^{-1})_{y=f(x)}=(df)_x^{-1},
\] the term on the right denoting the inverse matrix to \((df)_x\).

title: Partition of Unity
text:
\(\newcommand{\R}{\mathbf{R}}\) \(\newcommand{\B}{\operatorname{B}}\) \(\newcommand{\d}{\operatorname{d}\!}\)
We now go into the proof of existence of a differentiable partition of unity subordinate to a given covering by coordinate neighborhoods of a compact differentiable manifold \(M^n\) (we will require no orientability for that).
In what follows, \(\B_r(0)=\{p\in\R^n: |p|<r\}\).

Lemma 1
There exists a differentiable function \(\varphi:\B_3(0)\rightarrow \R\) such that:

\(\varphi(p)=1\), if \(p\in\B_1(0)\);
\(0<\varphi(p)\leq 1\), if \(p\in \B_2(0)\);
\(\varphi(p)=0\), if \(p\in\B_3(0)\setminus \B_2(0)\).




Proof. We first consider the function \(\alpha:\R\rightarrow\R\) given by \[
\begin{aligned}
\alpha(t) & = \exp(\frac{1}{(t+1)(t+2)}), \quad t\in (-2,-1); \\
\alpha(t) & =0,\quad t\notin(-2,-1).
\end{aligned}
\] Notive that \(\alpha\) is \(C^\infty\) everywhere.
Now take the integral \[
\gamma(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{t} \alpha(s)\d s
\] to obtain a differentiable function \(\gamma\) whose maximum value (at point \(-1\)) is given by \(\int_{-2}^{-1}\alpha(s)\d s=A\). Then, by setting \(\beta(t)=\gamma(t)/A\), we obtain a differentiable function with the following properties: \[
\begin{aligned}
\beta(t)=0, & \quad \text{if } t\leq -2; \\
0<\beta(t)\leq 1, & \quad \text{if } t\in (-2,-1), \\
\beta(t)=1, & \quad \text{if } t\geq -1.
\end{aligned}
\] The required function \(\varphi:\B_3(0)\rightarrow \R\) is obtained by \(\varphi(p)=\beta(-|p|)\), \(p\in\B_3(0)\).


Lemma 2
Let \(M^n\) be a differentiable manifold, let \(p\in M\) and let \(g:U\subset \R^n\rightarrow M\) be a parametrization around \(p\). Then it is possible to obtain a parametrization \(f:\B_3(0)\rightarrow M\) around \(p\) in such a way that \(f(\B_3(0))\subset g(U)\) and that \(f^{-1}(p)=(0,\dots,0)\).



Proof. Let \((x_1^0,\dots,x_n^0)\in U\) be such that \(g(x_1^0,\dots,x_n^0)=p\). Since \(U\) is open, there exists an \(r>0\) such that \(\B_r(x_1^0,\dots,x_n^0)\subset U\). Let \(T\) be the translation in \(\R^n\) that takes \(x_1^0,\dots,x_n^0\) to \((0,\dots,0)\), and let \(H:\R^n\rightarrow \R^n\) be the map that to each \(p\in \R^n\) associates the point \(\frac{3}{r}p\). Then \(H\circ T\) takes \(\B_r(x_1^0,\dots,x_n^0)\) to \(\B_3(0)\).
We define the parametrization \(f:\B_3(0) \rightarrow M\) by \[
f=g\circ T^{-1} \circ H^{-1}
\] which is easily seen to satisfy the required conditions.


Proposition 3: Existence of a differentiable partition of Unity
Let \(M\) be a compact manifold and let \(\{V_\alpha\}\) be a covering of \(M\) by coordinate neighborhoods. Then there exist differentiable functions \(\varphi_1,\dots,\varphi_m\) such that:

\(\sum_{i=1}^{m}\varphi_i=1\)
\(0\leq \varphi_i \leq 1\), and the support of \(\varphi_i\) is contained in some \(V_{\alpha_i}\) of the covering \(\{V_\alpha\}\).




Proof. For each \(p\in M\) consider the parametrization \(f_p:\B_3(0)\rightarrow M\) given by the lemma above with \(f_p(\B_3(0))=V_p \subset V_\alpha\), for some \(V_\alpha\) of the covering \(\{V_\alpha\}\). Set \(W_p=f_p(\B_1(0))\subset V_p\).
The family \(\{W_p\}\) is an open covering of \(M\). Since \(M\) is compact we can select from it a finite covering \(W_1,\dots,W_m\). The corresponding \(V_1,\dots,V_m\) will make up a covering of \(M\).
Let us define functions \(\theta_i:M\rightarrow \R, \quad i=1,\dots,m\), by \[
\begin{aligned}
\theta_i &=\varphi\circ f_i^{-1} \text{ in } V_i \\
\theta_i &= 0 \text{  in  } M\setminus V_i
\end{aligned}
\] where \(\varphi:\B_3(0)\rightarrow \R\) is the function given by Lemma 1. The functions \(\theta_i\) are differentiable and the support of \(\theta_i\) is contained in \(V_i\).
Finally define \(\varphi_i\) by \[
\varphi_i(p)=\frac{\theta_i(p)}{\sum_{j=1}^{m}\theta_j (p)},\quad p\in M.
\] It is immediate to check that the functions \(\varphi_i\) so constructed satisfy the conditions (a) and (b).

title: Differential form on differentiable manifolds
text:
We now extend for differentiable manifolds the notion of a differential form of Chapter 1. Given a vector space \(V\), we will denote by \(\wedge^k(V)\) the set of alternate, \(k\)-linear maps \(w:V\times\dots\times V\rightarrow \mathbf{R}\), where \(V\times \dots \times V\) contains \(k\) factors.

Definition 1
Let \(M^n\) be a differentiable manifold. An exterior \(k\)-form \(w\) in \(M\) is the choice, for every \(p\in M\), of an element \(w(p)\) of the space \(\wedge^k(T_pM)^*\) of alternate \(k\)-linear forms of the tangent space \(T_pM\).


Given an exterior \(k\)-form \(w\) and a parametrization \(f_\alpha:U_\alpha\rightarrow M\), around \(p\in f_\alpha(U_\alpha)\), we define the representation of \(w\) in this parametrization as the exterior \(k\)-form \(w_\alpha\) in \(U_\alpha\subset \mathbf{R}^n\) given by \[
w_\alpha(v_1,\dots,v_k):=w\big((df)_\alpha(v_1),\dots,(df)_\alpha(v_k)\big),\qquad v_1,\dots,v_k \in \mathbf{R}^n\,.
\] If we change coordinates to \(f_\beta:U_\beta\rightarrow M^n,p\in f_\beta(U_\beta)\), we obtain that \[
\begin{aligned}
(f_\beta^{-1}\circ f_\alpha)^*w_\beta(v_1,\dots,v_k)&=w_\beta\big(d(f_\beta^{-1}\circ f_\alpha)(v_1),\dots,d(f_\beta^{-1}\circ f_\alpha)(v_k)\big)\\
&=w\big(df_\beta\circ(d(f_\beta^{-1}\circ f_\alpha)(v_1)),\dots,df_\beta\circ(d(f_\beta^{-1}\circ f_\alpha)(v_k))\big)\\
&=w_\alpha(v_1,\dots,v_k)\\
\end{aligned}
\] that is, \((f_\beta^{-1}\circ f_\alpha)^*w_\beta = w_\alpha\).

Definition 2
A differential \(k\)-form in a differentiable manifold \(M^n\) is an exterior \(k\)-form \(w\) such that for some parametrization \(f_\alpha:U_\alpha\rightarrow M^n\), the representation \(w_\alpha\) is a differential \(k\)-form in the open set \(U_\alpha\subset \mathbf{R}^n\) (hence, in all).


From the above, it follows that a differential \(k\)-form in \(M^n\) is the choice, for each parametrization \((U_\alpha,f_\alpha)\) of \(M\), of a differential \(k\)-form \(w_\alpha\) in \(U_\alpha\) in such a way that for another parametrization \((U_\beta,f_\beta)\), we have \((f_\beta^{-1}\circ f_\alpha)^*w_\beta = w_\alpha\) in \(U_\alpha\cap U_\beta\).
It is an important fact that all the operations defined for differential forms in \(\mathbf{R}^n\) can be extended to differential forms in differentiable manifolds. In particular, if \(w\) is a differential \(k\)-form in \(M^n\), we can define the exterior derivative \(dw\) as the differential \((k+1)\)-form in \(M^n\) whose representation in a parametrization \((U_\alpha,f_\alpha)\) is the exterior derivative of the representation of \(w\) in that parametrization, that is, \((dw)_\alpha=d(w_\alpha)\). Since \[
dw_\alpha=d((f_\beta^{-1}\circ f_\alpha)^*w_\beta)=(f_\beta^{-1}\circ f_\alpha)^*dw_\beta
\] \(dw\) is well defined. The same holds for the wedge product of differential forms.

Definition 3
A vector field \(X\) on a differentiable manifold \(M^n\) is a correspondence that assigns to each point \(p\in M^n\) a tangent vector \(X(p)\in T_pM\). The vecote field \(X\) is said to be differentiable if for every different iable function \(\varphi:M^n\rightarrow R\), \(X(\varphi)\) is again a differentiable function.


Let \(f_\alpha:U_\alpha\rightarrow M\) be a parametrization of \(M\) and \(X_i=\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i},\, i=1,\dots,n\), the basis associatied to the parametrization. Then a vector field \(X\) can be written in \(f_\alpha(U_\alpha)\) as \[
X=\sum_{i=1}^n a_iX_i
\]
Since a vector field \(X\) on \(M\) is an operation on the space \(D\) of differentiable functions on \(M\), we can take the iterates of this operation. For instance, if \(X\) and \(Y\) are vector fields on \(M\), \(\varphi:M\rightarrow \mathbf{R}\) is a differentiable function, we can consider the functions \(Y(X(\varphi))\) and \(X(Y(\varphi))\). In general, such iterated opreations do not lead to a vector field, since they involve second derivatives of \(\varphi\). For instance:

Example 4
Let \(M\) be the real line with the standard differentiable structure. Let \(X=\frac{d}{dx}\) and \(Y=x\frac{d}{dx}\). Then \(X\) and \(Y\) are vector fields on \(M\). However, \(X\circ Y\) and \(Y\circ X\) are not vector fields, since they involve second derivatives of \(\varphi\). In fact, we have \(X(Y(x^3))=9x^2\). Assume that there is a vector field \(f(x)\frac{d}{dx}\) such that \(f(x)\frac{d}{dx}(\varphi)=X(Y(\varphi))\). Then we would have \(f(x)\frac{d}{dx}(x^3)=9x^2\), which implies \(f(x)=3\). Clearly, \(3\frac{d}{dx}\) is not equal to \(X\circ Y\). Similar with \(Y\circ X\).


However, the difference \(X\circ Y-Y\circ X\) is a vector field. In fact, we have

Lemma 1
Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be vector fields on a differentiable manifold \(M\). Then there exists a unique vector field \(Z\) on \(M\) such that for every differentiable function \(\varphi:M\rightarrow \mathbf{R}\), we have \(Z(\varphi)=X(Y(\varphi))-Y(X(\varphi))\).



Proof. We first prove that if such a \(Z\) exists, then it is unique. Let \(Z_1\) and \(Z_2\) be vector fields such that for every differentiable function \(\varphi:M\rightarrow \mathbf{R}\), we have \(Z_1(\varphi)=X(Y(\varphi))-Y(X(\varphi))=Z_2(\varphi)\). Then for every differentiable function \(\varphi\), we have \((Z_1-Z_2)(\varphi)=0\). Since \(Z_1-Z_2\) is a vector field, it follows that \(Z_1-Z_2=0\), hence \(Z_1=Z_2\).
To prove the existence of \(Z\), we take a parametrization \(f_\alpha:U_\alpha\rightarrow M\) and write \(X=\sum_{i=1}^n a_iX_i\) and \(Y=\sum_{i=1}^n b_iX_i\), where \(X_i=\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\) is the basis associated to the parametrization. Then we have \[
Z=\sum_{i=1}^n (a_iY_i-b_iX_i)
\] where \(Y_i\) and \(X_i\) are the components of \(Y\) and \(X\) respectively in the basis \(\{X_1,\dots,X_n\}\).
Write it in local coordinates, we have \[
\begin{aligned}
&XY\varphi=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\left(\sum_{j=1}^n b_j\frac{\partial \varphi}{\partial x_j}\right)=\sum_{i,j=1}^n a_i b_j\frac{\partial^2 \varphi}{\partial x_i \partial x_j}+\sum_{i,j=1}^n a_i\frac{\partial b_j}{\partial x_i}\frac{\partial \varphi}{\partial x_j} \\
&YX\varphi=\sum_{i=1}^n b_i\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\left(\sum_{j=1}^n a_j\frac{\partial \varphi}{\partial x_j}\right)=\sum_{i,j=1}^n b_i a_j\frac{\partial^2 \varphi}{\partial x_i \partial x_j}+\sum_{i,j=1}^n b_i\frac{\partial a_j}{\partial x_i}\frac{\partial \varphi}{\partial x_j}
\end{aligned}
\] hence \[
\begin{aligned}
(XY-YX)\varphi&=\sum_{i,j=1}^n \left(a_i\frac{\partial b_j}{\partial x_i}-b_i\frac{\partial a_j}{\partial x_i}\right)\frac{\partial \varphi}{\partial x_j}\\
&=\sum_{j=1}^n\left(\sum_{i=1}^n(a_i\frac{\partial b_j}{\partial x_i}-b_i\frac{\partial a_j}{\partial x_i})\frac{\partial}{\partial x_j}\right)\varphi\,.
\end{aligned}
\]


Definition 5
The vector field determined by the above lemma is called the bracket of the vector fields \(X\) and \(Y\) and is denoted by \([X,Y]\); clearly, it’s differentiable.



Proposition 2
Let \(X,Y\) and \(Z\) be differentiable vector fields on a differentiable manifold \(M\), \(a\) and \(b\) be real numbers, and \(\varphi\) and \(\theta\) be differentiable functions on \(M\). Then we have

\([X,Y]=-[Y,X]\)
\([aX+bY,Z]=a[X,Z]+b[Y,Z]\)
\([[X,Y],Z]+[[Y,Z],X]+[[Z,X],Y]=0 \qquad (\text{Jacobi's identity})\)
\([\theta X,\varphi Y]=\theta\varphi[X,Y]+\theta X(\varphi)Y-\varphi Y(\theta)X\)



The proof of these basic properties are straightforward.
There exists an interesting relation between exterior differentiation of differential forms and the bracket operation. For the case of \(1\)-forms, this relation is as follows.

Proposition 3
Let \(w\) be a differentiable \(1\)-form on a differentiable manifold \(M\) and \(X\) and \(Y\) be differentiable vector fields on \(M\). Then we have \[
dw(X,Y)=X(w(Y))-Y(w(X))-w([X,Y]).\qquad({\star})
\]



Proof. Set \(f:U\rightarrow M\) be a parametrization of \(M\) and let \[
X=\sum_i a_i\, \frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}, \quad Y=\sum_j b_j\,\frac{\partial}{\partial x_j}
\] be the expressions of \(X\) and \(Y\) in this parametrization. We first observe that \((\star)\) holds for \(X_i\) and \(Y_j\), then it also holds for \(\sum X_i\) and \(\sum Y_j\). Next we claim that if \((\star)\) holds for \(X\) and \(Y\), it also holds for \(\theta X\) and \(\varphi Y\), when \(\theta\) and \(\varphi\) are differentiable functions on \(M\).
To see that, we first notice that, by hypothesis, \[
dw(\theta X,\varphi Y)=\theta\varphi dw(X,Y)=\theta\varphi\left(X(w(Y))-Y(w(X))-w([X,Y])\right)\,.
\] It follows that \[
\begin{aligned}
&\theta X \left(w(\varphi Y)\right)-\varphi Y\left(w(\theta X)\right)-w\left([\theta X,\varphi Y]\right)\\
=&\theta X(\varphi w(Y))-\varphi Y(\theta w(X))-w\left(\theta\varphi[X,Y]+\theta X(\varphi)Y-\varphi Y(\theta)X\right)\\
=&\theta\varphi X(w(Y))+\theta X(\varphi)w(Y)-\varphi\theta Y(w(X))-\varphi Y(\theta)w(X)-\theta\varphi w([X,Y])-\theta X(\varphi)w(Y)+\varphi Y(\theta)w(X)\\
=&\theta\varphi\left(X(w(Y))-Y(w(X))-w([X,Y])\right)\\
=&dw(\theta X,\varphi Y)\,.
\end{aligned}
\]
Now it suffices to show that \[
dw(X_i,X_j)=X_i(w(X_j))-X_j(w(X_i))-w([X_i,X_j])=X_i(w(X_j))-X_j(w(X_i))\,. \qquad (\star^\prime)
\] To show this, we write \(w=\sum_k w_k dx_k\), where \(dx_k\) is the dual basis of \(\frac{\partial}{\partial x_k}\). Then we have \[
\begin{aligned}
dw(X_i,X_j)&=d\left(\sum_k w_k dx_k\right)(X_i,X_j)=\sum_k dw_k\wedge dx_k(X_i,X_j)\\
&=\sum_k\left(dw_k(X_i)dx_k(X_j)-dw_k(X_j)dx_k(X_i)\right)=\sum_k\left(\frac{\partial w_k}{\partial x_i}\delta_{kj}-\frac{\partial w_k}{\partial x_j}\delta_{ki}\right)\\
&=\frac{\partial w_j}{\partial x_i}-\frac{\partial w_i}{\partial x_j}=X_i(w(X_j))-X_j(w(X_i))\,.
\end{aligned}
\] and this proves \((\star^\prime)\), hence \((\star)\).


Remark. With essentially the same proof, we can show that if \(w\) is a differentiable \(k\)-form on a differentiable manifold \(M\) and \(X_1,\dots,X_{k+1}\) are differentiable vector fields on \(M\), then we have \[
dw(X_1,\dots,X_{k+1})=\sum_{i=1}^{k+1}(-1)^{i+1}X_i(w(X_1,\dots,\hat{X}_i,\dots,X_{k+1}))-\sum_{i<j}w([X_i,X_j],X_1,\dots,\hat{X}_i,\dots,\hat{X}_j,\dots,X_{k+1})\,.
\] where \(\hat{X_i}\) denotes the omission of \(X_i\).


Definition 6
A differentiable manifold \(M\) is said to be orientable if \(M\) has a differentiable atlas \(\{(U_\alpha,f_\alpha)\}\) such that for every pair of parametrizations \((U_\alpha,f_\alpha)\) and \((U_\beta,f_\beta)\), the Jacobian of the change of coordinates \(f_\beta^{-1}\circ f_\alpha\) is positive in \(U_\alpha\cap U_\beta\). Such an atlas is called an orientation of \(M\).

title: Tangent vectors/Differential of map between manifolds
text:
We will extend to differentiable manifolds the local differential calculus that holds for \(\mathbf{R}^n\). From now on, when we denote a differentiable manifold by \(M^n\), the upper index \(n\) will denote the dimension of \(M=M^n\).

Definition 1
Let \(M_1^n\) and \(M_2^n\) be differentiable manifolds. A map \(\varphi:M_1\rightarrow M_2\) is differentiable at a point \(p\in M_1\) if given a parametrization \(g:\mathbf{R}^m\supset V\rightarrow M_2\) around \(\varphi(p)\), there exists a parametrization \(f:\mathbf{R}^n\supset U\rightarrow M_1\) around \(p\) such that \(\varphi(f(U))\subset g(V)\) and the map \[
g^{-1}\circ \varphi \circ f:\mathbf{R}^n\supset U\rightarrow \mathbf{R}^m
\] is differentiable at \(f^{-1}(p)\). The map \(\varphi\) is differentiable in an open set of \(M_1\) if it is differentiable at all points of the set.


The map \(g^{-1}\circ \varphi \circ f\) is the expression of \(\varphi\) in the parametrizations \(f\) and \(g\);clearly the fact that \(\varphi\) is differentiable does not depend on the choice of parametrizations.
In particular, it follows from the above that we can talk about differentiable functions (\(\varphi:M^n\rightarrow \mathbf{R}\)) and differentiable curves (\(\psi:\mathbf{R}\supset I\rightarrow M^n\)) on a differentiable manifold (\(I\subset \mathbf{R}\) will always denote an open interval of the real line containing the origin);i.e. for any point \(\psi(p)\) on the curve and any parametrization around it \((U,f):\psi(p)\in f(U)\) the composition \(f^{-1}\circ \psi\) is differentiable at \(p\).
Now we would like to define the notion of a tangent vector to a differentiable curve on a differentiable manifold.

Definition 2
Let \(\alpha:I\rightarrow M\) be a differentiable curve on a differentiable manifold \(M\), with \(\alpha(0)=p\in M\), and let \(D\) be the set of functions of \(M\) which are differentiable at \(p\). The tangent vector to the curve at \(p\) is the map, denoted by \(\alpha^{\prime}(0):D\rightarrow \mathbf{R}\), given by \[
\alpha^\prime(0)\varphi=\frac{d}{dt}(\varphi\circ\alpha)\vert_{t=0}, \qquad \varphi\in D.
\] A tangent vector at \(p\in M\) is the tangent vector of some differentiable curve \(\alpha:I\rightarrow M\) with \(\alpha(0)=p\).


We want to show that the set of tangent vectors at a point \(p\in M^n\) makes up an \(n\)-dimensional real vector space.
For that, choose a parametrization \(f:U\subset \mathbf{R}^n\rightarrow M^n\) around \(p=f(0,\dots,0)\). Let \(\alpha^{\prime}(0)\) be a tangent vector at \(p\) which is tangent to \(\alpha:I\rightarrow M^n\) with \(\alpha(0)=p\). Let \(D\) be the set of functions of \(M\) which are differentiable at \(p\) and let \(\varphi\in D\) be any function in the set. Denote \(f^{-1}\circ\alpha\) by \((x_1(t),\dots,x_n(t))\) and \(\varphi\circ f\) by \(\varphi_f\). By definition of \(\alpha^\prime(0)\), we have: \[
\begin{aligned}
\alpha^\prime(0)\varphi&=\frac{d}{dt}(\varphi\circ\alpha)\vert_{t=0}=\frac{d}{dt}((\varphi\circ f)\circ(f^{-1}\circ\alpha))\vert_{t=0} \\
&=\frac{d}{dt}(\varphi_f \circ(k_1(t),\dots,k_n(t)))\vert_{t=0}\\
&=\sum_{i=1}^n \varphi_f^{i}\cdot\frac{dk_i}{dt}\vert_{t=0} \qquad \text{where } \varphi_f^i \text{ denotes the i'th partial derivative of } \varphi_f \text{ at the origin} \\
\end{aligned}
\]
Write \((-)_f^i\) in the form \(\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\vert_0\) where we omit \(f\).
Notice that \(\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\vert_0\) is the tangent vector to the coordinate curve at \(p\); i.e. \[
\frac{\partial(\varphi\circ f)}{\partial x_i}\equiv\alpha_i^\prime(0)(\varphi) \qquad \text{where }\alpha_i \text{ is the coordinate curve } x_i\rightarrow f(0,\dots,x_i,\dots,0),\, x_i\in \pi_i(U)
\]
This is straightforward for \[
\alpha_i^\prime(0)(\varphi)=\frac{d}{dt}(\varphi\circ \alpha_i)\vert_0=\frac{\partial (\varphi\circ f)}{\partial x_i}.
\]
Now we denote by \(T_fM\) the vector space spanned by \(\{\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\vert_0\}\) (depends on the parametrization \(f\)).
Indeed we note that the set \(T_pM\) of all tangent vectors at \(p\) is exactly the vector space \(T_fM\).

Lemma 1
\(T_fM=T_pM\)



Proof. Clearly \(T_pM\subseteq T_fM\) as \(\alpha^\prime(0)\in T_pM\) implies that it can be written as a linear combination of \(\{\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\vert_0\}\).
We show the reverse inclusion; Let \(v\in T_fM\), then \(v=\sum \lambda_i (\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i})_0\); let \(\alpha:I\rightarrow M\) be the following differentiable curve on \(M\): \[
\alpha:t\rightarrow f(\lambda_1t,\dots,\lambda_nt)
\] Then \(\alpha^\prime(0)=v\); which completes the proof.

It follows that \(T_pM\) is a vector space. Furthermore, the choice of a parametrization \(f\) determines a basis \(\{(\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i})\vert_0\}\) for \(T_pM\). Thus \(T_pM\) is an \(n\)-dimensional vector space which is called the tangent space of \(M\) at \(p\). The basis \(\{(\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i})\vert_0\}\) is called the associated basis to the parametrization \(f\).
With the notion of a tangent space we can define the notions of a differential of a map \(\varphi:M_1^n\rightarrow M_2^m\).

Definition 3
Let \(M_1^n\) and \(M_2^m\) be differentiable manifolds and let \(\varphi:M_1\rightarrow M_2\) be a differentiable map. For each \(p\in M\), the differential of \(\varphi\) at \(p\) is the linear map \((d\varphi)_p:T_pM_1\rightarrow T_{\varphi(p)}M_2\) which associates to each \(v\in T_pM_1\) the vector \((d\varphi)_p(V)\in T_{\varphi(p)}M_2\) defined as follows: Choose a differentiable curve \(\alpha:(-\epsilon,\epsilon)\rightarrow M_1\), with \(\alpha(0)=p,\alpha^\prime(0)=v\); then \((d\varphi)_p(v)=(\varphi\circ\alpha)^\prime(0)\).


For the definiton to make sense, it’s necessary to show that \((\varphi\circ\alpha)^\prime(0)\) does not depend on the choice of \(\alpha\) and that \((d\varphi)_p\) is in fact a linear map. This is proved by taking parametrizations around \(p\) and \(\varphi(p)\) thus reducing to the case of a map from \(\mathbf{R}^n\) to \(\mathbf{R}^m\), where the properties are well known.

Proposition 2
Let \(\varphi\) be a differentiable map from a manifold \(M_1\) into a manifold \(M_2\). If \(f\) is a differentiable function defined in a neighborhood of \(\varphi(p)\) (\(p\in M\)), then \(\varphi^*(f)=f\circ \varphi\) is a differentiable function defined in a neighborhood of \(p\). For \(v\in T_pM_1\), we have the charaterization of the differential: \[
(d\varphi)_p(v)(-)=v(\varphi^*(-))
\]
Sometimes we denote a differential by \((\varphi_*)_p\) to bring out this charaterization.



Proof. Let \(v=\alpha^\prime(0)\) and \(f\) is a differentiable function in a neighborhood of \(\varphi(p)\). Then \(\varphi^* f\) is a differentiable function in a neighborhood of \(p\); thus \(v(\varphi^*f)=\frac{d}{dt}(\varphi^*f\circ \alpha)\vert_{t=0}\); therefore we have \(v(\varphi^*(-))=(d\varphi)_p(v)(-)\)


Proposition 3
Let \(M\) and \(N\) be differentiable manifolds and \(p\in M\) and \(\varphi:M\rightarrow N\) be a differentiable map. Let \(f:\mathbf{R}^n\supset U\rightarrow M\) be a coordinate neighbourhood of \(p\) and \(g:\mathbf{R}^m\supset V\rightarrow N\) be a coordinate system of \(\varphi(p)\) such that \(g^{-1}\circ \varphi \circ f\) is a differentiable map. Let \(\{(\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i})_0\}\) be the basis of \(T_pM\) w.r.t the parametrization \(f\) and \(\{(\frac{\partial}{\partial y_j})_0\}\) be the basis of \(T_{\varphi(p)}N\) w.r.t the parametrization \(g\). Then \((d\varphi)_p\) admits the form in matrix (w.r.t the bases we choose before): \[
\begin{bmatrix}
\displaystyle\frac{\partial \varphi_1}{\partial x_1}& \dots& \displaystyle\frac{\partial \varphi_1}{\partial x_n} \\
\vdots &\ddots &\vdots \\
\displaystyle\frac{\partial \varphi_m}{\partial x_1} &\cdots& \displaystyle\frac{\partial \varphi_m}{\partial x_n}
\end{bmatrix}
\] where \((\varphi_1,\dots,\varphi_m)=g^{-1}\circ \varphi \circ f\).


The proof is clear.

Definition 4: diffeomorphism/local diffeomorphism
Let \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) be differentiable manifolds. A map \(\varphi:M_1\rightarrow M_2\) is a diffeomorphism if it is differentiable, bijective, and its inverse \(\varphi^{-1}\) is also differentiable.
The map is a local diffeomorphism at \(p\in M\) if there exist neighborhood \(U\) of \(p\) and \(V\) of \(\varphi(p)\) such that \(\varphi\restriction_U:U\rightarrow V\) is a diffeomorphism.


The linear map \((d\varphi)_p\) may be thought as a first order approximation of the map \(\varphi\) around \(p\). Probably the most important theorem in calculus is the inverse function therom which states that if \((d\varphi)_p\) is an isomorphism (locally) then \(\varphi\) is a local diffeomorphism at \(p\). Being a local theorem, it extends immediately to differentiable manifolds.

Theorem 4: Inverse function theorem on manifold
Let \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) be differentiable manifolds and \(x\in M_1\);let \(f:M_1\rightarrow M_2\) be a differentiable mapping. Suppose that \((df)_x；T_xM_1\rightarrow T_{f(x)}M_2\) is nonsingular (i.e. linear isomorphism), then there eixts a neighborhood of \(x\in U\subset M_1\) such that \(f\restriction_U:U\rightarrow f(U)\subset M_2\) is a diffeomorphism.


Let us consider a potentially confusing example.

Example 5
Let \(\mathbf{R}\) be equipped with the standard atlas; i.e. the atlas containing \((\mathbf{R},\operatorname{id})\); Let \(\tilde{\mathbf{R}}\) be a copy of the real line but we will define a new differentiable structure \((\mathbf{R},f)\) where \(f:\mathbf{R}\rightarrow \tilde{\mathbf{R}}; \quad x\mapsto x^{1/3}\) (carefully check that it’s a differentiable structure (non-maxiaml); since its inverse \(x \mapsto x^3\) is differentiable). Notice that \((\mathbf{R},f)\) is not in the standard atlas as \(\operatorname{id}^{-1}\circ f=x^{1/3}\) is not smooth. But \(f:x\mapsto x^{1/3}\) is a differentiable mapping between the two manifolds, for \((x^{1/3})^{-1}\circ f \circ \operatorname{id}=\operatorname{id}\) is a differentiable function. Indeed it’s a diffeomorphism as \(\operatorname{id}^{-1}\circ f^{-1}\circ f\) is a differentiable function.


The conclusion of this very boring example is that: \(x^{1/3}\) is not differentiable when it’s treated as real-valued function; but it’s differentiable, even diffeomorphic, when treated as a mapping between manifolds. This is a tricky point, because we often mix up words like mapping and function in some settings (like the example above). But usually we won’t hit this kind of boring-but-annoying thing again (What? \(x^{1/3}\) is smooth!). So we’re bothering to explain it, even though it looks kind of dumb.
In fact it’s easy to observe that the parametrizations are all diffeomorphisms when we view them as mappings between manifolds like the example above (\(\mathbf{R}^n\) always takes the standard differentiable structure).
And conversely, every diffeomorphism of an open subset of a manifold with an open subset of a Euclidean space can serve as a parametrization.

Proposition 5
If \((U,\varphi)\) is a coordinate system on a manifold \(M\) of dimension \(n\), then the parametrization \(\varphi:U\rightarrow\varphi(U)\subset M\) is a diffeomorphism (here we suppose that \(\mathbf{R}^n\) is equipped with the standard differentiable structue;i.e. the maximal atlas containing \((\mathbf{R}^n,\operatorname{id})\)).



Proof. By definition, \(\varphi\) is a homeomorphism, so it suffices to check that both \(\varphi\) and \(\varphi^{-1}\) are differentiable. To test the smoothness of \(\varphi\), we use the atlas \(\{(U,\operatorname{id})\}\) with a single chart on \(U\) and the atlas \(\{(U,\varphi)\}\) with a single chart on \(\varphi(U)\). Since \(\varphi^{-1}\circ \varphi \circ \operatorname{id}:U\rightarrow U\) is just the identity map, it is differentiable.


Proposition 6
Let \(U\) be an open subset of \(\mathbf{R}^n\) and \(M\) be a differentiable manifold with a differentiable structure \(\mathcal{A}\). Suppose that there is a diffeomorphism \(f\) from \(U\) onto an open subset \(f(U)\) of \(M\), then \((U,f)\) is a chart in the differentiable structure of \(M\).



Proof. For any chart \((U_\alpha,\phi_\alpha)\in\mathcal{A}\), both \(\phi_\alpha\) and \(\phi_\alpha^{-1}\) are differentiable by the proposition 5. As composites of differentiable maps, both \(f^{-1}\circ \phi_\alpha\) and \(\phi_\alpha^{-1}\circ f\) are differentiable. Hence, \((U,f)\in\mathcal{A}\) due to the maximality of the atlas.


Definition 6: immersion/embedding
Let \(M^m\) and \(N^n\) be differentiable manifolds. A differentiable map \(\varphi:M\rightarrow N\) is an immersion if \((d\varphi)_p:T_pM\rightarrow T_{\varphi{(p)}}N\) is injective for all \(p\in M\) (i.e. the rank of linear mapping is equal to \(\operatorname{dim} T_pM=\operatorname{dim} M\)). If, in addition, \(\varphi\) is a homeomorphism onto \(\varphi(M)\subset N\), where \(\varphi(M)\) has the topology induced by \(N\), \(\varphi\) is an embedding. If \(M\subset N\) and the inclusion \(i:M\subset M\) is an embedding, we say that \(M\) is a submanifold of \(N\).


To verify that \(\varphi:\mathbf{R}^1\supset I\rightarrow \mathbf{R}^n\) is an immersion it is necessary to check that the Jacobian has rank \(1\) at every point of \(I\), i.e. one of the derivatives with respect to \(t\) is different from zero for every value of \(t\) where the mapping \(\varphi\) is defined.

Example 7
The curve \(\varphi:\mathbf{R}^1\rightarrow \mathbf{R}^2\) given by \(\varphi(t)=(t^3,t^2)\) is a differentiable map but not an immersion.



Proof. We have \((\varphi\circ \alpha)^\prime(0) f=(f\circ \varphi\circ\alpha)^\prime(0)=(f\circ \varphi)^\prime_{0}\alpha^\prime_0\).
It follows that \((f\circ \varphi)^\prime(0)=\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1}_{(0,0)}\varphi_1^\prime(0)+\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_2}_{(0,0)}\varphi_2^\prime(0)=0\) where \(f\) is a differentiable function at the point \(\varphi(0)=(\varphi_1(0),\varphi_2(0))\).
Consider the tangent vectors at \(0\),\(\alpha_1:(-\epsilon,+\epsilon)\rightarrow \mathbf{R}^1;s\mapsto 0\) and \(\alpha_2:(-\epsilon,+\epsilon)\rightarrow \mathbf{R}^1;s\mapsto s\); clearly they are different in \(T_0M\); but they are the same tangent vector in \(T_{(0,0)}N\) as they have the entirely same action on the differentiable functions at \((0,0)\); i.e. they sends each function differentiable functions at \((0,0)\) to \(0\).
Thus \(T_0M\xrightarrow{(d\varphi)_0}T_{(0,0)}N\) is not an injective map; then not an immersion.
Or more easily, we observe the matrix of the differential: \[
\begin{bmatrix}
3t^2\\
2t
\end{bmatrix}
\] then we have the rank is \(0\) when \(t=0\); thus \(\varphi\) is not an immersion.


Example 8
The curve \(\varphi(t)=(t^3-4t,t^2-4)\) is an immersion that is not an embedding, since it has a self-intersection at \((0,0)\) (for \(t=2,t=-2\)).



Proof. The matrix of differential map is as follows: \[
\begin{bmatrix}
3t^2-4 \\
2t
\end{bmatrix}
\] the rank is always \(1\); then \(\displaystyle(d\varphi)_p\) is injective. But \(\varphi(2)=\varphi(-2)\), \(\varphi\) is not an injection thus not homeomorphism.


Example 9
\(\varphi:\mathbf{R}^1\rightarrow \mathbf{R}^2\) is given by \(t\mapsto (\sin 2\pi t,\,\cos 2\pi t)\). It’s easy to check it’s an immersion as \(\cos x,-\sin x\) cannot be zero at the same time. Notice that the image of this immersion is the unit circle on the plane:\(\{(x_1,x_2)\in\mathbf{R}^2:x_1^2+x_2^2=1\}\).



Example 10
\(\varphi:(1,+\infty)\rightarrow \mathbf{R}^2\) is given by \(t\mapsto (\frac{\cos 2\pi t}{t},\frac{\sin 2\pi t}{t})\) whose image is a curve spiraling to \((0,0)\) when \(t\to +\infty\) and tending to \((1,0)\) as \(t\to 1\).



Example 11
Change the parameter such that the curve spirals to a circle with center at origin and radius of \(\frac{1}{2}\): \(\varphi:(1,+\infty)\rightarrow \mathbf{R}^2\) which is given by: \[
t\mapsto (\frac{t+1}{2t}\cos 2\pi t,\frac{t+1}{2t}\sin 2\pi t).
\]



Example 12
\(\varphi:\mathbf{R}^1\rightarrow \mathbf{R}^2\) is given by \(t\mapsto (2\cos(t-\frac{\pi}{2}),\sin(2(t-\frac{\pi}{2})))\). The image is a “figure eight”.



Example 13
Change the parameter in the example before such that we obtain a curve which passes through the origin only once when \(t=0\) and tends to the origin as \(t\to\pm \infty\). Let \(\varphi\) be given as follows: \[
\begin{aligned}
&t\mapsto (2\cos(g(t)-\frac{\pi}{2}),\sin(2(g(t)-\frac{\pi}{2})))\\
&\text{where } g(t) \text{ is a monotone increasing differentiable function such that}\\
&g(0)=\pi,\lim_{t\to-\infty}g(t)=0,\lim_{t\to +\infty}g(t)=2\pi
\end{aligned}
\] For instance, we can take \(g(t)=\pi+2\arctan t,\quad t\in(-\infty,+\infty)\).



Example 14
Set \(F:\mathbf{R}\rightarrow \mathbf{R}^2\) given by \[
F(t)=
\begin{cases}
(\frac{1}{t},\sin \pi t) \qquad 1\leq t<\infty\\
\text{ a regular curve} \qquad  -1<t<1\\
(0,t+2) \qquad t\leq -1
\end{cases}
\] where the regular curve connected the two pieces smoothly such that \(F\) is an immersion. In the topology of \(\mathbf{R}^2\), a neighborhood of a point \(p\) in the vertical part of the curve has infinitely many connected components, where as in the topology induced by \(F\) it is a connected interval. This is a useful example to keep in mind.



Remark. We may draw some conclusions through the above examples about the nature of immersion.

An immersion need not to be a one-to-one(injective) map, like the example 7, example 8 and example 11.
Even through an immerison can be an one-to-one and continuous mapping onto its image, it need not to be a homeomorphism which requires it has a continuos inverse, like the example 12 and example 13, where the image is not locally connected.

There examples lead to a more restrictive concept—embedding (wirte imbedding sometimes) as we just have defined.


Example 15: The projective plane revisited
The set of straight lines of \(\mathbf{R}^3\) that pass through the origin may be looked upon as the quotient space of the unit sphere \(S^2=\{p\in \mathbf{R}^3:|p|=1\}\) by the equivalence relation that identifies \(p\) with the antipodal point \(-p\). For each line through the origin in \(S^2\) determines two antipodal points, and the correspondence thus obtained is bijective.
Taking this into account, let us introduce another differentiable structure in \(P^2(\mathbf{R})\). For that notice that we cover the regular surface \(S^2\subset \mathbf{R}^3\) by a family of parametrizations: \[
f_i^+:U_i\rightarrow S^2, \qquad f_i^-:U_i\rightarrow S^2, i=1,2,3
\] where \[
\begin{aligned}
&U_1=\{(x_1,x_2,x_3)\in \mathbf{R}^3:x_1=0,x_2^2+x_3^2<1\} \\
&f_1^+(x_2,x_3)=(+\sqrt{1-(x_2^2+x_3^2)},x_2,x_3);\\
&f_1^-(x_2,x_3)=(-\sqrt{1-(x_2^2+x_3^2)},x_2,x_3).
\end{aligned}
\] and similarily for \(i=2,3\). It is immediate to check that this is in fact a differentiable structure for \(S^2\)(see the Example and use the result about change of parameters).
Let \(\pi:S^2\rightarrow P^2(\mathbf{R})\) be the canonical projection, that is, \(\pi(p)=\{p,-p\}\) and notice that \(\pi(f_i^+(U_i))=\pi(f_i^-(U_i))\). We will define \(g_i:U_i\rightarrow P^2(\mathbf{R})\) by \[
g_i=\pi\circ f_i^+
\] Since the restriction of \(\pi\) to \(f_i^+(U_i)\) is injective, we obtain that \[
g_i^{-1}\circ g_j=(\pi\circ f_i^+)^{-1}\circ (\pi\circ f_j^+)=(f_i^+)^{-1}\circ (f_j^+).
\]
It follows that \(g_i^{-1}\circ g_j\) is differentiable for all \(i,j=1,2,3\), hence \(\{(U_i,g_i)\}\) is a differentiable structure for \(P^2(\mathbf{R})\).
Actually the above structure and that of example before will determine the same maxiaml structure. For the coordinate neightborhoods are the same and the diffeomorphism is given by \[
[(1,\frac{x_2}{x_1},\frac{x_3}{x_1})] \leftrightarrow [(+\sqrt{1-x_2^2-x_3^2},x_2,x_3)].
\]



Remark (Crossed-cap). We give an animation which visualizes the process of sewing the bowl continuously; i.e. the image of \(P(\mathbf{R}^2)\) in \(\mathbf{R}^3\) under a differentiable mapping (singular thus not an immersion), since \[
\{S^2/\sim  \xrightarrow{\tilde{f}} \mathbf{R}^3\} \leftrightarrows \{S^2\xrightarrow{f} \mathbf{R}^3:f(A)=f(B) \quad \text{when  } A\sim B\}.
\] The surface we obtained may be called crossed-cap. And notice that it has a self-intersection line where different points on the circle pass at different time.








Figure 1: image of \(P(\mathbf{R}^2)\) in \(\mathbf{R}^3\) under a differentiable mapping: crossed-cap with a bowl




Example 16: Immersion of the projective plane in \(\mathbf{R}^4\)
Let \(\varphi:\mathbf{R}^3\rightarrow \mathbf{R}^4\) be the map given by \[
\varphi(x,y,z)=(x^2-y^2,xy,xz,yz),\quad (x,y,z)\in \mathbf{R}^3
\] Let \(S^2\subset \mathbf{R}^3\) be the unit sphere and let \(\pi:S^2\rightarrow P^2(\mathbf{R})\) be the canonical projection of \(S^2\) onto the real projective plane (i.e. \((x,y,z)\rightarrow [(x,y,z)]\)). Notice that \(\varphi(p)=\varphi(-p)\), and define a map \(\theta:P^2(\mathbf{R})\rightarrow \mathbf{R}^4\) by \[
\theta([p])=\theta(\{p,-p\})=\varphi(p).
\] Since \(\pi\) is a local diffeomorphism (as restriction of it to the half sphere (without boundary) is injective), to show that \(\theta\) is an immersion, it suffices to show that the restriction of \(\varphi\) to the sphere \(S^2\) is an immersion. To see that, choose the parametrization of \(S^2\) given in the example. Then \(f_3^+\), for instance, is given by \[
f_3^+(x,y)=(x,y,+\sqrt{1-(x^2+y^2)})=(x,y,D)
\] and \[
\varphi\circ f_3^+(x,y,z)=(x^2-y^2,xy,xD,yD).
\] To show that \(d(\varphi\circ f_3^+)\) is injective, it suffices to show that the rank of the matrix (by proposition) \[
\begin{bmatrix}
2x & y & D+xD_x & yD_x \\
-2y & x & xD_y & D+yD_y
\end{bmatrix}
\] is equal to two at each point of \(\{(x_1,x_2,x_3)\in \mathbf{R}^3:x_3=0,x_1^2+x_2^2<1\}\), and this is easily checked (by its Jacobian determinants). Similarily, we can check that the same holds for all other parametrizations and this completes the example.

title: Concepts and examples in 3-dimensinal space
text:
We will start with the most familiar example of a differentiable manifold, namely a regular surface in \(\mathbf{R}^3\). Roughly speacking, a regular surface in \(\mathbf{R}^3\) is obtained by taking pieces of a plane, deforming them, and arranging them in such a way that the resulting figure has no sharp points, edges, or self-intersections and so that it makes sense to speak of a tangent plane at points of the figure. The idea is to define a set that is, in a certain sense, two-dimensional and that also is smooth enough so that the ususal notions of calculus can be extended to it.

Definition 1
A subset \(S\subset \mathbf{R}^3\) is called a regular surface if, for each \(p\in S\), there exist a neighbourhood \(V\) of \(p\) in \(\mathbf{R}^3\) and a map \(\mathbf{x}:U\rightarrow V\cap S\) of an open set \(U\) in \(\mathbf{R}^2\) onto \(V\cap S\) such that:

\(\mathbf{x}\) is a differentiable. This means that if we write \[
\mathbf{x}=(x(u,v),y(u,v),z(u,v)), \quad (u,v)\in U
\] the functions \(x,y,z\) have continuous partial derivatives of all orders in \(U\).
\(\mathbf{x}\) is a homeomorphism. This means that \(\mathbf{x}\) has an inverse \(\mathbf{x}^{-1}:V\cap S \rightarrow U\) which is continuous.
(The regularity condition) For each \(q\in U\), the differential \((d\mathbf{x})_q:\mathbf{R}^2\rightarrow\mathbf{R}^3\) is one-to-one (injective).

The mapping \(\mathbf{x}\) is called a parametrization or a system of local coordinates in a neighbourhood of \(p\). The neighbourhood \(V\cap S\) of \(p\) in \(S\) is called a coordinate neighbourhood.


Let’s explain condition 3 by computing the Jacobian matrix of the linear map \((d\mathbf{x})_q\) in the canonical basis (the canonical basis of \(\mathbf{R}^2\) is denoted by \(\{u,v\}\)). We have : \[
\begin{bmatrix}
\frac{\partial x}{\partial u}(q) &\frac{\partial x}{\partial v}(q) \\
\frac{\partial y}{\partial u}(q) &\frac{\partial y}{\partial v}(q) \\
\frac{\partial z}{\partial u}(q) &\frac{\partial z}{\partial v}(q) \\
\end{bmatrix}=(d\mathbf{x})_q
\] Thus the condition 3 is equivalent to saying that the rank of the matrix is \(2\) at each \(q\); i.e. one of the determinants \[
\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)},\frac{\partial(y,z)}{\partial(u,v)},\frac{\partial(x,z)}{\partial(u,v)}
\] is different from zero at each \(q\).

Remark 1
Note that the surface is created by covering \(S\) with the traces of parametrizations which satisfy conditions 1,2,3.
Condition 1 is natural as we wish to do differential geometry on the surface;
Condition 2 requires an inverse at first: this is necessary otherwise the surface may have self-intersection. Furthermore we require it to be continuous of which the necessity would be clear in the future.
Condition 3 will guarantee the existence of a tangent plane at all points of \(S\).


The most familiar example of regular surface is a sphere but we have to check condition carefully:

Example 2
Let us show that the unit sphere \[
S^2=\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbf{R}^3:x^2+y^2+z^2=1\}
\] is a regular surface.



Proof. Set \(\mathbf{x}_1\) as follows: \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{x}_1:\mathbf{R}^2\supset U=\{(x,y):x^2+y^2<1\} &\rightarrow S^2 \\
(x,y)&\mapsto (x,y,+\sqrt{1-x^2-y^2})
\end{aligned}
\]
Condition 1 is satisfied since component functions \(x,y,\sqrt{1-x^2-y^2}\) have partial derivatives of all orders.
Condition 2 is satisfied since \(\pi(x,y,z)=(x,y)\) is a differentiable inverse of \(\mathbf{x}_1\).
Condition 3 is satisfied since there exists one Jacobian determinant \(\frac{\partial (x,y)}{\partial (x,y)}=1\) which is non-zero.
It’s easy to see that we can cover the whole sphere with similar parametrizations and then we verify that sphere is a regular surface.

title: Concepts and examples in 3-dimensinal space
section: Change of parameters; Differentiable functions on surfaces
text:
Change of parameters; Differentiable functions on surfaces
It is important that we be able to define what it means for a function \(f:S\rightarrow R\) to be differentiable at a point \(p\) of a regular surface \(S\).
A natural way to proceed is to choose a coordinate neighborhood of \(p\), with coordinates \(u, v\), and say that \(f\) is differentiable at \(p\) if its expression (i.e. \(f\circ \mathbf{x}\) where \(\mathbf{x}\) is the corresponded parametrization such that \(p\in \mathbf{x}(U)\)) in the coordinates u and v admits continuous partial derivatives of all orders.
However, given a parametrization system (fixed) on a regular surface \(S\), we notice that one point can belong to various coordinate neighborhoods(in the sphere of Example 2 any point of the interior of the first octant belongs to three of the given coordinate neighborhoods);Moreover, other coordinate systems could be chosen in a neighborhood of p (the points referred to on the sphere could also be parametrized by geographical coordinates or by stereographic projection).
For the above definition to make sense, it is necessary that it does not depend on the chosen system of coordinates. In other words, it must be shown that when \(p\) belongs to two coordinate neighborhoods, with parameters \((u, v)\) and \((\xi,\eta)\), it is possible to pass from one of these pairs of coordinates to the other by means of a differentiable transformation.
The following proposition shows that this is true.

Proposition 1: Change of parameters
Let \(p\) be a point of a regular surface \(S\), and let \({x}:\mathbf{R}^2\supset U\rightarrow S;\quad {y}:\mathbf{R}^2\supset V \rightarrow  S\) be two parametrizations of S such that \(p\in  x(U) \cap y(V) = W\). Then the “change of coordinates” \(h=x^{-1}\circ y:y^{-1}(W)\rightarrow x^{-1}(W)\) is a difleomorphism; that is, \(h\) is differentiable and has a differentiable inverse \(h^{-1}\).

title: Exercises 1
text:
Exercise 1
Prove that a bilinear form \(\varphi: \mathbb{R}^3 \times \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}\) is alternate if and only if \(\varphi(v, v) = 0\), for all \(v \in \mathbb{R}^3\).



Proof. \[
\varphi(v,v)+\varphi(v,w)+\varphi(w,w)+\varphi(w,v)=\varphi(v+w,v+w)=0
\]


Exercise 2
Prove that if \(i_1 < i_2 < \ldots < i_k\) and \(j_1 < j_2 < \ldots < j_k\), then
\[
(dx_{i_1} \wedge \ldots \wedge dx_{i_k})(e_{j_1}, \ldots, e_{j_k}) =
\begin{cases}
1, & \text{if } i_1 = j_1, \ldots, i_k = j_k, \\
0, & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\]



Proof. \[
\begin{aligned}
& (dx_{i_1} \wedge \ldots \wedge dx_{i_k})(e_{j_1}, \ldots, e_{j_k}) \\
=&\operatorname{det}(dx_{i_s}(e_{j_t}))_{1\leq s,t \leq k}
\end{aligned}
\] If there exists some \(j_t\) is equal to none of \(i_s\), then the matrix has a zero column, \(\operatorname{det}=0\); Otherwise, \(i_1 = j_1, \ldots, i_k = j_k\) holds.


Exercise 3
Let \(\varphi\) be an exterior \(k\)-form, where \(k\) is an odd integer. Show that \(\varphi \wedge \varphi = 0\).



Proof. \[
\begin{aligned}
\varphi \wedge\varphi=(-1)^{k^2}(\varphi \wedge \varphi)
\end{aligned}
\]


Exercise 4
Let \(\varphi, \psi\) and \(\theta\) the following forms in \(\mathbb{R}^3\):
\[
\varphi = xdx - ydy,
\] \[
\psi = zdx \wedge dy + xdy \wedge dz,
\] \[
\theta = zdy.
\]
Compute: \(\varphi \wedge \psi\), \(\theta \wedge \varphi \wedge \psi\), \(d\varphi\), \(d\psi\), \(d\theta\).



Proof. \[
\begin{aligned}
&(xdx - ydy)\wedge(zdx \wedge dy + xdy \wedge dz)=x^2dx\wedge dy \wedge dz \\
&\theta \wedge \varphi \wedge \psi=0 \\
&d\varphi=0 \\
&d\theta=dz \wedge dy
\end{aligned}
\]


Exercise 5
Let \(\omega\) be the 2-form in \(\mathbb{R}^{2n}\) given by
\[
   \omega = dx_1 \wedge dx_2 + dx_3 \wedge dx_4 + \ldots + dx_{2n-1} \wedge dx_{2n}.
   \]
Compute the exterior product of \(n\) copies of \(\omega\).



Proof. claim: for any positive integer \(n\), \(dx_I=dx_1 \wedge \ldots\wedge dx_{2n}\) where \(dx_I\) is a form like \(\wedge_{k=1}^n(dx_{i_{2k-1}}\wedge dx_{i_{2k}})\); the proof is staightforward using induction on \(n\).
By claim, we know \[
\wedge^n \omega=\sum_{I}dx_I=n!dx_1 \wedge \ldots\wedge dx_{2n}
\]


Exercise 6
Let \(f\colon \mathbf{R}^{n}\to \mathbf{R}^{n}\) be a differentiable map given by
\[
f(x_{1},\ldots ,x_{n}) = (y_{1},\ldots ,y_{n}),
\]
and let \(\omega = d y_{1}\wedge \ldots \wedge d y_{n}\). Show that
\[
f^{*}\omega = \det(df) \, d x_{1}\wedge \ldots \wedge d x_{n}.
\]



Proof. \[
\begin{aligned}
f^*\omega&=df_1 \wedge \ldots \wedge df_n  \\
&=\wedge_{i=1}^{n}(\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac{\partial f_i}{\partial x_j}dx_j) \\
&=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j_k \text{ is a permutation}}\operatorname{sgn}((j_k)) \prod_{j=1}^{n}\frac{\partial f_i}{\partial x_{j_k}} dx_I\\
&=\det(df) \, d x_{1}\wedge \ldots \wedge d x_{n}
\end{aligned}
\]


Exercise 7: volume
Let \(\nu\) be the \(n\)-form in \(\mathbf{R}^{n}\) defined by
\[
\nu (e_{1},\ldots ,e_{n}) = 1,
\]
where \(\{e_{i}\} ,i = 1,\ldots ,n\), is the canonical basis of \(\mathbf{R}^{n}\). Show that:

If \(v_{i} = \sum a_{i j} e_{j}\), then

\[
\nu (v_{1},\ldots ,v_{n}) = \det(a_{i j}) = \operatorname{vol}(v_{1},\ldots ,v_{n}).
\]
(The form \(\nu\) is called the volume element of \(\mathbf{R}^{n}\).)

\(\nu = d x_{1}\wedge \ldots \wedge d x_{n}\).




Proof. 

CLear.
\(\nu(e_1,\ldots,e_n)=\det(dx_i(e_j))=1\)



Exercise 8: Hodge Star Operation
Given a \(k\)-form \(\omega\) in \(\mathbf{R}^{n}\) we will define an \((n - k)\)-form \(\ast \omega\) by setting
\[
\ast (d x_{i_{1}}\wedge \ldots \wedge d x_{i_{k}}) = (-1)^{\sigma}(d x_{j_{1}}\wedge \ldots \wedge d x_{j_{n - k}})
\]
and extending it linearly, where \(i_{1}< \ldots < i_{k}\), \(j_{1}< \ldots < j_{n - k}\), \((i_{1},\ldots ,i_{k},j_{1},\ldots ,j_{n - k})\) is a permutation of \((1,2,\ldots ,n)\), and \(\sigma\) is 0 or 1 according as the permutation is even or odd, respectively. Show that:

If \(\omega = a_{12}d x_{1}\wedge d x_{2} + a_{13}d x_{1}\wedge d x_{3} + a_{23}d x_{2}\wedge d x_{3}\) is a 2-form in \(\mathbf{R}^{3}\), then

\[
\star \omega = a_{12}d x_{3} - a_{13}d x_{2} + a_{23}d x_{1}.
\]

\[

  d(xc-za)\wedge dy&=(c+xc_x-za_x)dx\wedge dy +(za_z+a-xc_z)dy\wedge dz \\
  d(ya-zb)\wedge dz&=(a+ya_y-xb_y)dy\wedge dz+(ya_x-b-xb_x)dx \wedge dz
  d(zb-yc)\wedge dx+d(xc-za)\wedge dy+d(ya-zb)\wedge dz&=(k+2)c \, dx\wedge dy+(k+2)b \,dx\wedge dz +(k+2)a \,dy\wedge dz
  \end{aligned}
  \]

title: tensor product of algebras
text:
We will introduce the tensor product of several modules.

Definition 1: tensor product of several modules
Let \(M_1,\dots,M_n\) be \(R\)-modules. Let \(T\) be a \(R\)-module and \(M_1\times\dots\times M_n\xrightarrow{\otimes } T\) be an \(n\)-linear map. We say that \((T,\otimes)\) has the universal property of tensor profuct if for any \(R\)-module \(K\) and \(n\)-linear map \(M_1\times\dots\times M_n\xrightarrow{\psi}K\), there exists a unique \(R\)-linear map \(\overline{\psi}\) such that the following diagram commutes:



Then \(T\) is said to be the tensor product denoted by \(M_1\otimes\dots\otimes M_n\) and \(\otimes(m_1,\dots,m_n)\) is denoted by \(m_1\otimes\dots\otimes m_n\).


Obviously the universal property is equivalent to

The elements \(m_1\otimes\dots\otimes m_n\) generate \(T\).
Every \(n\)-linear mapping \(M_1\times\dots\times M_n\xrightarrow{\psi}K\) (\(K\) is any \(R\)-module) can be written in the form of \[
\psi(m_1,\dots,m_n)=f(m_1\otimes\dots\otimes m_n)
\] where \(f:T\rightarrow K\) is a \(R\)-linear map.

Clearly the map \(f\) satisfying conditions 1 and 2 is unique.
Let’s prove the law of associativity which we don’t need to check in the case of two modules and we shall begin by product of \(3\) modules.

Lemma 1: associativity of tensor product
Given three arbitrary modules \(M_1,M_2,M_3\) there exists a \(R\)-linear isomorphism \[
f:M_1\otimes M_2\otimes M_3 \xrightarrow{\cong} (M_1\otimes M_2)\otimes M_3
\] such that \(f(x\otimes y\otimes z)=(x\otimes y)\otimes z\).

title: Technical Lemmas II
text: The lemmas here are mainly taken from I.Kaplansky-Commutative-Rings (1974.UCP).

title: Technical Lemmas II
text:
Charaterizations of Prime ideals
One should be familiar with the basic definitions of primes. Let \(\mathfrak{p}\) be an ideal and it’s said to be a prime if:

\(ab\in \mathfrak{p}\) implies that \(a\in \mathfrak{p}\) or \(b\in \mathfrak{p}\).
\(R/\mathfrak{p}\) is a domain.
\(_{R}\complement \mathfrak{p}\) is a multiplicatively closed set.


Clearly \(\mathfrak{m}\) is prime. The general observation below is due to Krull:

Lemma 1
Let \(S\) be a multiplicatively closed set in a ring \(R\) and \(I\) be an ideal in \(R\) maximal w.r.t the exclusion of \(S\). Then \(I\) is prime.


The proof by contradiction is standard.

Proof. Let \(I\) be such maximal ideal. Assume \(ab\in I\) but neither \(a\) nor \(b\) is in \(I\). Then the ideals \(I+(a)\) and \(I+(b)\) must intersect with \(S\). It follows that \((i_1+ar_1)(i_2+br_2)=i_1i_2+i_1br_2+i_2ar_1+abr_1r_2\in I\) with \((i_1+ar_1),(i_2+br_2)\in S\). This contradicts the fact that \(I\cap S=\emptyset\).


Corollary 2
Given any ideal \(J\) disjoint from a multiplicatively closed set \(S\), it’s contained in a maximal ideal w.r.t the exclusion of \(S\).



Proof. By Zorn’s lemma and lemma 1.

We impose a further property on the multiplicatively closed set \(S\): it’s said to be saturated multiplicatively closed if along with an element \(x\in S\) it contains all the divisors of \(x\). We are led to the following lemma, in essense a sharpening of lemma 1.

Remark. It would have been reasonable to exclude the possibility \(0\in S\).


Lemma 3
The following statements on a set \(S\) in a ring \(R\) are equivalent:
(a). \(S\) is a saturated multiplicatively closed set.
(b). the complement of \(S\) is a set-theoretic union of prime ideals in \(R\).



Proof. 

implies (1) is clear; To prove that (1) implies (2), take \(x\in _{R}\complement S\). Then the principle ideal \((x)\) is disjoint from \(S\) since \(S\) is saturated. Expand \((x)\) into a maximal ideal \(\mathfrak{p}_x\) w.r.t the exclusion of \(S\) by Corollary 2 and it follows that each element in \(_R\complement S\) is contained in some prime ideal by Lemma 1. Therefore \(_R\complement S=\bigcup_{x}\mathfrak{p}_x\).




Example 1
Let \(S\) be the set of all non-zero-divisors in \(R\). \(S\) is a saturated multiplicatively closed set. So the zero-divisors in \(R\) are a union of prime ideals. The prime ideals maximal among there might be called the maximal primes of zero-divisors.


Roughly speaking, lemma 1 allows us to construct a prime ideal from a multiplicatively closed set.

In the next two lemmas we exhibit two ways of constructing primes without using a multiplicatively closed set. Lemma 4 is due to Herstein; lemma 5 and its immediate corollary, lemma 7 are due to I.S.Cohen.

Lemma 4
Let \(R\) be a ring and \(A\) be an \(R\)-module. Let \(Z\) be an ideal in \(R\) that is maximal among all annihilators of non-zero elements of \(A\). Then \(Z\) is prime.



Proof. Suppose \(\operatorname{ann}(x)=Z\) is such a maximal ideal. Then we expect that \(ab\in Z\) implies \(a\in I\) or \(b\in I\). Assume that \(a\notin I\) then \(\operatorname{ann}(ax)\supset I\). Since \(I\) is maximal, \(\operatorname{ann}(ax)=I\). Thus \(b\in\operatorname{ann}(ax)=I\).


Lemma 5
Let \(Z\) be an ideal in \(R\). Suppose that \(Z\) is not finitely generated, and is maxiaml among all ideals in \(R\) that are not finitely generated. Then \(Z\) is prime.



Proof. Let \(Z\) be such a maximal ideal. We make a indirect proof by the use of quotient of ideals. Assume that \(ab\in Z\) with neither \(a\) nor \(b\) in \(Z\). Then the ideal \(Z+(a)\) is properly larger than \(Z\) and consequently is finitely generated. As generaters for it we may pick elements of the form \(i_1+x_1a,\dots,i_n+x_na\,(i_1,\dots,i_n\in Z)\). Now let \(J\) be the set of all \(y\) in \(R\) such that \(ya\in Z\);i.e. the quotient of \(Z\) and \((a)\): \(J=[Z:a]\). Then \(J\supset I\) and \(J\supset (b)\), hence is properly larger than \(J\), hence is finitely generated.

Claim 6
Let \(Z\trianglelefteq R\) be any ideal and \(a\in R\). If \(Z+(a)\) is finitely generated, say its generators \(i_1+x_1a,\dots,i_n++x_na\), then it follows that \[
Z=(i_1,\dots,i_n,Ja)
\] where \(J=[Z:a]\).


Clearly we have \((i_1,\dots,i_n,Ja)\subset Z\); it remains to show the reverse inclusion. Take an arbitrary element \(z\in Z\). Then all the more so \(z\) lies in \(Z+(a)\) where we can use the generators to express \(z\) as: \[
z=u_1(i_1+x_1a)+\dots+u_n(i_n+x_na),\qquad u_1,\dots,u_n\in R
\] Since \[
(u_1x_1+\dots+u_nx_n)a=z-(u_1i_1+\dots+u_ni_n)\in Z
\] by definition, we have \((u_1x_1+\dots+u_nx_n)\in J\). Hence \(z\in (i_1,\dots,i_n,Ja)\), as required.
By the claim we obtained that \(Z=(i_1,\dots,i_n,Ja)\), which implies that \(Z\) is finitely generated, a contradiction.

title: Technical Lemmas II
section: Ordering structure on the set of prime ideals
text:
Ordering structure on the set of prime ideals
Let \(\mathcal{S}\) be the set of all prime ideals of a commutative ring. It seems reasonable to think of the partial ordering on \(\mathcal{S}\) as its first, basic structure.

Question 1
Can an arbitrary partially ordered set be the partially ordered set of prime ideals in a ring?


There is a first negative answer by the following lemma:

Lemma 7
Let \(\mathfrak{p}_i\) be a chain of primes in a ring \(R\). Then both \(\cup \mathfrak{p}\) and \(\cap \mathfrak{p}\) are primes in \(R\).



Proof. It’s clear that they are ideals. Our task becomes easier when we pass to the complements \(S_i\), it being quite evident that \(\cap S_i\) and \(\cup S_i\) are multiplicatively closed. Then they are prime ideals.

The partially ordered set \(\mathclose{S}\) of prime ideals has an another (slightly unexpected) property: between any two elements we can find a pair of immediate neighbors.

Lemma 8
Let \(\mathfrak{p}\subsetneq \mathfrak{q}\) be distinct prime ideals in a ring \(R\). Then there exist distinct prime ideals \(\mathfrak{p}_1,\mathfrak{q}_1\) with \[
\mathfrak{p}\subseteq \mathfrak{p}_1\subsetneq \mathfrak{q}_1\subseteq \mathfrak{q} \qquad (\star)
\] such that there is no prime ideal properly between \(\mathfrak{p}_1\) and \(\mathfrak{q}_1\).



Proof. Using Zorn’s lemma, we can insert a chain \(\{\mathfrak{p}_i\}\) of prime ideals between \(\mathfrak{p},\mathfrak{q}\) such that for any \(i\), if \(\mathfrak{p}_i\subsetneq \mathfrak{b}\subseteq \mathfrak{p}_{i+1}\) (\(\mathfrak{b}\) is a prime ideal) then \(\mathfrak{b}=\mathfrak{p}_{i+1}\). Take any element \(x\) that is in \(Q\) but not in \(P\). Define \(Q_1\) to be the intersection of all \(\mathfrak{p}_i\)’s containing \(x\), \(P_1\) the union of all \(\mathfrak{p}_i\)’s not containing \(x\). By lemma , \(P_1\) and \(Q_1\) are prime. Then clearly \((\star)\) holds. None of the \(\mathfrak{p}_i\)’s can be properly between \(P_1\) and \(Q_1\), for if \(x\in \mathfrak{p}_i\) then \(\mathfrak{p}_i\supseteq Q_1\) and if \(x\notin \mathfrak{p}_i\) then \(\mathfrak{p}_i\subseteq P_1\). By the maximality of the chain \(\{\mathfrak{p}_i\}\), no prime ideal at all can lie properly between \(P_1\) and \(Q_1\).


Lemma 9
Let \(T\) be an algebra over the commutative ring \(R\). Suppose that \(u,v\in T\) are commutating integral elements. Then \(u+v\) and \(uv\) are integral.



Theorem 10
Let \(T\) be a commutative algebra over the commutative ring \(R\). Then the elements of \(T\) integral over \(R\) form a subring of \(T\).



Lemma 11
Let \(R\) be a commutative ring, \(u\) an invertible element of a ring containing \(R\). Then \(u^{-1}\) is integral over \(R\) if and only if \(u^{-1}\in R[u]\).



Lemma 12
Let \(R\) be an integral domain contained in a field \(L\). If \(L\) is integral over \(R\), then \(R\) is a field.



Proof. For \(u\neq 0\) in \(R\) we have that \(u^{-1}\in L\) is integral over \(R\). By the lemma above, \(u^{-1}\in R[u]=R\). Hence \(R\) is a field.


Lemma 13
If \(R\) is an integral domain algebraic over a field \(K\) then \(R\) is a field.



Lemma 14
Let \(T\) be a commutative algebra over the commutative ring \(R\). The following statements are equivalent:

\(T\) is a finitely generated \(R\)-module.
\(T\) is a finitely generated ring over \(R\) annd is integral over \(R\).

title: Dimension
text:
A topological space \(X\) is said to have dimension \(\leq n\) if, for any strictly decreasing chain \(Z_p\subsetneq Z_{p-1}\subsetneq \dots \subsetneq Z_0\) of non-empty irreducible closed subsets of \(X\), the length \(p\) of the chain \(\leq n\). The minimum \(n\) that satisfies this condition is called the dimension of \(X\). Clearly, for a noetherian topological space \(X\), \(\operatorname{dim}X=\text{maximum of dimensions of the components of } X\).
In algebraic geometry, this naive notion of dimension is quite good. An affine variety of dimension zero is a finite collection of points. An affine variety of dimension one is a finite union of irreducible curves plus a finite number of isolated points.

title: Dimension
section: How finite morphisms behave w.r.t. dimension
text:
How finite morphisms behave w.r.t. dimension
We will first study how finite morphisms behave with respect to dimension.

Lemma 1
Let \(f:X\rightarrow Y\) be a finite surjective morphism between varieties. Then \(\operatorname{dim}X = \operatorname{dim} Y\).



Proof. Let \(Z_p\supsetneq Z_{p-1}\supsetneq \dots \supsetneq Z_0\) be a chain of non-empty irreducible closed subsets of \(X\). Set \(W_i=f(Z_i)\). Then \(W_p\supsetneq W_{p-1}\supsetneq \dots \supsetneq W_0\) is a strictly decreasing chain of closed subsets of \(Y\) (by lemma 2 and lemma 3). Therefore \(\operatorname{dim}X\leq \operatorname{dim} Y\).
Conversely let \(W_p\supsetneq \dots \supsetneq W_0\) be a sequence in \(Y\). We need to see that we can find a sequence of \(Z_i\) in \(X\) such that \(f(Z_i)=W_i\). The variety \(f^{-1}(W_p)=K_1\cup\dots\cup K_i\) where the \(K_i\)’s are the irreducible components of \(f^{-1}W_p\). Thus as \(f\) is surjective \(W_p=f(K_1)\cup\dots\cup f(K_i)\) where the \(f(K_j)\) are closed and irreducible. As \(W_p\) is irreducible, \(W_p=f(K_j)\) for some \(j\). Set \(Z_p=K_j\). Consider the finite surjective morphism \(f\restriction_{Z_p}: Z_p\rightarrow W_p\). By induction on \(p\) we may find the required \(Z_{p-1}\supsetneq \dots \supsetneq Z_0\) in \(Z_p\). This constructs the required sequence \(Z_i\).

Next we will check that we have the right definition of dimension in the simplest case.

title: Irreducible Components
text:
A topological space \(X\) is said to be irreducible if whenever \(X=X_1 \cup X_2\) where \(X_1,X_2\) are closed subsets then \(X=X_1 \text{ or } X_2\). An irreducible topological space is necessarily connected but not conversely as the following example shows.

Example 1
The plane curve \(x(y-x^2)=0\) is connected but not irreducible.
This curve is the union of the line \(x=0\) and the parabola \(y=x^2\) but they meet at the origin.








Warning



Notice that in the definition of irreducible space we don’t require that the two closed subsets have an empty intersection. Therefore it’s stronger than connected spaces and one may called it Hyperconnected. However in some cases we may prove that they are equivalent.→


We have an algebraic criterion for an affine variety to be irredicuble and the proof is clear.

Lemma 1
An affine variety \(X\) is irreducible if and only if the ring \(\mathcal{O}(X)\) is an integral domain.


Before we discuss components we will do two lemmas.

Lemma 2
Let \(Z\) be an irreducible closed subset of a topological space \(X\). If \(Z\) is contained in the finite union \(W_1\cup\dots\cup W_p\) for some closed subsets of \(X\), then \(Z \subseteq W_i\) for some \(i\).



Proof. We have \(Z=(Z\cap W_1)\cup\dots\cup(Z\cap W_p)\) and \(Z\cap W_i\) is a closed subset of \(Z\); as \(Z\) is irreducible, \(Z=Z\cap W_i\) for some \(i\); thus, \(Z \subset W_i\).



We will next see that a noetherian space is not too far removed from being irreducible.

Lemma 3
Any noetherian space \(X\) is a finite union of irreducible closed subspaces.



Proof. If \(X\) is irreducible, there is nothing to prove; otherwise, \(X\) is the union \(Z\cup W\) of proper closed subsets;if \(Z\) and \(W\) are unions of irreducible closed subsets, then so is \(X\).
Therefore if \(X\) were not a finite union of irreducible closed subsets, then we could find a proper clsoed subset \(X_1\) (either \(Z\) or \(W\)) with the same property. Continuing in this way, one could produce an infinite strictly decreasing chain \(X_1\supseteq X_2 \supseteq \dots\) of closed subsets, which is contradiction as \(X\) is noetherian. Thus \(X\) must be a finite union of irreducibles.

title: Irreducible Components
text:
