title: Irreducible Components
text:
Component
To be more precise about the structure of a noetherian space, one introduces the idea of components. A component of \(X\) is just a maximal irreducible closed subspace of \(X\). In fact, we have:

Proposition 4
A noetherian space \(X\) has only finitely many components. The union of these components is all of \(X\); furthermore, if \(X=X_1\cup\dots\cup X_n\) is a finite union closed irreducible subspaces, then the components of \(X\) are exactly the \(X_i\)’s which are not contained in any other.



Proof. We need only show the last statement. Let \(Z\) be any irreducible clsoed subset of \(X\). By lemma, \(Z\subset X_i\) for some \(i\). Therefore any component (maxiaml irreducible closed subset) must be one of \(X_i\), which is not contained in another; conversely, the big \(X_i\)’s must be maximal irreducibles (for \(X_i \subset Z\) implies \(X_i \subset Z \subset X_j\) and the \(X_j\) must be \(X_i\)); i.e. they are components.

Next we will study the algebraic interpretation of the components.

Proposition 5
Let \(X\) be an affine variety.

A closed subset \(Z\) of \(X\) is a component of \(X\) if and only if the ideal \(\operatorname{ideal}(Z)=\{f \in \mathcal{O}(X):f\restriction_Z=0\}\) is a minimal prime ideal of \(\mathcal{O}(X)\).
There is a one-to-one correspondence between the components of \(X\) and the minimal prime ideals of \(\mathcal{O}(X)\).
If \(X_1,\dots,X_r\) are the components of \(X\), the zero ideal is the intersection \(\bigcap_{i=1}^r\operatorname{idea}(X_i)\) of finitely many minimal primes.




Proof. Clearly the algebra of functions on \(Z\), i.e. \(\mathcal{O}_X(Z)\), admits a form \(\mathcal{O}(X)/\operatorname{ideal}(Z)\); if \(Z\) is irreducible, \(\operatorname{ideal}(Z)\) is prime. Furthermore suppose that \(X\) is maximal, then whenever \(\mathfrak{p} \subset \operatorname{ideal}(Z)\) we have \(\operatorname{zeroes}(\mathfrak{p}) \supset \operatorname{zeroes}(\operatorname{ideal}(Z))\supset Z\) thus \(\mathfrak{p} = \operatorname{ideal}(Z)\); i.e. \(\operatorname{ideal}(Z)\) is minimal. Conversely, \(\mathfrak{p}\) is minimal prime ideal, \(\operatorname{zeroes}(\mathfrak{p})\) is then a maximal irreducible closed subset; i.e. component of \(X\). Therefore the one-to-one correspondence is established.
As for 3, we have \[
\operatorname{zeroes}(\bigcap \operatorname{ideal}(X_i))=\bigcup\operatorname{zeroes}(\operatorname{ideal}(X_i))=X
\] then \(\bigcap \operatorname{ideal}(X_i)=\{0\}\).

title: Irreducible Components
text:
Exercise

Exercise 1
Show that a topological space \(X\) is irreducible if and only if any non-empty open subset of \(X\) is dense.



Proof. Let \(U\subset X\) be a non-empty open subset. Since \[
\overline{U} \cup \overline{X-U}=X,\qquad \overline{X-U}=X-U
\] if \(X\) is irreducible then \(\overline{U}=X\); Conversely, suppose that \(X=U\cup V\) where \(U\) and \(V\) are clopens, then \(\overline{U}=U\) and \(\overline{V}=V\); if \(U\neq \emptyset\) then \(\overline{U}=X\) which implies \(X\) is irreducible.


Exercise 2
Show that a topological space \(X\) is irreducible if and only if any two non-empty open subsets intersect.



Proof. 

If \(U \cap V=\emptyset\), then \(\complement U \cup \complement V=X\); contradiction.
Suppose that \(X=F\cup E\) where \(F\) and \(E\) are closed. Then \(\complement F \cap \complement E=\emptyset\); contradiction.



Exercise 3
Let \(X\) be an irreducible topological space. Show that any open subset \(U\) of \(X\) must be irreducible.



Proof. Using the first exercise, we need only show that the closure of any open subset \(V\) of \(U\) is \(U\). Since \(V\) is also an open subset of \(X\), \(\overline{V}=X\) and thus \(\overline{V}\cap U=U\).


Exercise 4
Let \(X\) be a topological space. If two irreducible non-empty open sets intersect, their union is irreducible.



Proof. Denote the two open sets by \(U\) and \(V\). Suppose \(W_1\) and \(W_2\) are two open subsets of \(U\Cap V\).

\(W_1\cap U\neq \emptyset\) and \(W_2\cap U \neq \emptyset\). As \(U\) is irreducible, \[
(W_1\cap U)\bigcap(W_2 \cap U)=(W_1\cap W_2) \bigcap U \neq \emptyset
\] thus \(W_1\cap W_2 \neq \emptyset\).
\(W_1\cap U\neq \emptyset\) and \(W_2\cap V \neq \emptyset\). As \(U \cap V \subset U\) is non-empty and \(U\) is irreducible, we have \((W_1\cap U)\cup(U\cap V)\neq \emptyset\); i.e. \(W_1\cap U\cap V \neq \emptyset\); As \(W_2\cap V \neq \emptyset\) and \(V\) is irreducible we have \((W_1\cap U\cap V)\cap(W_2\cap V)\neq \emptyset\); i.e. \((W_1\cap W_2)\bigcap (U\cap V)\neq \emptyset\) which implies that \(W_1\cap W_2\neq \emptyset\).



Exercise 5: 
Let \(X\) be a topological space which has an open covering \(\mathcal{U}\) by irreducible subspaces. Prove that \(X\) is connected if and only if it is irreducible.



Proof. Suppose that \(X\) is irreducible then closure of any non-empty and proper open subset is \(X\), thus there is no clopen subset in \(X\), which means \(X\) is connected.
To show the opposite direction, we need the following lemma:

Lemma 6
A topological space \(X\) is connected if and only if every open covering \(\mathcal{U}=\{U_{\alpha}\}\) has the following property:
For each pair of sets \(U\) and \(V\) in \(\mathcal{U}\) there is a sequence of open sets \(U_0,U_1,\dots,U_n\) in \(\mathcal{U}\) such that \(U=U_0\) and \(V=U_n\), and \(U_i \cap U_{i+1}\neq \emptyset\) for all \(i\).


we wish to show that any two non-empty open subsets \(W_1\) and \(W_2\) in \(X\) intersect. As \(\mathcal{U}\) is a covering, there exist \(U_{\alpha},U_{\beta}\in \mathcal{U}\) such that \(W_1\cap U_{\alpha}\neq \emptyset\) and \(W_2\cap U_{\beta}\neq \emptyset\). By the lemma, we know there exist a sequence \(U_{\alpha}=U_0,U_1,\dots,U_n=U_{\beta}\) in \(\mathcal{U}\) such that \(U_i\cap U_{i+1}\neq \emptyset\). By the exercise, we have \(\cup_{i=1}^n U_i\) is irreducible. Since \(W_1\cap U_0\) and \(W_2\cap U_n\) are non-empty open sets, it follows that \((W_1\cap U_0)\cap(W_2\cap U_n)\neq \emptyset\); i.e. \(W_1\cap W_2\neq\emptyset\).


Exercise 6

Let \(X\) be a topological space and \(Y \subseteq X\). Show that \(Y\) is irreducible if and only if \(\overline{Y}\) is irreducible.
A maximal irreducible subspace of \(X\) must be closed and thus it is a component.




Proof. We shall use the following lemma and the proof is clear:

Lemma 7
Let \(X\) be a topological space and \(Y\subset X\) be a subsapce. If an open subset \(U\) intersect \(\overline{Y}\), \(U\cap Y\neq \emptyset\).


Suppose that \(Y\) is irreducible; let \(U_1\) and \(U_2\) be any two non-empty open subsets in \(\overline{Y}\), by definition, we have \[
U_1=V_1\cap \overline{Y},\quad U_2=V_2\cap\overline{Y},\quad V_i\cap \overline{Y}\neq \emptyset \qquad \text{where } V_1,V_2 \text{ are open subsets } \subseteq X
\] By lemma it follows that \(V_i \cap Y \neq \emptyset\) and thus \[
U_1\cap U_2=(V_1\cap  \overline{Y})\cap(V_2\cap \overline{Y}) \supset (V_1 \cap Y)\cap(V_2\cap Y)\neq \emptyset
\]
Conversely; let \(U_1\) and \(U_2\) be any two non-empty open subsets in \({Y}\), then \[
W_1\cap Y=U_1,\quad W_2\cap Y=U_2
\] As \(\emptyset \neq W_i\cap Y\subset W_i\cap \overline{Y}\), \[
\emptyset\neq (W_1\cap \overline{Y})\cap (W_2\cap\overline{Y})=(W_1\cap W_2)\cap \overline{Y}
\] by lemma, we know \(W_1\cap W_2\cap Y \neq \emptyset\); i.e. \(U_1\cap U_2\neq \emptyset\).
The last statement follows immediately from the first result.


Exercise 7
Let \(X=\cup U_i\) be an open covering of a noetherian toppological space \(X\). Show that the components of \(X\) are precisely the closure of the components of the \(U_i\)’s.



Proof. As \(X\) is noetherian, it admits a representation: \(X=\cup_{j=1}^p W_j\) where \(W_j\) is irreducible closed subsapce of \(X\). For each open subset \(U_i\) we have \(U_i=\bigcup_{j=1}^p(W_j\cap U_i)\); since \(W_j\cap U_i\subset W_j\) is open in \(W_j\), we know that it’s irreducible; and \(W_j\cap U_i\) is closed in \(U_i\) then \(W_j\cap U_i\) are the components of \(U_i\). As \(X\) is quasi-compact, we can assume that \(i\) is finite. It follows that \(X=\bigcup_{i=1}^{q}\bigcup_{j=1}^p\overline{(W_j\cap U_i)}\).

title: The lemma
text:
Let \(f\) be a non-constant polynomial in \(k[X_1,\dots,X_n]\) where \(k\) is an algebraically closed field as usual.






NoteLemma



After making a linear change of variables of the form \[
X_1 \to X_1+\lambda_1X_n,\dots,X_{n-1}\to X_{n-1}+\lambda_{n-1}X_{n} \text{ and } X_n \to \lambda_n X_n, \lambda_n \neq 0
\]
we may assume that \(f\) is monic in \(X_n\); i.e. f admits the form \[
X_n^d+\sum_{0 \leq i <d}f_iX_n^{i}
\] where \(d>0\) and the \(f_i\)’s are polynomials in the \(n-1\) variables \(X_1,\dots,X_{n-1}\).



Proof. Suppose that the highest degree of the homogeneous component of \(f\) is \(d > 0\) and the corresponding piece is \(f_d\); Then \(f=f_d+g\) where the total degree of polynomial \(g\) is less than \(d\). Consider the new polynomial \(f^\prime =f(X_1+\lambda_1X_n,\dots,\lambda_nX_n)\), we have \[
f^\prime=f_d(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n)X_n^d+g^\prime，\operatorname{deg}(X_n)<d \text{ in any monomial of } g^\prime
\] If \(f_d\) is a non-zero function on \(\mathbb{A}^n\), suitable \(\lambda\)’s make the homogeneous polynomial \(f_d\) take the value \(1\).
Thus we wish to show that a non-zero polynomial \(g\) in variables \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) defines a non-zero function on \(\mathbb{A}^n\).
The proof is by induction:

if \(n=1\), \(g\) has finitely many zeores on \(k\) which is infinite; thus the result is clear.
if \(n>1\), write \(g=\sum_{0\leq i \leq d}g_iX_n^{i}\) where \(g_i\) are polynomials in variables \(X_1,\dots,X_{n-1}\) and \(g_d\neq0\). By induction, we may find \(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_{n-1}\) such that \(g_d(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_{n-1})\neq 0\); thus the polynomial of variable \(X_n\), \(g(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_{n-1},X_n)\), is not zero; by the case \(n=1\), we may find \(\lambda_n\) such that \(g(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_{n-1},\lambda_n)\neq 0\).

This completes the proof.







ImportantLemma



If \(A\) is a non-zero finitely generated \(k\)-algebra then we have an injection \(B \subseteq A\) such that \(B\) is a polynomial ring and \(A\) is a \(B\)-module of finite type.



Proof. Let \(k[X_1,\dots,X_n]\to A\) be a surjectice homomorphism with kernel \(I\). If \(I=0\), take \(B=A\). Otherwise let \(i\) be a nonzero element of \(I\). By assumption \(i \neq 0\), otherwise \(A=0\); By the first lemma, we may assume that \(i\) is monic of degree \(>0\) in \(X-n\) after changing the coordinates. Let \(A^\prime=\operatorname{im}(k[X_1,\dots,X_{n-1}])\) in \(A\).
Claim: \(A\) is a \(A^\prime\)-module of finite type.
\[
k[X_1,\dots,X_n]/(i) \rightarrow A
\] is a surjective homomorphism. \(k[X_1,\dots,X_n]/(i)\) is a free \(k[X_1,\dots,X_{n-1}]\)-module of finite type; where the basis is \(1,X_n,\dots,X_n^{d-1} (\operatorname{mod}i)\); this proves the claim as expected.
As \(A^\prime\) has fewer generators than \(A\), by induction on \(n\), we may find a polynomial ring \(B \subseteq A^\prime\) such that \(A^\prime\) is a \(B\)-module of finite type. Hence by the claim \(A\) is a \(B\)-module of finite type.

We will need to know a special case of this argument.






NoteLemma



Let \(i\) be a non-constant regular function on \(\mathbb{A}^n\). We may find a morphism \(\pi:\{i=0\} \to \mathbb{A}^{n-1}\) which is surjective such that, via \(\pi^*\), \(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{A}^n}(\{i=0\})\) is a \(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{A}^n}(\mathbb{A}^{n-1})\)-module of finite type.



Proof. Let \(V(i)=\{p \in \mathbb{A}^{n}:i(p)=0\}\), then by nullstellensatz, \[
\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{A}^n}(V(i))=k[X_1,\dots,X_n]/\sqrt{(i)} \simeq \frac{k[X_1,\dots,X_n]/(i)}{\sqrt{(i)}/i}\equiv B/\sqrt{0}
\]
By the second lemma, \(B/\sqrt{0}\) is a \(k[X_1,\dots,X_{n-1}]\equiv A\)-module of finite type and indeed we have \(k\hookrightarrow A\hookrightarrow B\); By theorem，there is a surjective map induced by composition: \[
\operatorname{Hom}_{k}(B/\sqrt{0},k) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}_{k}(B,k)\twoheadrightarrow \operatorname{Hom}_{k}(A,k)
\] where the first equality follows from \(\sqrt{0} \subseteq \operatorname{ker}(f)\) for any \(f \in  \operatorname{Hom}_{k}(B,k)\) (nilpotents must be killed since \(k\) has no nilpotents);
Since \(V(i)=\operatorname{Spec }(B/\sqrt{0})\), we have found the surjective map.

title: Examples
text:
We shall introduce two important and basic examples of varieties: \(\mathbb{A}^{n}\) and \(\mathbb{P}^{n}\).






NoteDefinition



\(\mathbb{A}^n\) is defined as \(\Spec (k[X_1, \dots, X_n])\) where \(k\) is an algebraically closed field.


Set-theoretically, \(\mathbb{A}^n=\{(x_1, \dots, x_n): x_i \in k, 1 \leq i \leq n\}\) since every \(k\)-algebra homomorphism is determined by the images \(x_{i}\) of \(X_{i}\) which can be arbitrary in \(k\). As a variety \(\mathbb{A}^n\) is called an affine \(n\)-space.
Furthermore if X is a space with functions and \(f:X \to \mathbb{A}^n\) is a mapping given by \(f(x)=(f_1(x),\dots,f_{n}(x))\) then \(f\) is a morphism if and only if each \(f_i\) is regular function on X.






Tip 1: Proof




We will use the already proven lemma:

If \(X\) is a space with functions then \(X \xrightarrow{f}\mathbb{A}^{1}\) is a morphism if and only if it’s a regular function on \(X\).

\(\mathbb{A}^{n} \xrightarrow{p_{i}}\mathbb{A}^{1}\) is a morphism as \(p_i=X_i \in k[X_1,\dots,X_n]\). If \(f\) is a morphism from \(X\) to \(\mathbb{A}^n\), then \(f_i=p_{i} \circ f\) is a morphism.
Conversely suppose that \(f_{i}\) is morphism for each \(i\). First we show that \(f\) is continuous. Let \(V(P)\) be a closed set of \(\mathbb{A}^n\). We have \[
f^{-1}(V(P))=\{x \in X: p(f_1(x),\dots, f_n(x))=0, \forall p \in P\}
\] Since \(f_i\) is regular on \(X\) and \(p(f_1(x),\dots, f_n(x))\) is a function obtained by algebraic operations without division in \(\mathcal{O}(X)\), \(p \circ f\) is a regular funciton on \(X\). Hence \(X-D(p \circ f)\) is a closed subset and so is \(f^{-1}(V(p))= \bigcap_{p\in P} {(X-D(p \circ f))}\). As expected \(f\) is continuous.
Next We show that \(f^*(g)=g\circ f\) is a regular function on \(f^{-1}(U)\) where \(g \in \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{A}^n}(U)\). Wlog we assume that \(U=D(h)\), then \(g\) admits a form \(\frac{a(x_1,\dots,x_n)}{h(x_1,\dots,x_n)}\) on \(U\). Then \(g \circ f\) admits a form \(\frac{a(f_1(x),\dots,f_n(x))}{h(f_1(x),\dots,f_n(x))}\) on \(f^{-1}(U)\). Since \(f_{i}:X \rightarrow \mathbb{A}^1\) is a morphism, it is indeed a regular function on \(X\). Therefore functions which admit the form \(a(f_1(x),\dots,f_n(x))\) are regular on \(X\). Moreover since \(D(h(f_1(x),\dots,f_n(x)))=f^{-1}(U)\), \(1/h(f_1(x),\dots,f_n(x))\) is regular on \(f^{-1}(U)\). Hence \(\frac{a(f_1(x),\dots,f_n(x))}{h(f_1(x),\dots,f_n(x))}\) is regular on \(f^{-1}(U)\) as expected.



Another fact is that any affine variety \(X\) is isomorphic (non-canonically) to a closed subvariety of \(\mathbb{A}^{n}\) corresponding to a surjection \(k[X_1,\dots,X_n]\rightarrow A\) where \(A=\mathcal{O}(X)\). A subvariety of \(\mathbb{A}^n\) (or any other affine variety) is called quasi-affine.
For instance the punctured affine space \(\mathbb{A}^{n}-\{0\}\).






Note 1: Lemma




\(\mathcal{O}(\mathbb{A}^1-\{0\})=k[X_1,X_1^{-1}]\)
If \(n>1\), \(\mathcal{O}(\mathbb{A}^n-\{0\})=k[X_1,\dots,X_n]\)









TipProof



If \(n=1\), \(\mathbb{A}^{1}-\{0\}\) is the open subvariety \(D(X)\) of \(\mathbb{A}^1\). So \(\mathbb{A}_1-\{0\} \cong \Spec (k[X]_{(X)})\) as spaces with functions. Hence \(\mathcal{O}(\mathbb{A}^1-\{0\})=\mathcal{O}(\Spec (k[X]_{(X)}))=k[X]_{(X)}=k[X,X^{-1}]\)
If \(n>1\), \(\mathbb{A}^n-\{0\}=\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}{D(X_i)}\) and \[
\mathcal{O}(D(X_i))=k[X_1,\dots,X_n,X_i^{-1}]
\] Thus we have
\(\mathcal{O}(\mathbb{A}^n-\{0\})=\bigcap_{i}{k[X_1,\dots,X_n,X_i^{-1}]}=k[X_1,\dots,X_n]\) .








CautionExericse



Prove that the quasi-affine variety \(\mathbb{A}^2-\{0\}\) is not affine.








TipProof




There is a natural isomorphism \(\operatorname{id}(X_i)=X_i\) in \(\operatorname{Hom}_{k}(\mathcal{O}(\mathbb{A}^2),\mathcal{O}(\mathbb{A}^2-\{0\}))\). \[
\mathcal{O}(\mathbb{A}^2) \xrightarrow{\operatorname{id}} \mathcal{O}(\mathbb{A}^2-\{0\})
\] Since \(\mathbb{A}^2\) is affine, there is a unique morphism \(f\) in \(\operatorname{Mor}(\mathbb{A}^2-\{0\},\mathbb{A}^2)\) such that \(f^*=\operatorname{id}\) i.e. \[
\mathbb{A}^2-\{0\} \xrightarrow{f} \mathbb{A}^2 \xrightarrow{X_i} k
\] in which \(f^*(X_i)=\operatorname{id}(X_i)=X_i=X_i \circ f\) and we thus have \(X_i(P)=(X_i \circ f)(P)\) which means that \(f\) must be the natural inclusion map.
But we know if \(\mathbb{A}^2-\{0\}\) is affine then there is a morphism \(g\) in \(\operatorname{Mor}(\mathbb{A}^2,\mathbb{A}^2-\{0\})\) such that \(g^*=\operatorname{id}\) as above.
Consider \(g \circ f\in \operatorname{Mor}(\mathbb{A}^2-\{0\},\mathbb{A}^2-\{0\})\). It follows that \((g \circ f)^*=\operatorname{id}=(\operatorname{id}_{\mathbb{A}^2-\{0\}})^*\). If \(\mathbb{A}^2-\{0\}\) is affine, we have \(g \circ f \equiv \operatorname{id}_{\mathbb{A}^2-\{0\}}\).
Similarily we have \(f \circ g \equiv \operatorname{id}_{\mathbb{A}^2}\). Therefore \(f\) is an isomorphism and thus must be surjective. This is a contradiction!



Set-theoretically \(\mathbb{P}^n\) is the quotient set \[
(\mathbb{A}^{n+1}-\{0\})/k^{\times}=\{(x_0,x_1,\dots,x_n)\neq 0: x_i \in k\} / \sim \text{ where } (x_0,\dots,x_n) \sim \lambda(x_0,\dots,x_n) \text{ for any } \lambda \in k-\{0\}
\] We want to define it as a quotient space with functions. Let \(\pi:\mathbb{A}^{n+1}-\{0\} \to \mathbb{P}^{n}\) send a vector to all vectors with the same direction. A subset \(U\) of \(\mathbb{P}^n\) is open if and only if \(\pi^{-1}(U)\) is open. A function \(f\) on \(U\) is regular if and only if \(\pi^*(f)\) is regular on \(\pi^{-1}(U)\). We claim that with this definition of a space with functions \(\mathbb{P}^n\) is a variety. Let \(0\leq i \leq n\). Let \(E_i=\{(x_0,\dots,x_n)\in \mathbb{P}^n:x_i \neq 0\}\).






ImportantClaim



The \(E_i\) form an open covering of \(\mathbb{P}^n\) by open affine subvarieties. In fact, \(E_i=\Spec (k[X_0/X_i,\dots,X_i/X_i,\dots,X_n/X_i])\).


Proof:
It suffices to show the second fact. Let \(D_i=D(X_i)\) in \(\mathbb{A}^{n+1}\). Then \(\pi^{-1}E_i=D_i\). So \(E_i\) is open. And we have the following: \[
\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^n}(E_i)=\{f:\pi^*f \in \mathcal{O}(\pi^{-1}(E_i))\}=\{f:f \circ \pi \in k[X_0,\dots,X_n,1/X_i]\} \simeq \{f\in k[X_0,\dots,X_n,1/X_i] \text{ such that }f(\lambda x)=f(x) \text{ for all } \lambda \neq 0\}
\]






TipScrutiny





As \((f \circ \pi )(\lambda x)=(f \circ \pi )(x)\) we have $f f $, denoted by \(\varphi\). Define \(\varphi^{-1}\): \(f \mapsto f^\prime\) where \(f^{\prime}\) is defined as below: \[
\begin{aligned}
f^\prime: E_i & \rightarrow k \\
[v_1] & \mapsto f(v_1)
\end{aligned}
\] We shall check that \(f^\prime\) is well-defined: Suppose that \([v_1]=[v_2]\) then \(v_1=\lambda v_2\) for some \(\lambda\neq 0\), thus \(f^{\prime}(v_1)=f(v_1)=f(\lambda v_2)=f(v_2)=f^{\prime}(v_2)\).
\[
\begin{aligned}
&(\varphi \circ \varphi^{-1})(f)=\varphi(f^{\prime})=f^{\prime} \circ \pi \equiv f \\
&(\varphi^{-1} \circ \varphi)(f)=\varphi^{-1}(f \circ \pi)=([v] \mapsto (f \circ \pi)(v)) \equiv f \\
& \varphi(f_1+(\times)f_2)=(f_1+(\times)f_2) \circ \pi=f_1 \circ \pi +(\times)f_2\circ \pi=\varphi(f_1)+(\times)\varphi(f_2) \\
&\varphi^{-1}(f_1+(\times)f_2)=([v]\mapsto (f_1+(\times)f_2)(v))=([v]\mapsto f_1(v))+(\times)([v]\mapsto f_2(v))=\varphi^{-1}(f_1)+(\times)\varphi^{-1}(f_2)
\end{aligned}
\]



If \(f \in k[X_0,\dots,X_n,1/X_i]\), \(f\) admits the form (c.f.): \[
f=f_{d_1}+\dots+f_{d_m}, f_{d_i} \text{ is the homogeneous component}
\] As \(f(\lambda x)=f(x), \forall \lambda\neq0\), we have
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\lambda^{d_1}f_{d_1}+\dots+\lambda^{d_m}f_{d_m}=f_{d_1}+\dots+f_{d_m} \\
& \Rightarrow\sum_{i=1}^{m}(\lambda^{d_i}-1)f_{d_i}=0
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(k\) is infinite, \(f_{d_i}\) must be zero if \(d_i \neq 0\); thus \(f\) is a homogeneous element of degree \(0\) and belongs to \(k[X_0/X_i, \dots,X_i/X_i,\dots,X_n/X_i]\). Denote it by \(B\); Thus we have \(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^n}(E_i)\cong B\) as f.g.\(k\)-algebras with no nilpotents. Thus we have \(E_i \cong \Spec (k[X_0/X_i, \dots,X_i/X_i,\dots,X_n/X_i])\) as affine varieties.
\(\mathbb{P}^n\) is called projective n-space.
A closed subvariety of a projective space is called projective. An arbitrary subvariety of a projective space is called quasi-projective. We may compute the global regular fucntions on \(\mathbb{P}^n\): they are just constants.






NoteLemma



\(\mathbb{P}^n=k\).



Proof. If \(n=0\), \(\mathbb{P}^0\) is just a point and the result is clear; Assume that \(n \geq 1\), then \(\pi^{*}\) is injective, for \[
\mathbb{A}^{n+1}-\{0\} \xrightarrow{\pi} \mathbb{P}^{n} \xrightarrow{f}k
\] if \(f \circ\pi =0\) then \(f \equiv 0\) since \(\pi\) is surjective.
Since \(\pi^*:\mathcal{O}(\mathbb{P}^{n}) \rightarrow \mathcal{O}(\mathbb{A}^{n+1}-\{0\})\) and by lemma, \[
\mathcal{O}(\mathbb{A}^{n+1}-\{0\})=k[X1,\dots,X_{n+1}]
\] \(\mathcal{O}(\mathbb{P}^{n})\) is identified with the homogeneous polynomials of degree zero; i.e. constants.







NoteExercise



Let \(f: \mathbb{P}^n \to X\) be a morphism where \(X\) is a quasi-affine variety. Prove that the image of \(f\) is a single point.



Proof. By the exercise, \(f\) is a morphism if and only if \(\mathbb{P}^n \xrightarrow{\iota \circ f} \mathbb{A}^{n}\) is; Then the component functions (by the lemma) are regular functions which are constant and thus the image is just a single point.







NoteExercise



Let \(X\) be a subset of \(\mathbb{P}^n\). Then \(X\) is closed if and only if it has the form \[
\{(X_0,\dots,X_n) \in \mathbb{P}^{n}:f_i(X_0,\dots,X_n)=0 \text{ for some set of homogeneous polynomials } f_i\}
\]



Proof. 

Assume that \(X\) has the desired form, and \(\operatorname{deg}f_i=d_i \in \mathbb{N}\); On \(E_k \cap X\), \(f_i/X_k^{d_i}\) is regular. Then by condition (b) the subset of zeroes of these \(f_i\) is closed in each \(E_k\) and thus \(X\) is closed.
Assume that \(X\) is a closed subset of \(\mathbb{P}^n\); \(X \cap E_k\) is closed in \(E_k \cong \mathbb{A}^n\) which implies that \(X \cap E_k\) has the form: \[
\{(x_0, \dots,x_n):x_k \neq 0;f_{k,r}(\frac{x_0}{x_k},\dots,\frac{\hat{x_k}}{x_k},\dots,\frac{x_n}{x_k})=0\}
\] Denote \(X_k^{d_{k,r}}f_{k,r}\) by \(F_{k,r}\) where \(d_{k,r}\) is the highest total degree of \(f_{k,r}\). Since \(X_k\) vanishes nowhere in \(E_k\), \(\operatorname{zeroes}(f_{k,r}) = \operatorname{zeroes}(F_{k,r})\) in \(E_k\). Clearly then we have \(X \subseteq \operatorname{zeroes}(F_{k,r})_{1 \leq k \leq n}\) (because \(X_{t}^{d_{t,r}}f_{t,r}(p)=0\) if \(p \in E_t \cap X\) and also zero when \(p \notin E_t\) for \(X_t(p)=0\)); Suppose that there exists a point \(p \in \mathbb{P}^n\) such that \(F_{k,r}(p)=0\), \(p\) must belongs to some \(E_{t}\); \(p\) is then a zero of \(f_{t,r}\); thus \(p \in X\).

title: The Nullstellensatz
text:
The objective of this note is to prove the Hilbert’s Nullstellensatz which says that \(\operatorname{Spec} A\) has enough points so that the following morphism is injective.
\[
\phi:A \rightarrow \mathcal{O}(\Spec A)
\]






Warning



In this theorem, we need to impose that 1. base field \(k\) is algebracially closed 2. \(A\) is a finitely generated \(k\)-algebra without nilpotents
For several statements in this note, the imposed condition turns out to be superfluous. Nevertheless, we should still clarify the prerequisites of Nullstellensatz and resist the temptation to generalize it in certain directions, so as to concentrate our attention on the main theorem.


To the end, we need few technical lemmas from commutative algebra as follows.






ImportantTheorem



Noether’s Normalization Lemma
Let \(k\) be a field and \(A\) be a non-zero finitely-generated \(k\)-algebra. Then there exists an injection \(B\xrightarrow{\subset}A\) where \(B\) is a polynomial ring \(k[X_1,\dots,X_d]\) i.e there exist \(d\geq0\) algebraically independent elements \(x_1,\dots,x_d \in A\), such that \(A\) is a finitely generated \(B\)-module.



Preparation:
Suppose that \(B \subseteq A\) are rings and \(A\) is finitely generated as \(B\)-algebra. Then we have: \[
A \ \text{is integral over} \ B  \iff A \ \text{is finitely generated as} \ B \text{-module}
\]







NoteProof



this proof is from Andrea Ferretti’s Commutative Algebra
Let \(y_1,\dots,y_m\) be a minimal set of generators of \(A\). We argue by induction over \(m\), the base case \(m=0,1\) is trivial.
If \(y_1,\dots,y_m\) are already algebracially independent then there is nothing to prove (just take \(B=A\) which is obviously finite), so assume that there is some polynomial \(f\) over \(k\) such that \(f(y_1,\dots,y_m)=0\). (wlog. we can also assume that \(y_{i}\) is not nilpotent) We can try to alter the set of generators and use the relation given by \(f\) to write one of the generators in terms of the other ones.
We perform the change of variable \[
z_i=y_i-y_1^{r^{i-1}}
\] for \(i\geq 2\), where \(r\) to be chosen later. This is clearly an invertible change of variable which has the effect of increasing the degree of \(y_1\) inside \(f\). More precisely, in the equation \[
f(y_1,z_2+y_1^{r},\dots,z_m+y_1^{r^{m-1}})=0
\] we can look at the exponent of \(y_1\) in the various monomials. For a monomial of multidegree \((\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_m)\) (in the \(y_{i}\)), the highest exponent of \(y_1\) in \(c_{(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_m)}y_{1}^{\alpha_1} \dots (z_{m}+y_1^{r^{m-1}})^{\alpha_{m}}\) after the change of variables is \[
\alpha_1+\alpha_2r+\dots+\alpha_mr^{m-1}
\] And the corresponding term is \[
c_{(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_m)}y_{1}^{\alpha_1+\alpha_2r+ \dots +\alpha_{m}r^{m-1}}
\] Suppose that \[
M=\max{\{c_{(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_m)}y_1^{\alpha_1}\dots y_m^{\alpha_m} \ \text{is a monomial in} \ f :(\alpha_1+\alpha_2r+ \dots +\alpha_{m}r^{m-1})\}}
\] Then we collect all the terms like \(cy_1^{M}\) : \[
M=\alpha_1^{1}+\alpha_2^{1}r+ \dots +\alpha_{m}^{1}r^{m-1}=\dots=\alpha_1^{t}+\alpha_2^{t}r+ \dots +\alpha_{m}^{t}r^{m-1}
\]
Then we get the term: \[
(\sum_{i=1}^{t} c_{(\alpha_1^{i},\dots,\alpha_m^{i})}) y_{1}^{M}
\]
In fact, there is some trouble: \[
\sum_{i=1}^{t} c_{(\alpha_1^{i},\dots,\alpha_m^{i})}
\] might vanish. But we can fix the trouble easily:
For \(r\) big enough (such that \(t=1\)), we see that this single monomial which will be of maximum degree for \(y_1\) such that the \(z_i\) do not appear in this monomial. This means that the transformed equation shows that \(y_1\) is integral over \(B:=k[z_1,\dots,z_m]\).
By induction, \(B\) already has the desired form of an integral extension of a polynomial ring and the thesis follows.


When \(k\) is infinite one can use a linear change of variables in the above proof. The only thing that is needed is that in the resulting polynomial relation, \(y_1\) appears with maximum degree in a monomial that contains no other indeterminates.
Consider a change of variables of the form: \[
z_i=y_i-\lambda_iy_1
\] This change of variables preserves the total degree of monomials, so consider the homogeneous part of maximum degree of \(f\), call it \(F\). We want to ensure that in \(F\) there appears a monomial containing only \(y_{1}\). Let \(t\) be the degree of \(F\).
The coefficient of \(y_{1}^{t}\) in \[
F(y_{1},z_{2}+\lambda_{2}y_{1},\dots,z_{m}+\lambda_{m}y_{1})
\] is a nonzero polynomial in \(\lambda_2,\dots,\lambda_m\). Since \(k\) is infinite, there exists a choice of \(\lambda_2,\dots,\lambda_m\) such that the coefficient don’t vanish, which is enough to show that \(y_{1}\) is integral over \(k[z_2,\dots,z_m]\).






ImportantTheorem



Assume that \(k\) is an algebracially closed field. Let \(k \subseteq B \subseteq A\) be \(k\)-algebras such that \(A\) is a finitely generated \(B\)-module. Then composition gives a surjection \[
Hom_{k}(A,k) \rightarrow Hom_{k}(B,k)
\]



Preparation:

\(A\hookrightarrow B\), \(I\unlhd A\), denote \(I \cdot B\) by \(I^{e}\); \(J\unlhd B\),denote \(J \cap A \unlhd A\) by \(J^{c}\), then we have \[
I^{ec}\supseteq I,J^{ce}\subseteq J
\]

Hence we have \(A/I\hookrightarrow B/I^e\).

Let \(I\unlhd \mathfrak{M} \unlhd R\) where \(\mathfrak{M}\) is a maximal ideal. Then we have \(R/I \hookrightarrow R/\mathfrak{M}\).
Let \(A \in R^{n \times n}\) over a commutative ring \(R\). The adjugate \(\operatorname{adj}(A)\) is defined by:

\[
[\operatorname{adj}(A)]_{ij} = (-1)^{i+j} \det(A_{ji})
\]
Then:
\[
A \cdot \operatorname{adj}(A) = \operatorname{adj}(A) \cdot A = \det(A) \cdot I_n
\]
If \(\det(A)\) is a unit in \(R\), then:
\[
A^{-1} = \frac{\operatorname{adj}(A)}{\det(A)}
\]







NoteProof



Let \(\psi :B \rightarrow k\) be a \(k\)-algebra homomorphism. Let \(m\) be the kernel of \(\psi\). Consider the ideal \(mA\) in \(A\). If \(mA \neq A\), we can find a maximal ideal \(n\) of \(A\) such that \(mA \subseteq n\). Then \(A/n\) is a finite field extension of \(B/m=k\), for (by preparation) \[
k \cong B/m\hookrightarrow A/m^{e}\hookrightarrow A/n
\]
Thus \(A/n=k\) as \(k\) is algebraically closed and the quotient mapping \(A \rightarrow k\) is an extension of \(\psi\) i.e. the diagram commutes





It remains to show that \(mA=A\) is impossible. Let \(A=B^{r}/R\) as a \(B\)-module where \(R\) is a \(B\)-submodule of \(B^{r}\) where \(r\) is finite. Let \(e_1,\dots,e_r\) be the unit vectors in \(B^r\) and we have \(\bar{e_1},\dots,\bar{e_r}\) generates \(A=mA\). Then for \(1 \leq i \leq r\), it follows that \(\bar{e_i}=\sum_{j=1}^{t}m_{j}^{i}(\sum_{l=1}^{r}b_{l}^{i}\bar{e_l})=\), thus we can write \(e_i=\sum_{k=1}^{r}m_{k}^{i}e_{k}+r_{i},m_{k}^{i}\in m,r_{i}\in R\). We have \[
\begin{bmatrix}
b_1^1 & \dots & b_r^1 \\
\vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
b_r^1 & \dots & b_r^r
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
e_1 \\
\vdots \\
e_r
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
r_1 \\
\vdots \\
r_r
\end{bmatrix}
\] where \[
b_{u}^{v}=
\begin{cases}
1-m_u^v, & \text{if } u=v \\
-m_u^v, & \text{if } u \neq
\end{cases}
\]
And hence, by easy calculus, \[
det(b_u^v)\equiv 1_B (\operatorname{mod}m)
\]
By the following lemma (called Cramer’s rule on the textbook): \[
\operatorname{adj}(M)\cdot M =M\cdot\operatorname{adj}(M)  =\operatorname{det}(M)\cdot I_n
\]
It follows that \(det(b_u^v)e_i\) is a linear combination of \(r_j\), and thus \(det(b_u^v)A=0\). In particular, \(det(b_u^v)\cdot1_A=0\) in \(A\) which implies that \(det(b_u^v)=0\) in \(A\) and also in \(B\). This is a contradiction to the fact that \(det(b_u^v)\equiv 1_B (\operatorname{mod}m)\) since \(0 \notin m\).


Now it’s not hard to prove the Nullstellensatz i.e. \[
\phi:A \rightarrow \mathcal{O}(\Spec A)
\] is injective for finitely generated \(k\)-algebra \(A\)(\(k\) is algebraically closed) without nilpotents. 






TipProof of Nullstellensatz



Let \(a\) be a non-zero element of \(A\). Consider the localization \(A_{(a)}\). This is non-zero since \(A\) has no nilpotents. In fact, by the exercise in the last section, \(A_{(a)}\) is also \(k\)-f.g (and reduced). Thus by the Noether’s Normalization Lemma, we have an inclusion \(k[X_1,\dots,X_r]\subseteq A_{(a)}\).
We need to find a point \(x\) of \(\Spec A\) such that \(\phi(a)(x) \equiv x(a)\) is non-zero where \(x: A \rightarrow k\) is a \(k\)-algebra homomorphism (this means non-zero element \(a\) cannot be sent to a non-zero function on \(\Spec A\) by \(\phi\)).
Let \(z:k[X_1,\dots,X_r] \rightarrow k\) be any \(k\)-algebra homomorphism (it clearly always exists). By the second lemma, we may lift (by composition) \(z\) to a \(k\)-algebra homomorphism \(y:A_{(a)} \rightarrow k\). Let \(x\) be the composition \(A \rightarrow A_{(a)} \rightarrow k\). Then \[
1_k=x(1_A)=y(1_A/1_A)=y(a/a)=y(a/1_A)y(1_A/a)=x(a)y(1_A/a)
\]
Therefore \(x(a)\) is non-zero. This proves the Nullstellensatz.


We use the trick called determinant trick again in the next famous and useful lemma:






NoteExercise.Nakayama’s Lemma



Let \(M\) be a f.g module over a commutative ring \(A\). Assume that there is an ideal \(I \unlhd A\) such that \(M=I \cdot M\). Then there is an element \(a\) of \(1+I\) such that \(aM=\{0\}\).








TipProof



Suppose that \(M=A[x_1,\dots,x_n]\). Then we have (totally same with the second lemma) \[
x_j=\sum_{k=1}^{n}y_k^jx_k \Rightarrow \sum_{k\neq j}(-y_k^j)x_k+(1-y_j^j)x_j=0
\]
Then we write it in the form of matrix: \[
(I_n-M)\vec{x}=0 \Rightarrow \operatorname{det}(I_n-M)\vec{x}=0
\]
And we know that \(\operatorname{det}(I_n-M)\equiv 1 (\operatorname{mod}I)\), then take \(a=\operatorname{det}(I_n-M)\).


Henceforth, by Nullstellensatz, we shall identify \(A\) with a ring of regular functions, as \(a \neq b \in A \Rightarrow \phi(a) \neq \phi(b) \in \mathcal{o}(\Spec A)\). Next we will give a reformulation of the Nullstellensatz which resembles Hilbert’s original statement.






ImportantTheorem



Suppose that \(k\) is algebraically closed and \(A\) is a f.g. \(k\)-algebra without nilpotents. If \(I\) is an ideal of \(A\), \[
\{a\in A: a(x)=0 \ \text{for all} \ x \in \ \text{zeroes}(I)\}=\sqrt{I}
\] where \(\sqrt{I}=\{a \in A: a^n \in I \ \text{for some} \ n>0\}\).








NoteProof



One checks that \(\sqrt{I}\) is an ideal. Then \(A^\prime=A/\sqrt{I}\) is a f.g. \(k\)-algebra which has no nilpotents. Let \(b\) be an element of \(A-\sqrt{I}\), then \(b^\prime=b+\sqrt{I}\) is a non-zero element of \(A^\prime\). Hence there exists a homomorphism \(x^\prime:A^\prime \rightarrow k\) such that \(x^\prime(b^\prime) \neq 0\). Let \(x:A \rightarrow A^\prime \xrightarrow{x^\prime} k\) be the composition. Then by construction \(x\) is a point of \(zeroes(I)\) and \(b(x) \neq 0\). This proves the desired inclusion “\(\subseteq\)”. The reverse inclusion is trivial because \(b^n(x)=0 \iff b(x)=0 \ \text{if } n >0\).


Some special cases will be useful.






NoteCorollary



Given a subset \(J\) of \(A\) then \(zeroes(J)=\emptyset \iff 1=\sum_{\text{finite}}a_kj_k \ \text{where } a_k \in A, j_k \in J\).








TipProof



Set \(I=JA\). Hence if \(\text{zeroes}(J)=\emptyset\), then \(\text{zereos}(I)=\emptyset\). Then \[
\{a\in A: a(x)=0 \ \text{for all} \ x \in \ \text{zeroes}(I)\}=A=\sqrt{I}
\] i.e. \(1=1^n \in JA\) which is the second statement. The converse is obvious.








NoteCorollary



Let \(f_{i}\) be elements of \(A\) and \(n_i\) be any positive integers. Then there exist \(a_i\) such that: \[
\Spec A=\bigcup D(f_i) \iff 1=\sum_{\text{finite}} a_if_i
\]








TipProof



\[
\Spec A=\bigcup D(f_i) \iff \emptyset=\bigcap{D(f_i)^{c}}=\bigcap{\operatorname{zeroes}(f_i)}=\bigcap{\operatorname{zeroes}(f_i^{n_i})}=\operatorname{zeroes}(\{f_i^{n_i}\})
\]
Then by the corollary above (take \(\{f_i^{n_i}\}\) as \(J\)) it’s equivalent to \(1=\sum_{\text{finite}}a_if_i^{n_i}\) for some \(a_i \in A\).


This result has an interesting topological consequence.






ImportantTheorem



\(\Spec A\) is quasi-compact.








NoteProof



By the exercise in the last section \(D(f_i)\) is a basis for the topology of \(\Spec A\). If \(\Spec A=\bigcup {D(f_i)}\) is an open cover by this then \(1=\sum_{J \text{ is finite}}a_jf_j\) for some \(a_j \in A\). Then \(\Spec A= \bigcup_{j \in J}D(f_j)\) is a finite subcover.








NoteExercise



Prove that a point of \(\Spec A\) is a closed subset.



Preparation:

If \(A\) is a \(k\)-algebra, \(A\xrightarrow{\varphi}k\) is onto where \(\varphi \in \operatorname{Hom}_k(A,k)\). Then \(\operatorname{ker}(\varphi)\) is maximal ideal.
If \(x,y \in \operatorname{Hom}_{k}(A,k)\) and further \(\operatorname{ker}(x)=\operatorname{ker}(y)\), then \(x \equiv y\).

Proof: \[
\begin{aligned}
&\overline{x} \circ \overline{y}^{-1} \equiv id_{k} \\
& \Rightarrow \overline{x} \circ \overline{y}^{-1} \circ \overline{y} \equiv id_{k} \circ \overline{y}  \\
& \Rightarrow \overline{x} \equiv \overline{y}\\
& \Rightarrow \overline{x} \circ \pi \equiv \overline{y} \circ \pi \\
& \Rightarrow x \equiv y
\end{aligned}
\]







TipProof



Let \(x \in \Spec A\), we expect that \(\overline{\{x\}}=\{x\}\). If \(y\neq x \in \overline{\{x\}}\), then \(a(x)=0 \implies a(y)=0\) which is equivalent to \(\operatorname{ker}(x) \subseteq \operatorname{ker}(y)\). Then by preparation we know that \(x\equiv y\).

title: Varieties
text:
We shall assume the field \(k\) is algebraically closed in this note.
Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be spaces with functions. The global effect of pull-back defines a mapping
\[
*: Morphism(X,Y) \to k \text{-}Alg \text{-} Hom_{k}(\mathcal{O}(Y),\mathcal{O}(X))
\]






ImportantDefintion




Affine Variety
Provided that \(\mathcal{O}(Y)\) is a finitely generated \(k\)-algebra, a space with functions \(Y\) is said to be an affine variety if the mapping \(*\) defined above is bijective for every space with functions \(X\).


Algebraic Variety
An algebraic variety \(X\) is defined to be a space with functions \(X\) which has a finite open covering \(U_{1},\dots,U_{n}\) where each \(U_{i}\) is affine. (Recall that an open subset of a space with functions carries the structure of space with functions naturally)


Morphism
A morphism between algebraic varieties is just a morphism of spaces with functions.



Next we give the first examples of varieties: the affine line \(\mathbb{A}^{1}\) and the projective line \(\mathbb{P}^{1}\).






NoteExample



\(\mathbb{A}^{1}\)
The underlying set of \(\mathbb{A}^{1}\) is just the field \(k\).
The topology of it is the cofinite topology, i.e. the closed subsets of \(\mathbb{A}^{1}\) are the whole set and the finite subsets.
The regular functions on open set \(U\): if \(U\) is empty, \(\mathcal{O}(U)=\{0\}\). Otherwise, if \(U=\mathbb{A}^{1}-\{x_{1},\dots,x_{n}\}\) then \(\mathcal{O}(U)\) consists of the rational functions \(g\) such that \(g\) has no poles anywhere in \(U\); i.e. \(g\) admits a representation: \[
U\to k, x \mapsto \frac{p(x)}{\prod(x-x_{i})^{m_{i}}} \ \text{where $p$ is a polynomial and the $m_{i}$ non-negative integers.}
\]
In particular, \(\mathcal{O}(\mathbb{A}^{1}) \cong k[T]\) is (isomorphic to) a polynomial ring in one variable.








NoteExercise



Verify that \(\mathbb{A}^{1}\) is a space with functions.








TipProof




Suppose that open set \(U=k-\{x_{1},\dots,x_{n}\}\) is the union of a family of open subsets \(U_{\alpha}\) where \(U_{\alpha}=k-\{x_{\alpha_{1}},\dots,x_{\alpha_{k_{\alpha}}}\}\) where \(k_{\alpha}\) is finite for each \(\alpha\) and \(\bigcap{\{x_{\alpha_{1}},\dots,x_{\alpha_{k_{\alpha}}}\}=\{x_{1},\dots,x_{n}\}}\). If \(f\) is a regular function on \(U\) then \(f\) admits a representation of \(\frac{p(x)}{\prod_{i=1}^{n}(x-x_{i})^{m_{i}}}, m_{i} \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}\), then clearly \(f\) adimits a form \(\frac{p(x)}{\prod_{i=1}^{n}(x-x_{i})^{m_{i}}}\) on \(U_{\alpha}\) since \(U_{\alpha} \subseteq U\) and \(f \restriction_{U_{\alpha}} \in \mathcal{O}(U_{\alpha})\) since \(\{x_{1},\dots,x_{n}\} \subseteq\{x_{\alpha_{1}},\dots,x_{\alpha_{k_{\alpha}}}\}\).







CautionObservation




Given \(U=k-\{x_1,\dots,x_n\}\), we observe that we characterize \(f=\frac{p(x)}{\prod_{i=1}^{n}(x-x_{i})^{m_{i}}}, m_{i} \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}\) as \(\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}\) where polynomial \(q(x)\) vanishes nowhere in \(U\).
Given any two open sets \(U_1,U_2\), \(U_1 \cap U_2\) is an infinite set since \(k\) is infinite.



 Conversely, if \(f:U \to k\) takes the form of \(\frac{p_{\alpha}(x)}{q_{\alpha}(x)}\) (as we observed) on each \(U_{\alpha}\), then clearly \(\frac{p_{\alpha}(x)}{q_{\alpha}(x)}=\frac{p_{\beta}(x)}{q_{\beta}(x)}\) on \(U_{\alpha} \cap U_{\beta}\) since they are all restricted by \(f\) which implies that \(p_{\alpha}(x){q_{\beta}(x)}-{p_{\beta}(x)}{q_{\alpha}(x)}\) has infinitely many roots for observation 2. It follows that \(\frac{p_{\alpha}(x)}{q_{\alpha}(x)}=\frac{p_{\beta}(x)}{q_{\beta}(x)}\) on the whole \(U\) for any \(\alpha,\beta\), and thus the global function \(f\) admits a representation \(\frac{p(x)}{q(x)} \in k(x)\).
Now we show that \(q(x)\) has no roots in \(U\) which leads to that it’s a constant. Assume not: $q(x_0)=0,x_0 U_{_0} U $. Then in the field of fractional functions \(k(x)\) we have \(\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}=\frac{p_{\alpha_{0}}(x)}{q_{\alpha_{0}}(x)} \in \mathcal{O}(U_{\alpha_{0}})\) and here we can assume \(gcd(p,q)=1\) (implies that they have no commen roots in \(k\)). It follows that \(p(x)q_{\alpha_{0}}(x)=p_{\alpha_{0}}(x)q(x)\) which implies that \(q_{\alpha_{0}}(x_0)=0\). Contradiction with \(q_{\alpha_0}\) vanishes nowhere in \(U_{\alpha_0}\). Hence \(q(x)=c\prod(x-t_i)^{s_i},t_i \in k-U\) and we get the form \(\frac{1}{c}p(x)/\prod(x-t_i)^{s_i},t_i \in k-U\) as we expected.


Suppose that \[
g=\frac{p(x)}{\prod(x-x_i)^{m_i }}\in\mathcal{O}(U)
\]，then \(D(g)=\{x\in U:p(x) \neq0\}=k-\{x_{1},\dots,x_{n}\}-\{r_1,\dots,r_{m}\}\) where \(r_j\) are the roots of \(p\) in \(k\) is an open set. And \(\frac{1}{g(x)}=\frac{\prod(x-x_i)^{m_i}}{(x-r_{j})^{k_j}}\in D(g)\) where \(p\) splits into \(\prod(x-r_{j})^{k_j}\) in \(k\) since \(k\) is algebraically closed.



This is a technical and detailed proof. We may need the following elementary result (use Bézout theorem to verify): \[
(f, g) = 1 \text{ in } k[x]   \Longleftrightarrow  (f, g) = 1 \text{ in } K[x] \ \forall K/k \Longleftrightarrow  \nexists \alpha \in \bar{k} : f(\alpha) = g(\alpha) = 0.
\]
Next we show that \(\mathbb{A}^{1}\) is indeed an affine variety.
Let \(Y\) be any space with functions. A mapping \(f:Y \to \mathbb{A}^{1}=k\) is just a \(k\)-valued function.






ImportantClaim



\(f\) is a morphism if and only if \(f\) is regular on \(Y\).






NoteProof



“Only if”: The coordinate function \(x:k\to k; t \mapsto t\) is regular on \(\mathbb{A}^1\) and then \(f(x)\) is regular on \(Y\) since \(f\) is a morphism and \(f^{-1}(k)=Y\).
“if”: Suppose that \(f\) is regular on \(Y\). \(f\) is continuous since \(f^{-1}(\{t_1,\dots,t_n\})=Y-D(F)\), where \(F=\prod_{i=1}^{n} (f-t_{i})\), is the complement of an open set \(D(f)\). To show that \(f\) pulls back regualr function \(g=\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}\) on \(U=\mathbb{A}^1-\{t_1,\dots,t_n\}\), we notice that: \[
g \circ f=\frac{p(f(y))}{q(f(y))}=\frac{p(f(y))}{\prod_{i=1}^{n} (f(y)-t_i)^{m_{i}}}
\] which is regular on \(D(f)=f^{-1}(k-\{t_1,\dots,t_n\})\) by definition.


At last we obtain that \(\mathbb{A}^{1}\) is affine: \[
*:Morphism(Y,\mathbb{A}^{1}) \cong \mathcal{O}(Y) \cong k \text{-} Alg \text{-} Hom (\mathcal{O}(\mathbb{A}^1),\mathcal{O}(Y))
\] The last equality holds for that \(\mathcal{O}(\mathbb{A}^1)=k[T]\) and the \(k\)-algebra maps are totally determined by the regular functions on \(Y\) as the images of \(T\).








ImportantExample



As a set \(\mathbb{P}^{1}=k \cup \{\infty\}\) where \(\infty\) is a set disjoint from \(\mathbb{P}^{1}\).
Topolgy:The closed subsets are finite sets, i.e. the open sets are like \(\mathbb{P}^{1}-\{x_1,\dots,x_n\}\).
Regular functions: The regular functions \(g\in \mathcal{O}(\mathbb{P}^1-\{x_1,\dots,x_n\})\) admit a form of rational functions without poles except at \(x_1,\dots,x_n\) where \(g\) has no poles at \(\infty\) is equvalent to saying \(g(\frac{1}{y})\) has no pole at \(y=0\).
It is a space with functions.
To see that it is indeed a variety, it has an open covering \((\mathbb{P}^{1}-\{\infty\})\cup (\mathbb{P}^{1}-\{0\})\) isomorphic to two affine lines: \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}^{1}-\{\infty\} & \xrightarrow[Id]{\simeq} \mathbb{A}^1 \\
\mathbb{P}^{1}-\{0\} & \xrightarrow[\frac{1}{x}]{\simeq} \mathbb{A}^1 \quad \text{where} \frac{1}{\infty}=0
\end{aligned}
\]








NoteExercise



Verify that \(\mathcal{O}(\mathbb{P}^{1})=k\)








TipProof



Suppose that \(f \in \mathcal{O}(\mathbb{P}^{1})\), then \(f \restriction_{(\mathbb{P}^{1}-\{\infty\})\cap(\mathbb{P}^{1}-\{0\})=k^{\times}}\) admits a representation
\(f \restriction_{(\mathbb{P}^{1}-\{\infty\})}\) admits a representation \(\frac{p_{1}(x)}{q_{1}(x)}\) where \(deg(p_{1}(x)) \leq deg(q_{1}(x)) \quad \text{or} \quad =\text{constant}\) and $ f _{(^{1}-{})}$ admits a representation \(p_{2}(x)\). Therefore, \(\frac{p_{1}(x)}{q_{1}(x)}=p_{2}(x)\) or \(p_{2}(x)=\text{constant}\) on \((\mathbb{P}^{1}-\{\infty\})\cap(\mathbb{P}^{1}-\{0\})=k^{\times}\) which only happens when \(f \restriction_{(\mathbb{P}^{1}-\{\infty\})}\) and \(f \restriction_{(\mathbb{P}^{1}-\{0\})}\) are constant. Hence \(f \in \mathcal{O}(\mathbb{P}^{1})\) if and only if \(f=\text{constant}\in k\).








NoteExercise



Show that \(\mathbb{P}^{1}\) is not affine.








TipProof



Suppose not, \(\mathbb{P}^{1}\) is an affine variety. By definition, for the field \({k}\) we have \(Mor(\mathbb{A}^{1},\mathbb{P}^{1}) \cong Hom_{k}(\mathcal{O}(\mathbb{P}^{1}),\mathcal{O}(\mathbb{A}^{1})) \cong Hom_{k}(k,k[T])\). But the latter corresponds to the ideals (\(0,k\)) of \(k\) which contradicts the fact that the first has at least two nontrivial morphisms (\(0,\mathbb{A}^{1} \to \mathbb{P}^{1}-\{0\},\mathbb{A}^{1} \to \mathbb{P}^{1}-\{\infty\}\)).








NoteExercise



Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be two affine varieties. Show that \(X \cong Y\) as spaces with functions if and only if \(\mathcal{O}(X) \cong \mathcal{O}(Y)\) as \(k\)-algebras.








TipProof



Suppose that \(X \cong Y\), then for some morphism \(g:X \to Y\), we have \(f: Y \to X\) such that \(f\circ g=id_{X}\) and \(g \circ f=id_{Y}\). Then \(g^{*} \circ f^{*}=id_{\mathcal{O}(X)}\) and \(f^{*} \circ g^{*}=id_{\mathcal{O}(Y)}\) where \(g^{*}:\mathcal{O}(Y) \to \mathcal{O}(X)\) and \(f^{*}:\mathcal{O}(X) \to \mathcal{O}(Y)\).
Conversely we suppose that \(X,Y\) are affine varieties and as \(k\)-algebras \(\mathcal{O}(X) \cong \mathcal{O}(Y)\). Then for some map \(G:\mathcal{O}(Y) \to \mathcal{O}(X)\) we have \(F:\mathcal{O}(X) \to \mathcal{O}(Y)\) such that \(F \circ G =id_{\mathcal{O}(Y)}, G \circ F =id_{\mathcal{O}(X)}\). Since \(X,Y\) are affine varieties (\(*\) is bijective), there exist unique morphisms \(g:X \to Y\) and \(f: Y \to X\) such that \(g^{*}=G,f^{*}=F\) and thus \(g\circ f=id_{Y},f\circ g=id_{X}\).

title: Exercise 1.1
text:
Exercise 1
Let \(R\) be a commutative ring where \(0\neq 1\). Suppose that every ideal \(\big(\neq (1)\big)\) is prime. Show that \(R\) is a field.



Proof. Clearly \(R\) is a domain. Let \(a\neq 0\in R\) be a non-unit. Then \((a^2)\) is a prime ideal and thus \(a^2\in(a^2)\) implies that \(a\in(a^2)\). It follows that there exists an element \(r\in R\) such that \(a=a^2r\). As \(R\) is a domain, we have \(1=ar\) which leads to contradiction.


Exercise 2
Let us say that a saturated multiplicatively closed set \(S\) is generated by \(\{x_i\}\) if \(S\) is the smallest such set containing the \(x\)’s. Prove that if \(S\) is finitely generated in this sense, then it can be generated by a single element.



Proof. Suppose that \(S\) is generated by \(x_1,\dots,x_n\); we show that \(S\) is also generated by \(x_1\dots x_n\);denote \(S^\prime\) the saturated multiplicatively closed set generated by this single element. \(S^\prime\subseteq S\) for \(S\) contains \(x_1\dots x_n\); \(S\subseteq S^\prime\) for \(S^\prime\) contains the \(x_i\)’s. Therefore \(S=S^\prime\).


Exercise 3
Let \(\mathfrak{p}\) be a finitely generated prime ideal with annihilator \(0\). Prove that the annihilator of the module \(\mathfrak{p}/\mathfrak{p}^2\) is \(\mathfrak{p}\).



Proof. Suppose that \(\mathfrak{p}\) is generated by \(x_1,\dots,x_r\). Clearly \(\mathfrak{p}\subseteq \operatorname{ann}(\mathfrak{p}/\mathfrak{p}^2)\); Let \(x\) be any element in \(\operatorname{ann}(\mathfrak{p}/\mathfrak{p}^2)\). The element in \(\mathfrak{p}^2\) admits the form \(\sum_{i=1}^{r}a_ip_i\) where \(a_i\in \mathfrak{p}\). Then it follows that \[
xp_i=\sum_{j=1}^{r}a_{ij}p_j,\qquad a_{ij}\in \mathfrak{p}
\] for \(i=1,\dots,r\).
Write the linear relations betwen \(p_i\)’s in the form of matrix: \[
\begin{bmatrix}
a_{11}-x & a_{12} & \ldots & a_{1r} \\
a_{21} & a_{22}-x &\ldots & a_{2r}\\
\vdots &\vdots &\ddots  & \vdots \\
a_{r1}& a_{r2} &\ldots &a_{rr}-x
\end{bmatrix}
\cdot
\begin{bmatrix}
p_1 \\
p_2 \\
\vdots \\
p_r
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
0\\
0\\
\vdots\\
0
\end{bmatrix}
\] Take determinant of the matrix \(M\); Since \(\operatorname{ann}(\mathfrak{p})=0\) we get \(\det M=0\);i.e. there exists a polynomial \(f\) with coefficients in the prime ideal \(\mathfrak{p}\) such that \(f(x)=0\). By induction on the degree of \(f\) (there we need the ideal being prime), we have \(x\in \mathfrak{p}\).

The purpose of the exercise below is to show that in Ex.3 we cannot drop the requirement that \(\mathfrak{p}\) is prime.

Exercise 4
Let \(k\) be a field. Let \(R\) be the ring of polynomials in one indeterminant \(x\) over \(k\), subject to the condition that they contain no terms in \(x\) or \(x^2\). Let \(I\) be the ideal in \(R\) generated by \(x^3\) and \(x^4\). Prove: \(x^5\notin I\), and \(x^5I\subset I^2\); i.e. \(I\subsetneq\operatorname{ann}(I/I^2)\).



Proof. Assume that \(x^5=f(x)x^3+g(x)x^4\); then \(x^2=f(x)+g(x)x\) which contradicts the fact that \(f\) and \(g\) contain no terms in \(x\) or \(x^2\). So \(x^5\notin I\). Any element in \(x^5I\) admits the form \(x^8f(x)+x^9g(x)\). As \(x^8\in I^2\) and \(f(x)\in R\), \(x^8f(x)\in I^2\); As \(x^6\in I^2\) and \(x^3g(x)\in R\), \(x^9g(x)\in I^2\). Hence \(x^5I\subset I^2\).


Exercise 5
Let \(\mathfrak{p}=(p)\) be a principal prime ideal and \(J=\bigcap_{n=1}\mathfrak{p}^n\).

If \(\mathfrak{q}\) is a prime ideal properly contained by \(\mathfrak{p}\), prove that \(\mathfrak{q}\subset J\).
Assume further that \(p\) is a non-zero-divisor. Prove: \(J=pJ\).
Again assuming that \(p\) is a non-zero-divisor, prove that \(J\) is prime.
Assume that \(R\) is a domain and \(J\) is finitely generated. Prove that \(J=0\) and that there is no prime ideal properly between \(P\) and \(0\).
Assume merely that \(J\) is finitely generated. Prove that there cannot exist a distinct chain \(\mathfrak{p}\supsetneq\mathfrak{q}_1\supsetneq \mathfrak{q}_2\) of prime ideals.




Proof. 

For any \(q\in \mathfrak{q}\), we show that \(q\in\mathfrak{p}^n\) for any \(n\) by induction; \(q\in\mathfrak{p}^1\) obviously; Assume \(q\in\mathfrak{p}^n=(p^n)\), then \(q=p^nq_1\) for some \(q_1\); As \(p^n\notin \mathfrak{q}\) (otherwise \(p\in \mathfrak{q}\)), we have \(q=p^{n+1}q_2\). By induction, it follows that \(\mathfrak{q}\subset J\).
For any \(j\in J\), we can write \(j=px_1\) since \(j\in\mathfrak{p}\). As \(j\in (p^n)\) for any \(n\), we have \(p^nx_n=px_1\). Then \(x_1=p^{n-1}x_n\) for any \(n\) since \(p\) is a non-zero-divisor. Hence \(x_1\in J\) and hence \(J\subseteq pJ\). The reverse inclusion is clear.
Suppose \(ab\in J\) with neither \(a\) nor \(b\) in \(J\). Since \(ab\in\mathfrak{p}\) which is prime ideal, we can assume that \(a\in\mathfrak{p}\). As \(a\notin \bigcap_{n=1} \mathfrak{p}^n\), there exists a positive integer \(m\) such that \(a\in \mathfrak{p}^m\) while \(a\notin\mathfrak{p}^{m+1}=p^m\mathfrak{p}\). So \(a\) has a form of \(a=p^ma_1\) where \(a_1\notin \mathfrak{p}\). Similarly \(b\) has the form of \(b=p^nb_1\) where \(b_1\notin \mathfrak{p}\) (here \(n\) could be zero). Then \(ab=p^{m+n}a_1b_1\) which is contained in \((p^{m+n+1})\). As \(p\) is a non-zero-divisor, \(a_1b_1=px\in\mathfrak{p}\). As \(\mathfrak{p}\) is a prime ideal, either \(a\) or \(b\) is in \(\mathfrak{p}\). We get a contradiction then.
Using determinant trick, it follows that there exists \(x\in R\) with \(x\equiv 1 (\operatorname{mod} \mathfrak{p})\) such that \(xJ=0\). Then \(J=0\) as \(x\neq0\) and \(R\) is a domain. The final statement is immediate from part (a).
Assume such a chain exists. Then we get a chain \(\mathfrak{p}\,\operatorname{mod}\mathfrak{q_2}\supsetneq \mathfrak{q_1}\,\operatorname{mod} \mathfrak{q_2}\supsetneq 0\) of prime ideals in the domain \(R/\mathfrak{q}_2\). This is impossible from part (d).



Exercise 6
Let \(\mathfrak{p}\) be a prime ideal in \(R\), \(I\) the ideal generated by all the idempotents in \(\mathfrak{p}\). Prove that \(R/I\) has no non-trivial idempotents. (This result is due to D.Lazard who studied under P.Samuel.)




Lemma 1
Let \(\{e_i\}_{i\in I}\) be some idempotents in \(R\) and \(I\) be the ideal generated by \(\{e_i\}_{i\in I}\). For any element \(x\in I\), there is an idempotent \(f\in I\) such that \(fx=x\).



Proof. Suppose that \(x=\sum_{i=1}^{r} r_ie_i\). It suffices to show that there exists an idempotent \(f\in I\) such that \(fe_i=e_i\) for \(i=1,\dots,r\). The expected \(f\) can be explicitly constructed as follows: \[
\begin{aligned}
f&=\sum e_i -  \sum e_ie_j + \dots +(-1)^{r-1}e_1\dots e_r.\\
&=\sum_{S\subseteq \{1,\dots,r\}}(-1)^{|S|-1}e_S
\end{aligned}
\] It’s clear that \(fe_k=e_k\) and hence \(f^2=f(\sum r_ie_i)=\sum r_ife_i=r_ie_i=f\).



Proof. Let \(e\in R/I\) be an idempotent. Pick \(u\in R\) such that \(u\,\operatorname{mod}I=e\). As \(e(1-e)=0\) in \(R/I\) it follows that \(u(1-u)\in I\); thus in \(\mathfrak{p}\). W.LO.G assume that \(u\in \mathfrak{p}\) since \(\mathfrak{p}\) is prime. By lemma above, we have \(f(u-u^2)=u-u^2\) for idempotent \(f\in I\). Then \([(1-f)u]^2=(1-f)u^2=(1-f)u\) and thus \((1-f)u\) is an idempotent in \(\mathfrak{p}\), hence in \(I\). As \(fu\in I\), \((1-f)u+fu=u\in I\). Thus \(u \,\operatorname{mod}I=0\) in \(R/I\) which is a trivial idempotent.


Exercise 7
Let \((p)\) and \((q)\) be non-zero principal prime ideals in a ring. Suppose that \((p)\subseteq (q)\) and that \(p\) is a non-zero-divisor. Prove that \((p)=(q)\).



Proof. It follows from \((p)\subseteq (q)\) that \(p=qr\) for some element \(r\in R\). As \(p\) is a prime element, either \(p|q\) or \(p|r\). If \(p|q\), then \(q=px\in(p)\) and the proof is complete; if \(p|r\), write \(r=pa\), then \(p(1-qa)=0\). Since \(p\) is a non-zero-divisor, \(1=qa\) which contradicts the fact that \(q\) is a prime element.


Exercise 8: A modernization of Euclid’s theorem on the infinitude of primes
Prove that an infinite integral domain \(R\) with a finite number of units has an infinite number of maximal ideals.



Proof. Notice that \((0)\) is not a maximal ideal as \((0)\subsetneq (a)\) for some \(a\notin R^\times\); Assume that \(R\) has a finite number of maximal ideals, say \(\mathfrak{m}_1,\dots,\mathfrak{m}_n\). Let \(a_i\in \mathfrak{m}_i\) be a non-zero element. Notice that any non-unit element is contained in one maximal ideal and thus the union of all maximal ideals. Since \((a_1\dots a_n+1)\notin \bigcup_{i}\mathfrak{m}_i\) (otherwise \(1\in\mathfrak{m}_i\) for some \(i\)), \((a_1\dots a_n+1)\) is a unit. Similarly all the elements in the form of \(ka_1\dots a_n+1, k\in\mathbb{N}\) are units. However, these elements are distinct for \(R\) is a domain. Hence \(R\) has infinitely many units which contradicts to the assumption that \(R\) has a finite number of units. The proof is then complete.


Exercise 9: A naive version of Gauss’s lemma
Let \(f\) and \(g\) be polynomials in an indeterminant over a ring \(R\). Suppose that the ideal generated by the coefficients of \(f\) is \(R\), and that the same is true for \(g\). Prove that the coefficients of \(fg\) also generate \(R\).



Proof. Assume that the coefficients of \(fg\) lie in a maximal ideal \(\mathfrak{m}\). Write \(f=a_nx^n+\dots+a_sx^s+\dots+a_0\) and \(g=b_mx^m+\dots+b_tx^t+\dots+b_0\) where \(a_s\) and \(b_t\) are the terms of highest degree which are not in \(\mathfrak{m}\). Consider the term of degree \(s+t\) in \(fg\). The coefficient of that term is \[
a_sb_t+\sum_{i>s}^{i+j=s+t}a_ib_j+\sum_{j>t}^{i+j=s+t}a_ib_j
\] which does not lie in \(\mathfrak{m}\). Thus we get a contradiction.


Exercise 10
In a ring \(R\) let \(I\) be maximal among non-principal ideals. Prove that \(I\) is prime. (a result from the famous finite theorist M.Isaacs)



Proof. Let \(I\) be such a maximal ideal. Assume that it’s not a prime ideal. Thus there exist \(a,b\notin I\) with \(ab\in I\). Since \(I+(a)\supsetneq I\), \(I+(a)\) is a principal ideal, say \((c)\). Take \(J=I:(c)\). Clearly \(I\subset J\) and \(b\in J\). It follows that \(J\supsetneq I\) and then it’s a principal ideal. Clearly \(Jc\subseteq I\); To show the reverse inclusion, choose any element \(i\in I\subsetneq I+(a)=(c)\). Hence \(i=cr\) for some \(r\in R\). As \(cr\in I\), we have \(r\in J\). Hence \(i\in Jc\) and hence \(I=Jc\). However, \(Jc\) is a principal ideal. Consequently we get a contradiction.


Exercise 11
In a ring \(R\) let \(I\) be maximal among ideals that are not countably generated. Prove that \(I\) is prime.



Proof. Let \(I\) be such a maximal ideal. Assume that it’s not a prime ideal. Thus there exist \(a,b\notin I\) with \(ab\in I\). Since \(I+(a)\subsetneq I\), it’s a countably generated ideal, say \(I+(a)=\sum_{i\in \mathbb{N}} R a_i+Ra\) with \(a_i\in I\). Take \(J=I:(a)\). It follows that \(J\supsetneq I\). Thus \(J\) is countably generated too. We claim that \(I=(a_{i\in\mathbb{N}},Ja)\). It’s clear that \((a_{i\in\mathbb{N}},Ja)\subseteq I\). To show the reverse inclusion, choose any element \(c\in I\subsetneq I+(a)\). Then \(c=\sum_{i\in\mathbb{N}} r_i a_i +ra\) with \(a_i\)’s contained in \(I\). Thus \(r\in J\). Consequently we obtain that \(I=(a_{i\in\mathbb{N}},Ja)\) which is a countably generated ideal. Contradiction.

title: Graded Modules and Rings
text:
This note is entirely taken from \(\S11.1,\S 11.2\) in Chapter \(\mathrm{II}\) of Bourbaki’s Algebra and is for my own review only.

GRADED COMMUTATIVE GROUPS






NoteDEFINITION



Graded Commutative Group of Type \(\Delta\)
Given a commutative group \(G\) written additively and a set \(\Delta\), a gradation of type \(\Delta\) on \(G\) is a family \((G_{\lambda})_{\lambda \in \Delta}\) of subgroups of \(G\), of which \(G\) is the direct sum, i.e \(G=\bigoplus_{\lambda \in \Delta}G_{\lambda}\). Then the set \(G\), with the structure defined by its group law and its gradation, is called a graded (commutative) group of type \(\Delta\).








Caution



There is an another way to understand where the type comes from. Let \(G\) be a commutative group; let \(G=\oplus_{i\in I}G_i\) be a decomposition of it. Suppose that there is another set \(J\) (may be equipped with some structures) such that there is an injection (set-theoretically) from \(I\) into \(J\). Then \((G_i)\) is said to be of type \(J\).


Some Notations:

\(\Delta\) is called the set of degrees of \(G\). An element \(x \in G\) is called homogeneous if it belongs to one of the \(G_{\lambda}\), homogeous of degree \(\lambda\) if \(x \in G_{\lambda}\).
The element \(0\) is therefore homogeneous of all degrees.
If \(x \neq 0\), it belongs to only one of the \(G_{\lambda}\)’s by definiton of direct sum; the index \(\lambda\) such that \(x \in G_{\lambda}\) is called the degree of \(x\) (or sometimes called weight) and is sometimes denoted by \(\operatorname{deg}(x)\).
Every \(0 \neq y \in G\) may be written uniquely as a finite sum \(\sum_{\lambda}y_{\lambda}\) of homogeneous elements with \(y_{\lambda}\in G_{\lambda}\); \(y_{\lambda}\) is called the component of degree \(\lambda\).


Examples of Graded Groups

Given any commutative monoid with identity \(0\) and a commutative group \(G\), a gradation \((G_{\lambda})_{\lambda \in \Delta}\) is defined on \(G\) by taking \(G_0=G\) and \(G_{\lambda}=\{0\}, \lambda \neq 0\); this gradation is called trivial.
Let \(\Delta,\Delta^{\prime}\) be two sets and \(\rho\) a mapping of \(\Delta \to \Delta^{\prime}\). Let \(G_{\lambda}\) be a gradation of type \(\Delta\) on a commutative group \(G\); for \(\mu \in \Delta^{\prime}\), let \(A_{\mu}\) be the sum of the \(G_{\lambda}\) such that \(\mu(\lambda)=\mu\); Clearly \(A_{\mu}\) is a gradation of type \(\Delta^{\prime}\) (by associativity of direct sum) on \(G\), said to be derived from \((G_{\lambda})_{\lambda \in \Delta}\) by means of the mapping \(\rho\).
(Product of gradations) If \(\Delta=\Delta_1 \times \Delta_2\) is a product of two sets, a gradation of type \(\Delta\) is called a bigradation of types \(\Delta_1,\Delta_2\).

Suppose that the bigradation of type \(\Delta=\Delta_1 \times \Delta_2\) is on some group \(G\). For all \(\lambda \in \Delta_1\), let \(A_{\lambda}=\bigoplus_{\mu \in \Delta_2}G_{(\lambda,\mu)}\) and for \(\mu \in \Delta_2\), let \(B_{\lambda}=\bigoplus_{\lambda \in \Delta_1}G_{(\lambda,\mu)}\). Clearly \((A_{\lambda})_{\lambda \in \Delta_1}\) is a gradation of type \(\Delta_1\) on \(G\) and \((B_{\mu})_{\mu \in \Delta_2}\) is a gradation of type \(\Delta_2\) on \(G\); these gradations are called the \(partial gradations\) derived from the bigradationn \((G_{(\lambda,\mu)})_{\Delta}\). Note that \(G_{(\lambda,\mu)}=A_{\lambda} \cap B_{\mu}\).
Conversely, if \((A_{\lambda})_{\lambda \in G_1}\) and \((B_{\mu})_{\mu \in \Delta_2}\) are two gradations on some group \(G\) such that \(G\) is the direct sum of \(G_{(\lambda,\mu)}=A_{\Lambda} \cap B_{\mu}\), then subgroups \(G_{(\lambda,\mu)}\) consist of a bigradation of types \(\Delta_1,\Delta_2\) on \(G\), of which \((A_{\lambda}),(B_{\mu})\) are the partial gradations.

Let \(\Delta_{0}\) be a commutative monoid written additively, with identity element denoted by \(0\); let \(I\) be any set and \(\Delta_{0}^{(I)}=\Delta\) denote the submonoid of the product \(\Delta_0^{I}\) consisting of the familys \((\lambda_{\iota})_{\iota \in I}\) of finite support. Let \(\rho:\Delta \to \Delta_0\) be the surjective homomorphism of \(\Delta\) onto \(\Delta_0\) defined by \(\rho((\lambda_{\iota})) \mapsto \sum_{\iota \in I}{\lambda_{\iota}}\). Given any gradation of type \(\Delta\), a gradation of type \(\Delta_0\) is derived by means of \(\rho\); it is called the total gradation associated with the given multigradation of type \(\Delta\).

For instance, consider the underlying group of \(k[x,y]\). Let \(\Delta_0\) be \(\mathbb{N}_{\geq0}\) and \(\Delta=\mathbb{N}^2\); let \((G_{(a,b)})\) be \(\{cx^ay^b:c \in k\}\);Clearly it’s a gradation of type \(\mathbb{N}^2\). By definition, the total gradation of this bigradution is just \((G_{\lambda})_{\lambda \in \mathbb{N}}=(\{cx^ay^b:c \in k,a+b=\lambda\})\).





GRADED RINGS AND MODULES
Henceforth we shall assume that \(\Delta\) is always a commutative mononid with identity \(0\).






ImportantDEFINITION



Graded Ring of Type \(\Delta\)
Given a ring \(A\) and a gradation \((A_{\lambda})\) of type \(\Delta\) on the additive group \(A\), this gradation is said to be compatible with the ring structure on \(A\) if \[
A_{\lambda}A_{\mu} \subseteq A_{\lambda +\mu} \text{ for all } \lambda,\mu \in \Delta
\] The ring \(A\) with this gradation is then called a graded ring of type \(\Delta\).








NotePROPOSITION



If every element of \(\Delta\) is cancellable and \((A_{\lambda})\) is a gradation of type \(\Delta\) compatible with the structure of a ring \(A\), \(A_0\) is a subring of \(A\) (and in particular \(1 \in A\)).
proof:
As \(A_0A_0 \subseteq A_0\) by definition, it suffices to show that \(1 \in A_0\). Let \(1=\sum_{\lambda \in \Delta}e_{\lambda}\) be the decomposition of \(1\) into its homogeneous components. If \(x \in A_{\mu}\), then \(x=x \cdot 1=\sum_{\lambda \in \Delta}e_{\lambda}x\). Since \(xe_0 \in A_{\mu}A_{0}\subseteq A_{\mu}\) (\(\lambda + \mu =\mu\) implies \(\lambda\) must be zero, this is why we require that \(\Delta\) be cancellable), by the uniqueness of decomposition, \(xe_i=0\) when \(i \neq 0\) and \(xe_0=x\) when \(i=0\). Since this relation holds ture for every homogeneous element of \(A\), it is true for all \(x \in A\); in particular, \(1=1 \cdot e_0=e_0\), and thus \(1 \in A_0\).








ImportantDEFINITION



Graded Module of Type \(\Delta\)
Let \(A\) be a graded ring of type \(\Delta\), \((A_{\lambda})\) its gradation and \(M\) a left \(A\)-module; a gradation \((M_{\lambda})\) of type \(\Delta\) on the additive group \(M\) is compatible with the \(A\)-module structure on \(M\) if \[
A_{\lambda}M_{\mu} \subseteq M_{\lambda + \mu} \text{ for all } \lambda,\mu \in \Delta
\] The module \(M\) with this gradation is then called a left graded module of type \(\Delta\) over the graded ring \(A\).


When the elements of \(\Delta\) are cancellable, it follows from Prop before that the \(M_{\lambda}\) are \(A_0\)-modules.
Clearly if \(A\) is a graded ring of type \(\Delta\) then the left module \(A_s\) is a graded module of type \(\Delta\).

Examples of Graded Rings and Modules

On any ring \(A\), the trivial gradation of type \(\Delta\) is compatible with its structure of ring. For a gradation \((M_{\lambda})\) of type \(\Delta\) on an \(A\)-module to be compatible with the \(A\)-module structure, it is necessary and sufficient that the \(M_{\lambda}\) be submodules of \(M\).
Let \(A\) be a graded ring of type \(\Delta\), \(M\) a graded \(A\)-module of type \(\Delta\) and \(\rho\) a homomorphism of \(\Delta\) into a commutative monoid \(\Delta^{\prime}\). Then \(A\) is also a graded ring of type \(\Delta^{\prime}\) for the gradation derived from \(\rho\); Same for \(M\). sketch of proof:
If \(A^{\prime}_{\lambda^{\prime}}=\sum_{\rho(\lambda)=\lambda^{\prime}}A_{\lambda}\), \((A^{\prime}_{\lambda^{\prime}})\) is the gradation derived from \(\Delta\) by means of \(\rho\) on the additive group \(A\).
Check this gradation is compatible with the ring structure of \(A\): \[
  A^\prime_{\lambda^\prime}A\prime_{\lambda^\prime}\subseteq(\sum_{\rho(\lambda)=\lambda^{\prime}}A_{\lambda})(\sum_{\rho(\mu)=\mu^{\prime}}A_{\mu}) \subseteq \sum_{\rho(\lambda)+\rho(\mu)=\rho(\lambda+\mu)=\lambda^\prime+\mu^\prime}A_{\lambda}A_{\mu}\subseteq \sum_{\rho(\lambda)+\rho(\mu)=\rho(\lambda+\mu)=\lambda^\prime+\mu^\prime}A_{\lambda+\mu}=A^\prime_{\lambda^\prime+\lambda^\prime}
  \]


if \(\Delta=\Delta_1 \times \Delta_2\) is a product of two commutative monoids, the projections \(\operatorname{pr}_1\) and \(\operatorname{pr}_2\) are homomorphisms and the corresponding gradations are just the partial gradations derived from the gradations of type \(\Delta\); these partial gradations are just compatible with the ring structure of \(A\) and the module structure of \(M\).
if \(\Delta=\Delta_0^{(I)}\), the total gradation of type \(\Delta_0\) derived from the gradation of type \(\Delta\) on \(A\)(\(M\)) by means of the codiagonal homomorphism is compatible with the ring structure of \(A\).(\(M\))


Let \(A\) be a graded ring of type \(\Delta\), \(M\) a graded module of type \(\Delta\) and \(\lambda_0\) be an element of \(\Delta\); for all \(\lambda \in \Delta\), let \(M^{\prime}_{\lambda}=M_{\lambda+\lambda_0}\) and let \(M^\prime=\sum_{\lambda\in \Delta}M^\prime_{\lambda}\). As \(A_{\lambda}M^\prime_{\mu}=A_{\lambda}M_{\mu +\lambda_0}\subseteq M_{\lambda+\mu}^\prime\), \(M^\prime\) is a \(A\)-module and the \(M^\prime_{\lambda}\)’s’ form a gradation of \(M^\prime\) of type \(\Delta\) compatible with the module strcuture of \(M^\prime\). This gradation is said to be obtained by shifting by \(\lambda_0\) and denoted by \(M(\lambda_0)\). Clearly when \(\Delta\) is a group the underlying set of \(M\) and \(M^\prime\) are the same.
Let \(B\) be a commutative ring. The polynomial ring \(B[X]\) in one indeterminate is graded of type \(\mathbb{N}_{\geq 0}\) by the subgroups \(BX^n,n\geq 0\).







TipRemark



The gradations most often used are of type \(\mathbb{Z}^{l}\); when we speak of \(graded modules and rings\) without mentioning the type, it is understood that we mean gradations of type \(\mathbb{Z}^{l}\).





GRADED POLYNOMIAL RINGS






NoteDEFINITION



Standard Grading
We will introduce a grading on the polynomial ring \(S=k[x_1,\dots,x_n]\) over a field \(k\). Set \(\operatorname{deg}(x_i)=1\) for each \(i\) and \(\operatorname{deg}({x_1^{c_1}\dots x_n^{c_n}})=\sum c_i\) for each monomial. For \(i \in \mathbb{N}_{\geq 0}\),we denote by \(S_i\) the \(k\)-vector space spanned by all monomials of degree \(i\). In particular, \(S_0=k\). A polynomial \(u\) is said to be homogeneous if \(u \in S_i\) for some \(i\), and in this case we say that \(u\) has degree \(i\) and write \(\operatorname{deg}(u)=i\). Clearly we have a direct sum decomposition \(S=\oplus_{i \in \mathbb{N}}S_i\) of \(S\) as a group. Moreover \(S_iS_j \subseteq S_{i+j}\) holds then \((S_i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}}\) is a gradation of type \(\Delta=\mathbb{N}\) on \(S\). We say that \(S\) with this gradation is standard graded. The ideal generated by all polynomials of positive degree \((x_1,\dots,x_n)\) and it is called the irrelevant maximal ideal.

for instance, let \(A=k[x,y]\). In this case, \(A_0=k\), \(A_1\) is the \(k\)-vector-sapce of all linear forms, \(A_2\) is the space of all quadrics, etc. The polynomial \(x^3y^2-2xy^4\) is homogeneous as its terms all of degree \(5\). The polynomial \(x^3y^2-2xy^4+2y^3-10x^4\) is not.
The Laurant polynomial ring

if \(A\) is a ring; let \(R=A[X,X^{-1}]\) be the ring of Laurant polynomials with the indeterminate \(X\). An element of \(R\) is of the form \(\sum_{i\geq m}a_iX^i\) with \(m \in \mathbb{Z}\) and finitely many non-zero \(a_i\)’s. Clearly \((AX^i)_{i \in \mathbb{Z}}\) is a gradation of type \(\mathbb{Z}\) on \(A\).

Generally consider the ring \(R=A[(X_{i},X_{j}^{-1})_{i,j\in I}]\) spanned by \(\prod_{i \in I}{X_i^{d_i}},d_i\in \mathbb{Z}\) where \(d_i=0\) for all but finite \(i\) as \(A\)-module. Set \(A_i\) be the subspace \(A\prod_{i \in I}{X_i^{d_i}}\) spanned by one monomial. Clearly \(A_iA_j \subseteq A_{i+j}\). Thus,by example 4 before we can obtain the total gradation of type \(\mathbb{Z}\) from the multigradation of type \(\mathbb{Z}^{I}\); explicitly, the gradation is the submodule generated by \(A^{\prime}_d=\prod_{i \in I}{X_i^{d_i}}\) where \(\sum d_i=d\).

An ideal \(I\) in \(S\) is said to be homogeneous or graded if the relation \(f \in I\) implies all homogeneous components of \(f\) are in \(I\). However, we shall not restrict ourselves to polynomial rings. We shall study homogeneous ideals in general graded rings. - In \(k[x,y]\), the ideal \(I=(x^2+y^2)\) is homogeneous and \(J=(x+y^2)\) is not.








NoteLemma



Let \(A\) be a graded ring of type \(\mathbb{N}\), \((A_i)\) the gradation and \(J\) a proper ideal of \(A\). The following statements are equivalent:

\(J\) is homogeneous.
If \(f \in J\), then every homogeneous piece of \(f\) is in \(J\).
\(J=\oplus_{i \in \mathbb{N}}J_i\), where \(J_i=A_i \cap J\).
If \(J^\prime\) is the ideal generated by all homogeneous elements in \(J\), then \(J=J^\prime\).
\(J\) has a system of homogeneous generators, i.e. \(J=\sum_{\iota \in I}Aj_{\iota}\) where \(j_{\iota} \in A_{\iota}\).

In this case, the \(J_i\)’s are called the homogeneous component of the ideal \(J\).
Proof:

\((1)\iff(2)\) holds by definition.
clearly \(\oplus_{i \in \mathbb{N}}(A_i \cap J) \subseteq J\) holds; Suppose that \((2)\) holds, \(f \in J\) implies that \(f_i \in J\) where \(f_i \in A_i\) and thus \(f_i \in A_i \cap J\); \(f \in \oplus_{i \in \mathbb{N}}(A_i \cap J)\) as \(f=\sum f_i, f_i \in A_i \cap J\); therefore \(J \subseteq \oplus_{i \in \mathbb{N}}(A_i \cap J)\).
clearly \(J^\prime \subseteq J\); if \((3)\) holds, \(\forall j \in J\), \(j=\sum a_{\iota}j_{\iota}\) where \(j_{\iota} \in A_i \cap J\) is homogeneous, then \(j\in J^\prime\); thus \(J \subseteq J^\prime\).
Assume that \((4)\) holds, clearly \((5)\) holds.
Suppose that \((5)\) holds; if \(f \in J\), since \(J=\sum_{\iota \in I}Aj_{\iota}\) is a direct sum decomposition, \(f=\sum_{\iota \in I}a_{\iota}j_{\iota}\) where \(a_{\iota} \in A\) is zero for all but finitely many \(\iota\). Write \(a_{\iota}\) in the form of sum of homogeneous pieces: \(a_{\iota}=\sum_{n \in \mathbb{N}}a_{\iota_{n}},a_{\iota_{n}}\in A_n\); Using the technique of swapping the order of summation, we have \[
f=\sum_{\iota \in I}a_{\iota}j_{\iota}=\sum_{\iota \in I}(\sum_{n \in \mathbb{N}}a_{\iota_{n}})j_{\iota}
=\sum_{n \in \mathbb{N}}(\sum_{\iota \in I}j_{\iota}a_{\iota_{n}})
\] As \(\sum_{\iota \in I}j_{\iota}a_{\iota_{n}}\) is a homogeneous element, if \(f_j\) is one homogeneous component, \(f_j\) admits a form of \(\sum_{n^\prime}\sum_{\iota \in I}j_{\iota}a_{\iota_{n^\prime}}\) where \(n^\prime\)’s are the indexs such that \(\sum_{\iota \in I}j_{\iota}a_{\iota_{n}} \in A_j\); Therefore \(f_j \in J\).

title: Cauchy’s Theorem
text:
Theorem 1: Integral Lemma of GOURSAT
Let \(f\) be holomorphic in the domain \(D\). Then for the boundary of every triangle \(\Delta \subset D\) we have \[
\int_{\partial\Delta}fd\zeta=0.
\]


For the proof we require two elementary facts about perimeters of triangles:

\(\max_{w,z\in\Delta}|w-z|\leq L(\partial\Delta)\).
\(L( \partial \Delta ^{\prime }) = \frac 12L( \partial \Delta)\) for each of the four congruent subtriangles \(\Delta ^{\prime }\) arising from connecting the midpoints of the three sides of \(\Delta\).


Proof. We now prove the integral lemma. As a handy abbreviation we use \(a(\Delta):=\int_{\partial\Delta}fd\zeta.\) By connecting with straight line segments the midpoints of the sides of \(\Delta\) we divide \(\Delta\) into four congruent sub-triangles \(\Delta_\nu,1\leq\) \(\nu\leq4;\) and then \[
a(\Delta)=\sum_1^4\int_{\partial\Delta_\nu}fd\zeta=:\sum_1^4a(\Delta_\nu),
\] because the segments connecting the midpoints of the sides of \(\Delta\) are each traversed twice, in opposite directions (as one sees clearly in the right-hand figure above), causing the corresponding integrals to cancel each other (the reversal rule), while the union of the remaining sides of the \(\Delta_\nu\) is just \(\partial\Delta\).From among the four integrals \(a(\Delta_\nu)\) we select one with the largest absolute value and label the corresponding triangle \(\Delta^1\). Thus \[
|a(\Delta)|\leq4|a(\Delta^1)|.
\] Apply the same subdivision and selection process to \(\Delta^1\) to get a triangle \(\Delta^2\) for which \(|a(\Delta)|\leq4|a(\Delta^1)|\leq4^2|a(\Delta^2)|\). Continuation of this procedure generates a descending sequence \(\Delta^1\supset\Delta^2\supset\cdots\supset\Delta^n\supset\cdots\) of compact triangles satisfying \[
|a(\Delta)|\leq4^n|a(\Delta^n)|,\quad n=1,2,\ldots
\tag{1}\] From preliminary remark (2) follows moreover that \[
L(\partial\Delta^n)=\frac{1}{2^n}L(\partial\Delta)\:,\quad n=1,2,\ldots
\tag{2}\] The intersection \(\cap_1^\infty\Delta^\nu\) consists of precisely one point \(c\in\Delta\). Because \(f\) lies in \(\mathcal{O}(D)\),there is a function \(g\in \mathcal{C}(D)\) such that \[
f(\zeta)=f(c)+f'(c)(\zeta-c)+(\zeta-c)g(\zeta)\:,\quad\zeta\in D,
\] and \(g(c)=0\). Then from the equations (which are valid on trivial grounds or can be justified by the evident existence of primitives) \[
\int_{\partial\Delta^n}f(c)d\zeta=0\quad\text{~and~}\quad\int_{\partial\Delta^n}f^{\prime}(c)(\zeta-c)d\zeta=0\quad\text{ for all }n\geq1,
\] it follows that \[
a(\Delta^n)=\int_{\partial\Delta^n}(\zeta-c)g(\zeta)d\zeta,\quad n=1,2,\ldots
\] From the standard estimate for curvilinear integrals together with the first preliminary remark, we get the inequality \[
|a(\Delta^n)|\leq\max_{\zeta\in\partial\Delta^n}(|\zeta-c||g(\zeta)|)L(\partial\Delta^n)\leq L(\partial\Delta^n)^2|g|_{\partial\Delta^n}\:,\quad n=1,2,\ldots
\] From Equation 1 and Equation 2, it follows that \[
|a(\Delta)|\leq4^n|a(\Delta^n)|\leq L(\partial\Delta)^2|g|_{\partial\Delta^n},\quad n=1,2,\ldots
\] Because \(g( c) = 0\) and \(g\) is continuous at \(c\), for every \(\epsilon>0\), there is a \(\delta>0\) such that \(|g|_{B_{\delta}(c)}\leq\epsilon\). To this \(\delta\) corresponds an \(n_{0}\) such that \(\Delta^{n}\subset B_{\delta}(c)\) for all \(n\geq n_0\). Accordingly, \(|g|_{\partial\Delta^n}\leq\epsilon\) for \(n\geq n_0\), and so \[
|a(\Delta)|\leq L(\partial\Delta)^2\epsilon.
\] Since \(L(\partial \Delta)\) is a fixed number and arbitrarily positive values can be chosen for \(\epsilon\), \(a(\Delta)=0\).

It is frequently and correctly maintained that all of Cauchy’s theory of functions can be developed, by and large without any additional calculation, from Goursat’s integral lemma.

Theorem 2: The Cauchy Integral Theorem for star regions
Let \(G\) be a star region with center \(c\) and let \(f: G \rightarrow \mathbb{C}\) be holomorphic in \(G\). Then \(f\) is integrable in \(G\) and \(F(z)=\int_{[c,z]}f d \zeta, \quad z \in G\) is a primitive of \(f\) in \(G\). In particular, \[
\int_{\gamma}f d\zeta =0, \quad \text{for evey closed path } \gamma \subset G.
\]

title: Wonderings of Lee
text:
Theorem 1: Weierstrass’s Theorem
Suppose that the terms in the series \(\sum_1^\infty f_n\left(z\right)\) are single-valued functions analytic in a domain \(G\) and that this series converges uniformly in every closed circle 1 belonging to \(G\). Then

the sum \(f(z)\) of the series is analytic in this domain,；
the series can be differentiated termwise any number of times, i.e. \(\sum _1^{\infty}f_n^{(k)}(z) = f^{(k)}(z)\)；
all the series obtained as a result of such differentiation converge uniformly in every closed circle belonging to \(G\).
In what follows, for the sake of brevity we will call a series that converges in every circle belonging to a domain \(G\) uniformly convergent inside domain \(G\). Using the Heine-Borel theorem on coverings, we can easily prove that uniform convergence inside a domain \(G\) is equivalent to uniform convergence on every closed, bounded point set belonging to \(G\). Note that uniform convergence inside \(G\) does not require that the series be convergent in the entire domain \(G\). For instance,
For the theorem to be valid it is essential that its hypothesis be satisfed for a domain in the plane. More precisely, it is essential that for each point of \(G\) there exists a circle with its center at that point and lying inside \(G\). For instance, if we consider a series whose terms are the simplest analytic functions, polynomials \(P_n(z)\) that uniformly converge in a segment of the real axis (this segment constitutes a set of points for which the hypothesis is not satisfed), the sum of such a series may be not differentiable in the segment, even if it is, we may not be able to justify termwise differentiation of the series.* Therefore, Weierstrass’s theorem expresses a specific property of analytic functions of a complex variable.
[another example]: c.f. remark of Theorem 1
