Therefore, we can identify \(A\otimes_k B\) with a supspace of \(\mathcal{O}(\operatorname{Spec}A \times \operatorname{Spec} B)\) which clearly contains no nilpotents.



Proof. If \(X=\bigcup_{i=1}^{r} X_i\) and \(Y=\bigcup_{j=1}^{s}Y_j\) are affine open covers then \(X\times Y=\bigcup_{i,j}X_i\times Y_j\) is a finite open covering. It (b) is true, each \(X_i\times Y_j\) is affine and (a) follows.
Suppose that \(X=\operatorname{Spec} A\) and \(Y=\operatorname{Spec} B\). By the lemma above, \(\operatorname{Spec} (A\otimes_k B)\) makes sense and it’s affine. By definition of affine variety, for any space \(X\), it follows that \[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Mor}(X,\operatorname{Spec}(A\otimes_k B))&\cong \operatorname{Hom}_k(A\otimes_k B,\mathcal{O}(X))\\
&=\operatorname{Hom}_k(A,\mathcal{O}(X))\times \operatorname{Hom}_k(B,\mathcal{O}(X)) \\
&=\operatorname{Mor}(X,\operatorname{Spec}A)\times \operatorname{Mor}(X,\operatorname{Spec}B)\\
&=\operatorname{Mor}(X,\operatorname{Spec}A\times\operatorname{Spec}B)
\end{aligned}
\] Hence \(\operatorname{Spec}(A\otimes_k B)\cong \operatorname{Spec}A \times \operatorname{Spec} B\).

The moral is: one computes easily with tensor products of \(k\)-algebras to prove the relevant properties about products, but set-theoretic properties about products are easy geometrically.

Exercise 2
Prove that the products of quasi-affine varieties are quasi-affine.



Proof. W.L.O.G. suppose that \(U\subset X,V\subset Y\) are open subspaces of affines. Thus by proposition it follows that \(U\times V\subset X\times Y\) is also an open subspace of the product \(X\times Y\) which is affine.


Exercise 3
Show \(\mathbb{A}^n=\mathbb{A}^1\times\ldots\times \mathbb{A}^1\) (\(n\) times).



Proof. It follows that \[
\mathcal{O}(\mathbb{A}^n)=k[x_1,\dots,x_n]=k[x_1]\otimes_k\ldots\otimes k[x_n]=\mathcal{O}(\mathbb{A}^1)\otimes_k\ldots\otimes_k\mathcal{O}(\mathbb{A}^1).
\] And the result holds for \(\operatorname{Spec}(A\otimes_k B)=\operatorname{Spec}A\times \operatorname{Spec}B\).


Theorem 5
If \(X\) and \(Y\) are varieties then \(\dim(X\times Y)=\dim X+\dim Y\) and \(X\times Y\) is irreducible if \(X\) and \(Y\) are.




Lemma 6: geometric interpretation of noether’s normalisation lemma
Let \(X\) be an affine variety with \(\dim X=n\). Then there exists a finite surjective morphism \(X\twoheadrightarrow  \mathbb{A}^n\).



Proof. Let \(\mathcal{O}(X)=A\) which is a finitely generated \(k\)-algebra. By Noether’s normalisation lemma, there is a polynomial ring \(k[x_1,\dots,x_t]\hookrightarrow A\) such that \(A\) is a \(k[x_1,\dots,x_n]\)-algebra of finite type. It follows that there exists a finite and surjective morphism \(X\twoheadrightarrow \operatorname{Spec}(k[x_1,\dots,x_t])=\mathbb{A}^t\). By lemma, \(n=\dim X=\dim \mathbb{A}^t=t\).



Proof. Reduce to the case of two affines \(X,Y\). By lemma above, there are \(f:X\twoheadrightarrow \mathbb{A}^n\) and \(g:Y\twoheadrightarrow \mathbb{A}^m\). Hence, there is finite and surjective morphism \(X\times Y\twoheadrightarrow \mathbb{A}^n\times\mathbb{A}^m=\mathbb{A}^{n+m}\). (since \(\mathcal{O}(X)\otimes_k\mathcal{O}(Y)\hookleftarrow k[x_1,\dots,x_n]\otimes_k k[y_1,\dots,y_m]\) is a \(k[(x_i,y_j)]\)-module of finite type.) Consequently \(\dim (X\times Y)=n+m=\dim X+\dim Y\).
Assume that \(X\times Y\) is not irreducible. Then there exist closed subsets \(Z,W\subsetneq X\times Y\) such that \(Z\cup W=X\times Y\). Choose any element \(x\in X\) and then \(\{x\}\times Y\) is irreducible as \(Y\) is irreducible. Since \[
\{x\}\times Y=(Z\cap \{x\}\times Y)\cup (W\cap \{x\}\times Y)
\] it follows that for each \(x\) either \(\{x\}\times Y\subseteq Z\) or \(\{x\}\times Y\subseteq W\). Set \[
X_1=\{x\in X:\{x\}\times Y\subseteq Z\}; X_2=\{x\in X:\{x\}\times Y\subseteq W\}
\] write \[
X_1=\bigcap_{y\in Y}\{x:(x,y)\in Z\}; X_2=\bigcap_{y\in Y}\{x:(x,y)\in W\}.
\] As for each \(y\in Y\), \(X\times\{y\}\) is closed, the intersection \(\{x:(x,y)\in Z\}=X\times\{y\}\cap Z\) is closed. Consequently, \(X_1,X_2\) are closed subsets in \(X\). And \(X_1\cup X_2=X\). Since \(X\) is irreducible, either \(X_1\) or \(X_2\) is equal to \(X\). Hence \(X\times Y\) is equal to \(Z\) or \(W\), which contradicts the assumption that \(Z,W\) are proper subset.

title: G-ideals, Hilbert rings, and the Nullstellensatz
text:
A modern style: the first thing to do with a maximal ideal \(\mathfrak{m}\) in \(R[x]\) is to contract it back to the ideal \(\mathfrak{m} \cap R\) in \(R\) where \(R\) is more or less aebitrary commutative ring. When we do this we certainly get a prime ideal in \(R\), but we wish it were a maximal ideal. A close examination of the facts leads to the sequence of ideals: G-domain, G-ideal, and Hilbert ring.

Theorem 1
Let \(R\) be an integral domain with quotient field \(K\). The following two statements are equivalent:

\(K\) is a finitely generated \(R\)-algebra.
as a ring, \(K\) can be generated over \(R\) by one element.




Proof. Of course, (b) implies (a). For the converse, let \(K=R[\frac{a_1}{b_1}, \ldots, \frac{a_n}{b_n}]\) where \(a_i, b_i \in R\) and \(b_i \neq 0\). Then \(K=R[\frac{1}{b_1 \cdots b_n}]\).


Definition 1
An integral domain satisfying either (hence both) of the statements in Theorem 1 is called a G-domain.



Remark. The name honors Oscar Goldman.

The next two theorems are simple but useful. Note that any G-domain has an element \(u\) of the type occurring in Theorem 2; note also that as a corollary of Theorem 2, in a G-domain the intersection of all non-zero prime ideals is non-zero.

Theorem 2
Let \(R\) be an integral domain with quotient field \(K\). For a non-zero element \(u\in R\) the following three statements are equivalent:

Any non-zero prime ideal contains \(u\).
Any non-zero ideal contains a power of \(u\).
\(K=R[\frac{1}{u}]\).




Proof. 

implies (2): Let \(I\) be a non-zero ideal. If \(I\) contains no power of \(u\), then by lemma 1 \(I\) can be expanded to a prime ideal \(\mathfrak{p}\) disjoint from \(\{u^n\}\), a contradiction.
implied (3): Take any \(b\neq 0\) in \(R\). By (2) there is a power \(u^n\in (b)\), so that \(\frac{1}{b}=\frac{r}{u^n}\in R[\frac{1}{u}]\) for some \(r\in R\).
implies (1): Let \(\mathfrak{p}\) be a non-zero prime ideal. Then \(\mathfrak{p}\) contains a non-zero element \(a\). By (3) we have \(\frac{1}{a}=\frac{r}{u^n}\) for some \(r\in R\). It follows that \(u^n=ar\in \mathfrak{p}\), so that \(u\in \mathfrak{p}\).



Lemma 3
Let \(R\) be a G-domain with quotient field \(K\) and let \(T\) be a ring lying between \(R\) and \(K\). Then \(T\) is a G-domain.



Proof. If \(K=R[\frac{1}{u}]\), then \(K=T[\frac{1}{u}]\) all the more so.


Lemma 4
A unique factorization domain is a G-domain if and only if it has only a finite number of primes (up to units).



Proof. Let \(R\) be a UFD. Suppose that \(R\) is a G-domain then \(K=R[\frac{1}{u}]\) for some \(u\neq 0\). Write \(u=cp_1^{r_1}\ldots p_n^{r_n}\) where \(r\) is unit and \(p_i\)’s are primes. Hence if it has an infinite number of primes, we can pick a \(p\neq p_i\) such that \(\frac{1}{p_i}\neq \frac{a}{ru}\) for any \(a\in R\). The converse is clear.

To use the notion of a G-domain effectively, we need to know how it behaves under ring extensions. The next two theorems, together with exercise 1, give fairly complete information.

Theorem 5
If \(R\) is an integral domain and \(x\) is an indeterminate over \(R\), then \(R[x]\) is never a G-domain.



Proof. Let \(K\) be the quotient field of \(R\); if \(R[x]\) is a G-domain, so is \(K[x]\) since \(R[x]\subseteq K[x] \subseteq K(x)\). But \(K[x]\) is a principal ideal domain. So we will achieve our goal if we show that \(K[x]\) has an infinite number of primes. We can apply the Euclid’s trick. Suppose that \(p_1,\ldots,p_n\) are all the irreducible monic polynomials and form \(1+p_1\ldots p_n=q\). Then \(q\) is divisible by none of the \(p_i\)’s, a contradiction.


Theorem 6
Let \(R\subset T\) be integral domains and suppose that \(T\) is algebraic over \(R\) and finitely generated as a ring over \(R\). Then \(R\) is a G-domain if and only if \(T\) is a G-domain.



Proof. Let \(K\) and \(L\) be the quotient field of \(R\) and \(T\). Suppose first that \(R\) is a G-domain; say \(K=R[\frac{1}{u}]\) for some \(u\in R\). Then \(T[\frac{1}{u}]\) is a domain algebraic over \(R[\frac{1}{u}]=K\), hence is itself a field (by lemma 11), necessarily equal to \(L\). Thus \(L\) is a G-domain.
We assume that \(T\) is a G-domain, \(L=T[\cfrac{1}{v}]\) and \(T=R[w_1,\ldots,w_k]\). The elements \(\frac{1}{v},w_1,\ldots,w_k\) are algebraic over \(K\) and consequently satisfy equations with coefficients in \(R\) which lead off, say \[
\begin{aligned}
av^{-m}+\cdots & =0 \\
b_iw_i^{n_i}+\cdots & =0 \qquad (i=1,\cdots,k)
\end{aligned}
\] Adjoin \(a^{-1},b_1^{-1},\cdots,b_k^{-1}\) to \(R\), obtaining a ring \(R_1\) between \(R\) and \(K\). The field \(L\) is generated over \(R\) by \(w_1,\cdots,w_k,v^{-1}\). A fortiori these elements generate \(L\) over \(R_1\). Now over \(R_1\) we have arranged that \(w_1,\cdots,w_k,v^{-1}\) are integral. Hence \(L\) is integral over \(R_1\). By lemma 12, \(R_1\) is a field and necessarily equal to \(K\). So \(K\) is a finitely generated ring over \(R\) and \(R\) is a G-domain, as required.

For convenience we add a theorem, which is immediate from the theorems above.

Theorem 7
Let \(R\) be a domain, \(u\) an element of a larger domain. If \(R[u]\) is a G-domain, then \(u\) is algebraic over \(R\) and \(R\) is a G-domain.



Proof. Theorem 5 and 6 apply.

So far there has been no sign that G-domains have anything to do with maximal ideals in polynomial rings. The next theorem exhibits the connection.

Theorem 8
An integral domain \(R\) is a G-domain if and only if there exists in the polynomial ring \(R[x]\) an ideal \(\mathfrak{m}\) which is maximal and satisfies \(\mathfrak{m}\cap R=\{0\}\).



Proof. Suppose that \(R\) is a G-domain, say \(K=R[u^{-1}]\) where \(K\) is the quotient field of \(R\). We can map \(R[x]\) homomorphically into \(K\) by sending \(x\) into \(u^{-1}\). The image is all of \(K\) so the kernel \(\mathfrak{m}\) is maxiaml. Since the homomorphism is one-to-one on \(R\), we have \(\mathfrak{m}\cap R=\{0\}\).
Conversely, let \(\mathfrak{m}\) be maxiaml in \(R[x]\) and satisfy \(\mathfrak{m}\cap R=\{0\}\). Denote the image of \(x\) in the natural homomorphism \(R[x]\rightarrow R[x]/\mathfrak{m}\) by \(v\). Then \(R[v]\) is a field. By theorem 7, \(R\) is a G-domain.


Definition 2
A prime ideal \(\mathfrak{p}\) in a commutative ring \(R\) is a G-ideal if \(R/\mathfrak{p}\) is a G-domain.



Theorem 9: Krull’s Theorem
The nilradical \(N\) of any commutative ring \(R\) is the intersection of all prime ideals in \(R\).



Theorem 10: strengthened Krull’s theorem
The nilradical \(N\) of any commutative ring \(R\) is the intersection of all G-ideals in \(R\).



Proof. Clearly a nilpotent element lies in every prime ideal, hence every G-ideal. Conversely, suppose \(u\notin N\). We must construct a G-ideal excluding \(u\). The ideal \(\{0\}\) is disjoint from \(\{u^n\}\); We can expand it to an ideal \(\mathfrak{p}\) maxiaml w.r.t disjointness from \(\{u^n\}\). We know that \(\mathfrak{p}\) is prime (Lemma 1). We show that \(\mathfrak{p}\) is a G-ideal. In the domain \(\overline{R}=R/\mathfrak{p}\), let \(\overline{u}\) denote the image of \(u\). Suppose that \(\overline{\mathfrak{q}}\) is a non-zero prime ideal in \(\overline{R}\). Assume that \(\overline{u}\notin \mathfrak{q}\). Then \(u\notin \mathfrak{q}\) and hence \(\mathfrak{q}\) is in the exclusion of \(\{u^n\}\). As \(\mathfrak{q}\supseteq \mathfrak{p}\) and \(\mathfrak{p}\) is maximal, it follows that \(\mathfrak{p}=\mathfrak{q}\) and then \(\overline{\mathfrak{q}}=0\), a contradiction. Therefore, every non-zero prime ideal in \(\overline{R}\) contains \(\overline{u}\). By Theorem 2, \(\overline{R}\) is a G-domain, and \(\mathfrak{p}\) is a G-ideal.


Corollary 11
Let \(I\) be any ideal in a commutative ring \(R\). Then the radical of \(I\) is the intersection of all G-ideals containing \(I\).



Proof. Notice that \(\sqrt{I}/I\) is the nilradical of \(R/I\) and then apply the strengthened Krull’s theorem.

Let \(I\) be any ideal in a ring \(R\). We write \(\overline{R}\) for the quotient ring \(R/I\). In the polynomial ring \(R[x]\) there is a smallest extension \(I\,R[x]\) of \(I\). The quotient ring \(R[x]/I\, R[x]\) is in a natural way isomophic to \(\overline{R}[x]\). In treating many problems, we can in this way reduce to the case \(I=\{0\}\), and we shall often do so.

Theorem 12
An ideal \(I\) in a ring \(R\) is a G-ideal if and only if it is the contraction of a maximal ideal in the polynomial ring \(R[x]\).



Proof. Assume that there is a maxiaml ideal \(\mathfrak{m}\trianglelefteq\overline{R}[x]\) such that \(\mathfrak{m}\cap \overline{R}=\{0\}\). Denote by \(\pi\) the canonical homomorphism \(R\rightarrow \overline{R}\). It follows that \(\pi^{-1}(\mathfrak{m}\cap\overline{R})=\pi^{-1}(\{0\})=I\). Define \(R[x]\twoheadrightarrow \overline{R}[x]\) by \(\sum a_i x^i \mapsto \sum \overline{a_i}x^i\) and denote it by \(\pi^\prime\) which is clearly an extension of \(\pi\). Then \((\pi^\prime)^{-1} (\mathfrak{m}\cap \overline{R})=\pi^{-1}(\mathfrak{m}\cap \overline{R})\) as \(\pi^\prime \equiv \pi\) on \(R\). Thus \(I=\pi^{-1}(\mathfrak{m})\cap R\). Via the natural isomorphism \(R[x]/I\, R[x]\cong \overline{R}[x]\), it follows that \(\pi^{-1}(\mathfrak{m})\) is a maximal ideal in \(R[x]\).
Therefore it suffices to show the theroem when \(I=\{0\}\) and Theorem 8 applies.


Theorem 13
Let \(\mathfrak{m}\) be a maxiaml ideal in \(R[x]\) and suppose that the contraction \(\mathfrak{m}\cap R=\mathfrak{n}\) is maxiaml in \(R\). Then \(\mathfrak{m}\) can be generated by \(\mathfrak{n}\) and one more element \(f\). We can select \(f\) to be a monic polynomial which maps \(\mod{\mathfrak{n}}\) into an irreducible polynomial over the field \(R/\mathfrak{n}\).



Proof. Since \(\overline{R}[x]\cong R[x]/\mathfrak{n}R[x]\), \(\overline{\mathfrak{m}}=(\overline{f})\) for some irreducible \(\overline{f}\in (R/\mathfrak{n})[x]\). Apply \(\pi^{-1}\). It follows that \(\mathfrak{m}=(f,\mathfrak{n})\). (Indeed we can generate any maxiaml ideal containing \(\mathfrak{n}R[x]\) in this way.)


Corollary 14
Suppose, in addition to the hypothesis of Theorem above, that \(R/\mathfrak{n}\) is algebraically closed. Then \(\mathfrak{m}=(\mathfrak{n},x-a)\) for some \(a\in R\).


Any maximal ideal is a G-ideal. The nice class of rings is where the reverse holds.

Definition 3
A commutative ring \(R\) is a Hilbert ring if every G-ideal in \(R\) is maximal. (Krull’s designation was Iacobson ring, and Bourbaki has followed this terminology.)



Lemma 15
Any homomorphic image of a Hilbert ring is a Hilbert ring.



Proof. Let \(R\) be a Hilbert ring and let \(\pi:R\rightarrow S\) be a surjective homomorphism. Let \(\mathfrak{p}\) be a G-ideal in \(S\). Then \(\pi^{-1}(\mathfrak{p})\) is a G-ideal in \(R\) and hence maximal. It follows that \(\mathfrak{p}\) is maximal in \(S\).


Theorem 16
In a Hilbert ring the radical of any ideal is the intersection of maximal ideals containing it.



Theorem 17
A commutative ring \(R\) is a Hilbert ring if and only if the polynomial ring \(R[x]\) is a Hilbert ring.



Proof. If \(R[x]\) is a Hilbert ring, then the homomorphic image \(R\) is also a Hilbert ring.
Conversely, suppose that \(R\) is a Hilbert ring. Let \(\mathfrak{m}\) be a G-ideal in \(R[x]\). Let \(\mathfrak{p}=\mathfrak{m}\cap R\) which is a prime ideal. Denote by \(\overline{R}[x]\) \((R/\mathfrak{p})[x]\) and by \(\overline{m}\) the image of \(\mathfrak{m}\). It suffices to show that \(\overline{\mathfrak{m}}\) is maxiaml. Consider the canonical homomorphism \(\overline{R}[x]\twoheadrightarrow \overline{R}[x]/\overline{\mathfrak{m}}\) and let \(u\) be the image of \(x\). Then \(\overline{R}[u]\) is a G-domain. It follows that \(u\) is algebraic over \(\overline{R}\) and \(\overline{R}\) is a G-domain. Then \(\overline{R}\) is a field since the G-ideal \(\{0\}\) is maximal. But this makes \(\overline{R}[u]=\overline{R}[x]/\overline{\mathfrak{m}}\) a field, proving \(\overline{\mathfrak{m}}\) to be maxiaml.


Theorem 18
Let \(K\) be an algebraically closed field and let \(x_1,\dots,x_n\) be indeterminates over \(K\). Then any maximal ideal in \(K[x_1,\dots,x_n]\) is of the form \((x_1-a_1,\dots,x_n-a_n)\), \(a_i\in K\); i.e. it consists of all polynomials vanishing at a point.



Proof. Let \(R=K[x_1,\dots,x_{n-1}]\). \(R\) is a Hilbert ring by iterated use of Theorem 17 . We are given a mamixal ideal \(\mathfrak{m}\) in \(R[x_n]\). By Theorem 12, \(\mathfrak{n}=\mathfrak{m}\cap R\) is a G-ideal in \(R\), and hence maximal. We make an induction on \(n\), assuming that \(\mathfrak{n}=(x_1-a_1,\dots,x_{n-1}-a_{n-1})\). Therefore \(R/\mathfrak{n}\cong K\) is algebraically closed. By Corollary 14, \(\mathfrak{m}=(\mathfrak{n},x_n-a_n)\) for some \(a_n\in K\).


Theorem 19
Let \(K\) be an algebraically closed field and \(f,g_1,\dots,g_r\) in \(n\) variables with coefficients in \(K\). Assume that \(f\) vanishes at all common zeros of \(g_1,\dots,g_r\). The some power of \(f\) lies in the ideal \((g_1,\dots,g_r)\).



Proof. By the theorem above, our hypothesis says that \(f\) lies in the intersection of all maxiaml ideals containing \((g_1,\dots,g_r)\). Since \(K[x_1,\dots,x_r]\) is a Hilbert ring; Theorem 16 is applicable and shows that \(f\) is in the radical of \((g_1,\dots,g_r)\).

title: Technical Lemmas I
text:
We recall two important and useful technical lemmas.

Lemma 1: Fields and algebraic algebras
Let \(A\) be an algebra over a commutative field \(k\).

If \(A\) is a domain and algebraic over \(k\), then \(A\) is a field.
If \(A\) is a field and is contained in a finitely generated \(k\)-domain, then A is algebraic.




Corollary 2: Zariski Lemma
Let \(k\) be a commutative field and \(A\) is a finitely generated \(k\)-algebra which is also a field. Then \(A\) is a field extension over \(k\) of finite degree.



Lemma 3
Let \(k\) be a commutative field and \(A\) be a finitely generated \(k\)-algebra. For any prime ideal \(\mathfrak{p}\trianglelefteq A\) we have \(\mathfrak{p}=\bigcap_{\mathfrak{m}\supset \mathfrak{p},\mathfrak{m}\text{ maxiaml}}\mathfrak{m}\).



Proof. W.L.O.G we may suppose that \(A\) is a finitely generated \(k\)-domain and we only need show that \(\bigcap_{\mathfrak{m} \text{ maximal}} \mathfrak{m}=\{0\}\). Assume that \(0\neq f\in \bigcap \mathfrak{m}\). Set \(\mathfrak{m}=\mathfrak{n}\cap A\) where \(\mathfrak{n}\) is a maximal ideal of \(A_f\). Notice that \[
A/\mathfrak{n}\cap A\rightarrow A_f/\mathfrak{n}; \qquad a (\operatorname{mod}\,  {\mathfrak{n}\cap A}) \mapsto a(\operatorname{mod} \mathfrak{n})
\] is an injection.
By Zariski lemma, we know that \(A_f/\mathfrak{n}:=L\) is a finite extension of \(k\) and \(A/\mathfrak{n}\cap A\) is a f.g. \(k\)-subalgebra of \(L\); i.e. \(k\subset A/\mathfrak{n}\cap R \subset L\); \(A/\mathfrak{n}\cap A\) is thus a field and \(\mathfrak{m}\) is then a maximal ideal of \(A\) which does not contain \(f\); this is a contradiction and the proof completed.



Proof. Let \(A[X]\) be the polynomial ring with coefficients in \(A\). Clearly \(\bigcap_{\mathfrak{m}\in A[X]}\mathfrak{m}=\{0\}\) (use \(y\in \operatorname{Jab}(R)\iff \forall x\in R,\, 1-yx\, \in R^{\times}\)). Let \(\mathfrak{n}=\mathfrak{m}\cap A\). It suffices to show that \(\mathfrak{n}\) is maximal in \(A\). Notice that \[
A/\mathfrak{n}\hookrightarrow A[X]/\mathfrak{m}
\] is an injection. Then by Zariski lemma, it follows that \(A[X]/\mathfrak{m}\) is a field extension of finite degree over \(k\) and thus algebraic over \(k\). Therefore the subalgebra is also a field. This completes the proof.

It’s straightforward to generalize the above case where \(A\subset B,\, \mathfrak{m}\trianglelefteq B\) implies that \(\mathfrak{m}\cap A\) is maximal too.

Proposition 4: Preimages of maximal ideals
Let \(\varphi:A\rightarrow B\) be a homomorphism of algebras over a field \(k\), and let \(\mathfrak{m}\subset B\) be a maximal ideal. If \(B\) is finitely generated, then the preimage \(\varphi^{-1}(\mathfrak{m})\subset A\) is also a maximal ideal.


The simple example below shows that it’s necessary to require that \(B\) is finitely generated.

Example 1
A maximal ideal of \(k(x)\) is \(\{0\}\). But \(\{0\}\cap k[x]\) is not a maximal ideal in \(k[x]\subset k(x)\).



Lemma 5
Let \(k\) be an algebraically closed field and \(A=k[T_1,\dots,T_n]\). Then the maximal ideal of \(A\) admits the form \((T_1-a_1,\dots, T_n-a_n)\) where \(a_i\)’s are arbitrary elements of \(k\).



Proof. It follows that \(k[T_1,\dots,T_n]/\mathfrak{m}\cong k\) as \(k\) is algebraically closed. Then \(T_i(\operatorname{mod}\mathfrak{m})\simeq a_i\). Since \(a_i(\operatorname{mod}\mathfrak{m})\simeq a_i\) it follows that \(T_i\equiv a_i (\operatorname{mod} \mathfrak{m})\). Thus \((T_1-a_1,\dots,T_n-a_n)\subset \mathfrak{m}\) and then \(\mathfrak{m}=(T_1-a_1,\dots,T_n-a_n)\).

title: Differential Forms in Euclidean Space
text:
Warning



Here by differentiable functions we mean smooth functions in the most textbooks.
It’s quite important for beginners to make the convention: \((dx_i)_p \in  (\mathbb{R}^n_p)^*\) denotes the differential of the coordinate function \(x_i\) at the point \(p \in \mathbb{R}^n\) which is a linear mapping;
\(dx_i\) denotes the differential form of degree 1, as we shall define below.
\[
\begin{aligned}
dx_i:\mathbb{R}^n&\rightarrow\bigsqcup_{p\in \mathbb{R}^n} (\mathbb{R}^n_p)^*\\
p &\mapsto (dx_i)_p
\end{aligned}
\]





\(\mathbb{R}^{3}\) is defined to be the set of all real triples; the element of it is called point.
Let \(p\) be a point of \(\mathbb{R}^3\); The set of vectors which have origin at \(p\), i.e., \(\{q-p: q \in \mathbb{R}^3\}\), is called the tangent space of \(\mathbb{R}^3\) at \(p\) and will be denoted by \(\mathbb{R}_{p}^3\); Clearly it has the structure of \(\mathbb{R}\)-vector-sapce of which the canonical basis is denoted by \(\{e_1,e_2,e_3\}\) (with subtle abuse of notations, we will drop the subscript \(p\)).
A vector field in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) is a map \[
  v:\mathbb{R}^3 \rightarrow \bigsqcup_{p \in \mathbb{R}^3}{\mathbb{R}_{p}^3}
  \] which associates to each point \(p\) a vector \(v(p)\in \mathbb{R}_{p}^3\); Thus we can write \(v\) as \[
  v(p)=a_1(p)e_1+a_2(p)e_2+a_3(p)e_3
  \] thereby defining three functions \(a_i:\mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}\) that characterize the vector field \(v\).
We say that a vector field \(v\) is differentiable if the functions \(a_i\) which define it are differentiable.
To each tangent space \(\mathbb{R}_{p}^3\) we can associate its dual space \((\mathbb{R}_p^3)^{*}\); i.e. the set of all linear maps (also called linear forms) \(\varphi: \mathbb{R}_{p}^3 \to \mathbb{R}\).
The canonical dual basis of \((\mathbb{R}_p^3)^{*}\) is denoted by \(\{(dx_1)_p,(dx_2)_p,(dx_3)_p\}\); by definition of dual basis we have: \[
(dx_i)_p(e_j)=1 \text{ if } i=j; \ =0 \text{ if } i\neq j
\]

Indeed, \((dx_i)_p\)’s as dual basis defined above are the differentials of the coordinate functions \(x_i\)’s at the point \(p\).

clearly, \((df)_p \in (\mathbb{R}_p^3)^{*}\) for any \(f\) differentiable at \(p\).


Definition 1: A field of linear forms
A field of linear forms (also called exterior form of degree 1) in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) is a map \(\omega\) that associates to each point \(p\in \mathbb{R}^3\) an element \(\omega(p) \in (\mathbb{R}_p^3)^{*}\); \(\omega\) can be written as: \[
\omega(p)=a_1(p)(dx_1)_p+a_2(p)(dx_2)_p+a_3(p)(dx_3)_p
\] thus we may write \[
\omega=\sum_{i=1}^{3}a_idx_i
\] where \(a_i\) are real functions in \(\mathbb{R}^3\).
If the functions \(a_i\) are differentiable, \(\omega\) is called a differential form of degree \(1\).
As the convention we made at first, \(dx_i\) is the differential form of degree form of degree \(1\) which associates to each point \(p\) the differential of the \(i\)-th coordinate function; i.e. \((dx_i)_p\)


Note that field of linear forms and vector field are the same except for the codomain.




\(\wedge^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3}_{p})^*\)
\(\wedge^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3}_{p})^*\) is defined to be the set of maps \(\varphi: \mathbb{R}^3_p \times \mathbb{R}^3_p \rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) that are bilinear and alternate;i.e. \(\varphi(x_1,x_2)=-\varphi(x_2,x_1)\).
With the usual opeartions of functions the set \(\wedge^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3}_{p})^*\) becomes a vector space naturally.
Conversely, when two functions \(\varphi_1,\varphi_2 \in (\mathbb{R}^3_p)\) are given, we can obtain an element \(\varphi_1 \wedge \varphi_2 \in \wedge^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3}_{p})^*\) by setting: \[
  (\varphi_1 \wedge \varphi_2)(v_1,v_2)=\operatorname{det}(\varphi_i({v_j}))
  \]
The element \((dx_1)_p \wedge (dx_2)_p \in \wedge^{2}(\mathbb{R}^3_{p})^*\) will be denoted by \((dx_1 \wedge dx_2)_p\). It is easy to see that the set \(\{(dx_i \wedge dx_j)_p: 1 \leq i < j \leq 3\}\) is a basis for \(\wedge^2(\mathbb{R}^3_p)^*\); Furthermore we have \[
  (dx_i \wedge dx_j)_p=-(dx_i \wedge dx_j)_p, \ i \neq j; \ (dx_i \wedge dx_i)_p=0
  \]
Geometric Interpretation \[\
  (\omega_ \wedge \nu )(V_1,V_2)=\pm \operatorname{area}[(\omega(V_1),\nu(V_1)),(\omega(V_2),\nu(V_2))]
  \] where \(\omega,\nu \in (\mathbb{R}^3_p)^*\)


Definition 2: Field of bilinear alternating forms
A field of bilinear alternating forms or exterior form of degree of 2 in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) is a map \(\omega\) that associates to each \(p \in \mathbb{R}^3\) an element \(\omega(p) \in \wedge^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3}_{p})^*\); thus \(\omega\) admits the form: \[
\omega(p)=a_{12}(p)(dx_1 \wedge dx_2)_p + a_{13}(p)(dx_1 \wedge dx_3)_p +a_{23}(p)(dx_2 \wedge dx_3)_p
\] or \[
\omega=\sum_{i <j }a_{ij}dx_i \wedge dx_j \qquad  i,j=1,2,3
\] where \(a_{ij}\) are real functions in \(\mathbb{R}^3\). When the functions \(a_{ij}\) are differentiable, \(\omega\) is said to be a differential form of degree 2.

title: Differential Forms in Euclidean Space
text:
Substitution of Variables
One of the most important features of differential forms is the way they behave under differentiable maps.

Definition 5
Let \(f: \mathbb{R}^n \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^m\) be a differentiable map. Then \(f\) induces a map \(f^*\) that takes \(k\)-forms in \(\mathbb{R}^m\) into \(k\)-forms in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) and is defined as follow;let \(\omega\) be a \(k\)-form in \(\mathbb{R}^m\). By definition, \(f^*(\omega)\) is the \(k\)-form in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) given by \[
(f^*\omega)(p)(v_1,\dots,v_k)=\omega(f(p))(df_p(v_1),\dots,df_p(v_k))
\] Here \(p \in \mathbb{R}^n\), \(v_1,\dots,v_k\in \mathbb{R}^n_p\), and \(df_p: \mathbb{R}^n_p \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^m_{f(p)}\) is the differential of the map \(f\) at \(p\)
We set the convention that if \(g\) is a \(0\)-form, \[
f^*(g)=g\circ f
\]



Proposition 3
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^m\) be a differentiable map, \(\omega\) and \(\varphi\) be \(k\)-forms on \(\mathbb{R}^m\) and \(g:\mathbb{R}^m\rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) be a \(0\)-form on \(\mathbb{R}^m\). Then: 1. \(f^*(\omega+\varphi)=f^*\omega+f^*\varphi\) 2. \(f^*(g\omega)=f^*(g)f^*(\omega)\) 3. If \(\varphi_1,\dots,\varphi_k\) are \(1\)-forms in \(\mathbb{R}^m\), \(f^*(\varphi_1\wedge\dots\wedge\varphi_k)=f^*(\varphi_1)\wedge\dots\wedge f^*(\varphi_k)\).



Proof. 

\[
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
f^*(\omega+\varphi)(p)(-)&=(\omega+\varphi)(f(p))(df_p(-))
\\
&=\omega(f(p))(df_p(-))+\varphi(f(p))(df_p(-))
\\
&=f^*(\omega)(p)(-)+f^*(\varphi)(p)(-)
\end{split}
\end{equation}
\]
\[
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
f^*(g\omega)(p)(-)&=(g\omega)(f(p))(df_p(-))
\\
&=g(f(p)) \cdot \omega(f(p))(df_p(-))
\\
&=f^*(g)f^*(\omega)
\end{split}
\end{equation}
\]
\[
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
f^*(\varphi_1\wedge\varphi_2)(p)(v_1,v_2)&=(\varphi_1\wedge\varphi_2)(f(p))(df_p(v_1),df_p(v_2))
\\
&=\operatorname{det}(\varphi_i(df_p(v_j)))
\\
&=\operatorname{det}(f^*(\varphi_i)(p)(v_j))
\\
&=(f^*(\varphi_1)\wedge f^*(\varphi_2))(p)
\end{split}
\end{equation}
\]



We can now present the promised interpretation of \(f^*\). Let \((x_1,\dots,x_n)\) br coordinates in \(\mathbb{R}^n\), \((y_1,\dots,y_m)\) be coordinates in \(\mathbb{R}^m\) and let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^m\) be written as \[
y_1=f_1(x_1,\dots,x_n),\dots,y_m=f_m(x_1,\dots,x_n)  \quad \tag{$\star$}
\] Let \(\omega=\sum_{I}a_Idy_I\) be a \(k\)-form in \(\mathbb{R}^m\). By using the above properties of \(f^*\), we obtain: \[
f^*\omega=\sum_{I}f^*(a_I)(f^*dy_{i_1})\wedge\dots\wedge(f^*dy_{i_k})
\] Since \[
f^*(dy_i)(p)(v)=(dy_i)_{(f(p))}((df)_p(v))=((dy_i)_{(f(p))} \circ (df)_p)(v)=(d(y_i \circ f))_p(v)=({df_{i}})_{p}(v),
\] we have \[
f^*\omega=\sum_Ia_I(f_{1}(x_1,\dots,x_n),\dots,f_m(x_1,\dots,x_n))df_{i_1}\wedge\dots\wedge f_{i_k}
\] Thus to apply \(f^*\) to \(\omega\) is equivalent to ‘substitute’ in \(\omega\) the variables \(y_i\) and their differentials by the functions of \(x_k\) and \(dx_k\) obtained from \(\star\).

Remark 1
In various situations, it is convenient to use differential forms defined only on some open set \(U\subset \mathbb{R}^n\) and not on the entire \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
It is clear that everything done so far extends trivially to this situation.



Example 6: Polar coordinates
Let \(\omega\) be the \(1\)-form in \(\mathbb{R}^2-\{(0,0)\}\) by \[
\omega=-\frac{y}{x^2+y^2}dx+\frac{x}{x^2+y^2}dy
\] Let \(U\) be the set in the plane \((r,\theta)\) given by \[
U=\{r>0;0<\theta<2\pi\}
\] And let \(f:U \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^2\) be the map: \[
f(r,\theta)=
\begin{cases}
x=r\cos \theta \\
y=r\sin \theta
\end{cases}
\] Let us compute \(f^*\omega\). Since \[
\begin{aligned}
&dx=d(r\cos \theta)=\cos\theta dr-r\sin \theta d\theta \\
&dy=d(r \sin \theta)=\sin \theta dr+r\cos \theta d\theta
\end{aligned}
\] Doing substitution and we obtain \[
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
&f^*(-\frac{y}{x^2+y^2}dx+\frac{x}{x^2+y^2}dy) \\
=&-\frac{r\sin \theta}{r^2}(\cos \theta dr-r\sin\theta d\theta)+\frac{r\cos\theta}{r^2}(\sin\theta dr+r\cos \theta d\theta)\\
=&d\theta
\end{split}
\end{equation}
\]


Notice that the addition of differential forms commutes with the substitution of variables; We will now show that the same holds for the exterior product.

Proposition 4
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^m\) be a differentiable map. Then - \(f^*(\omega \wedge \varphi)=(f^*\omega)\wedge(f^*\varphi)\), where \(\omega\) and \(\varphi\) any two forms in \(\mathbb{R}^m\). - \((f\circ g)^*\omega=g^*(f^*\omega)\), where \(g:\mathbb{R}^p \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^n\) is a differentiable map.



Proof. The proof are straightforward.

title: Differential Forms in Euclidean Space
text:
Exterior Differential
We are now going to define an operation on differential form that generalizes the differentiation of functions. Let \(g:\mathbb{R}^n \rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) be a \(0\)-form (i.e. a differentiable function). Then the differential: \[
dg=\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{\partial g}{\partial x_i}dx_i
\] is a \(1\)-form. We want to generalize this process by defining an operation that takes \(k\)-forms into \((k+1)\)-forms.

Definition 7
Let \(\omega=\sum_{I}a_Idx_I\) be a \(k\)-form in \(\mathbb{R}^n\). The exterior differential \(d\omega\) of \(\omega\) is defined by \[
d\omega=\sum_Ida_I\wedge dx_I
\]



Example 8
Let \(\omega=xyzdx+yzdy+(x+z)dz\) and let us compute \(d\omega\): \[
\begin{aligned}
d\omega&=d(xyz)\wedge dx+d(yz) \wedge dy +d(x+z)\wedge dz \\
&=(yzdx+xzdy+xydz)\wedge dx+(ydz+zdy)\wedge dy+(dx+dz)\wedge dz \\
&=-xzdx\wedge dy+(1-xy)dx\wedge dz-ydy\wedge dz
\end{aligned}
\]


We now present some properties of exterior differentiation. (3) is probably the most important one and (4) means that the operation \(d\) commmutes with substitution of variables.

Proposition 5

\(d(\omega_1+\omega_2)=d\omega_1+d\omega_2\), where \(\omega_1,\omega_2\) are \(k\)-forms
\(d(\omega\wedge\varphi)=d\omega\wedge\varphi+(-1)^k\omega\wedge d\varphi\), where \(\omega\) is a \(k\)-form and \(\varphi\) is an \(s\)-form
\(d(d\omega)=d^2\omega=0\)
\(d(f^*\omega)=f^*(d\omega)\), where \(\omega\) is a \(k\)-form in \(\mathbb{R}^m\) and \(f:\mathbb{R}^n \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^m\) is a differentiable map.




Proof. 

Let \(\omega=\sum_Ia_Idx_I\) and \(\varphi=\sum_Jb_Jdx_J\); then \(\omega \wedge \varphi=\sum_{IJ}a_Ib_Jdx_I\wedge dx_J\); thus \[
\begin{aligned}
d(\sum_{IJ}a_Ib_Jdx_I\wedge dx_J)&=\sum_{IJ}d(a_Ib_J)\wedge dx_I \wedge dx_J \\
&=\sum_{IJ}a_Idb_J\wedge dx_I \wedge dx_J +\sum_{IJ}b_Jda_I\wedge dx_I\wedge dx_J \\
&=(-1)^k\omega\wedge d\varphi+d\omega\wedge\varphi
\end{aligned}
\]
Let us first assume that \(\omega\) is a \(0\)-form, i.e., \(\omega\) is a function \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) that associates to each \((x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in\mathbb{R}^n\) the value \(f(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\). Then

\[
\begin{aligned}
d(df)
&=d\left(\sum_{j=1}^n\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_j}\,dx_j\right)\\
&=\sum_{j=1}^n d\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_j}\right)\wedge dx_j\\
&=\sum_{j=1}^n\left(\sum_{i=1}^n
\frac{\partial^2f}{\partial x_i\partial x_j}\,dx_i\right)\wedge dx_j.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since
\[
\frac{\partial^2f}{\partial x_i\partial x_j}
=
\frac{\partial^2f}{\partial x_j\partial x_i}
\]
and
\[
dx_i\wedge dx_j=-dx_j\wedge dx_i,\qquad i\neq j,
\]
we obtain that
\[
d(df)
=
\sum_{i<j}
\left(
\frac{\partial^2f}{\partial x_i\partial x_j}
-
\frac{\partial^2f}{\partial x_j\partial x_i}
\right)
dx_i\wedge dx_j
=0.
\]
Now let
\[
\omega=\sum_i a_i\,dx_i.
\]
By 1, we can restrict ourselves to the case \(\omega=a_1dx_1\) with \(a_1\neq0\). By 2, we have that
\[
d\omega
=
da_1\wedge dx_1+a_1d(dx_1).
\]
But
\[
d(dx_1)=d(1)\wedge dx_1=0.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\begin{aligned}
d(d\omega)
&=d(da_1\wedge dx_1)\\
&=d(da_1)\wedge dx_1+da_1\wedge d(dx_1)\\
&=0,
\end{aligned}
\]
since \(d(da_1)=0\) and \(d(dx_1)=0\), which proves 3.

We will first prove the result for a \(0\)-form. Let \(g:\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}\) be a differentiable function that associates to each \((y_1,\ldots,y_m)\) the value \(g(y_1,\ldots,y_m)\). Then

\[
\begin{aligned}
f^*(dg)
&=f^*\left(\sum_i\frac{\partial g}{\partial y_i}\,dy_i\right)\\
&=\sum_{ij}\frac{\partial g}{\partial y_i}
\frac{\partial f_i}{\partial x_j}\,dx_j\\
&=\sum_j\frac{\partial(g\circ f)}{\partial x_j}\,dx_j\\
&=d(g\circ f)
=d(f^*g).
\end{aligned}
\]
Now, let
\[
\varphi=\sum_i a_i\,dx_I
\]
be a \(k\)-form. By using the above, and the fact that \(f^*\) commutes with the exterior product, we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
d(f^*\varphi)
&=d\left(\sum_i f^*(a_i)f^*(dx_I)\right)\\
&=\sum_i d(f^*(a_i))\wedge f^*(dx_I)\\
&=\sum_i f^*(da_i)\wedge f^*(dx_I)\\
&=f^*\left(\sum_i da_i\wedge dx_I\right)\\
&=f^*(d\varphi),
\end{aligned}
\]
which proves 4.

title: Line Integrals
text:
Differential forms are to be integrated. We will do that soon after some preliminaries on the natural ‘habitat’ of differential forms. However, the special case of integration of forms of degree one along curves (the so called line integral) is so simple that it can be treated independently of the general theory. We will do that in this chapter.
Let \(\omega=\sum a_id\omega_i\) be a differential form of degree one defined in an open set \(U\subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\) and let \(c:[a,b]\rightarrow U\) be a piecewise differentiable curve in \(U\); we recall that \(c\) is piecewise differentiable if \(c\) is continuous and there exists a partition \(a=t_0,t_1,\dots,t_k,t_{k+1}=b\) of \([a,b]\) such that the restriction \(c\restriction_{[t_j,t_{j+1}]}=c_j\) is differentiable, \(j=0,1,\dots,k\).

title: Differentiable Manifolds
text:
Definition 1
An \(n\)-dimensional differentiable manifold is a set \(M\) together with a family of injective maps \(f_{\alpha}:U_{\alpha}\rightarrow M\) of open sets \(U_{\alpha}\subset \mathbf{R}^n\) into \(M\) such that:

\(\bigcup_{\alpha}f_{\alpha}(U_{\alpha})=M\).
For each pair \(\alpha,\beta\), with \(f_{\alpha}(U_\alpha)\cap f_\beta(U_\beta)=W\neq \emptyset\), the sets \(f_\alpha^{-1}(W)\) and \(f_\beta^{-1}(W)\) are open sets in \(\mathbf{R}^n\) and the maps \(f^{-1}_\beta\circ f_\alpha,f^{-1}_\alpha\circ f_\beta\) are differentiable.
The family \(\{(U_\alpha,f_\alpha)\}\) is maximal relative to conditions 1,2.

A family \(\{(U_\alpha,f_\alpha)\}=\mathcal{A}\) satisfying the conditions 1 and 2 is called a differentiable structure (or atlas) on \(M\). A pair \((U_\alpha,f_\alpha)\in\mathcal{A}\) with \(p\in f_\alpha(U_\alpha)\) is called a parametrization (or coordinate system,or chart) of \(M\) at \(p\); \(f_\alpha(U_\alpha)\) is called a coordinate neighbourhood of \(p\).


Condition 3 is a technical condition. Actually we can always extend a differentiable structure into a maximal one, by adjoining to the given structure all parametrizations that together with some parametrization of the given structure satisfy condition 2.

Lemma 1
If \(\mathcal{A}=\{(U_\alpha,h_\alpha)\}\) is a differentiable structure on \(M\), then \(\mathcal{A}\) is contained in a unique maximal differentiable structure on \(M\).



Proof. Let \(\mathcal{A}^\prime\) be the following set; \[
\mathcal{A}^\prime=\{(V,g):\mathcal{A}\cup(V,g)\text{ is a differentiable structure}\}
\] We check that \(\mathcal{A}^\prime\) is a differentiable structure on \(M\) and then it’s clearly the unique maxiaml atlas containing \(\mathcal{A}\).
Let \((U,f),(V,g)\) be any two charts in \(\mathcal{A}\) with \(f(U)\cap g(V)=W\neq \emptyset\). We wish to show that \(g^{-1}\circ f:f^{-1}(W)\rightarrow \mathbf{R}^n\) and \(f^{-1}\circ g\) are differentiable.
Clearly we have \(W=\bigcup_{\alpha}h_{\alpha}(U_\alpha)\cap W=\bigcup_{\alpha}W_\alpha\) and thus \(f^{-1}(W)=\bigcup_\alpha f^{-1}(W_\alpha)\); Since \(F_\alpha=f(U)\cap h_\alpha(U_\alpha)\supset W_\alpha\), \(f^{-1}(F_\alpha)\supset f^{-1}(W_\alpha)\); then \(h_{\alpha}^{-1}\circ f\) is differentiable on \(f^{-1}(W_\alpha)\); Since \(G_\alpha=g(V)\cap h_\alpha(U_\alpha)\supset W_\alpha\), \(g^{-1}\circ h_\alpha\) is differentiable on \(h_{\alpha}(W_\alpha)\). Thus \(g^{-1}\circ f=g^{-1}\circ h_{\alpha}\circ h_{\alpha}^{-1}\circ f\) is differentiable on \(f^{-1}(W)\); this completes the proof.


Remark. 

A differentiable structure on a set \(M\) induces in a natural way a topology in \(M\). It suffices to define that \(A\subset M\) is an open set if \(f_{\alpha}^{-1}(A\cap f_{\alpha}(U_{\alpha}))\) is an open set in \(\mathbf{R}^n\), for all \(\alpha\). It is easily checked that this defines a topology in \(M\) in which the sets \(f_{\alpha}(U_{\alpha})\) are open and the maps \(f_\alpha\) are continuos.
The natural topology defined above can be very strange. In particular, it can happen that one (or both) of the following axioms do not hold:

Axiom of Hausdorff: Give two distinct points of \(M\) there exist neighbourhoods of these points that do not intersect.
Axiom of countable basis: \(M\) can be covered by a countable number of coordinate neighbourhoods (we say then that \(M\) has a countable basis)

Axiom 1 is essential to prove that the limit of a convering sequence is unique, and axiom 2 is essential for the existence of a partition of unity.
We shall assume, from now on, that all the manifolds to be considered are Hausdorff and have a countable basis.


After defining the natural topology on the manifold, we have the equivalent charaterization of differentiable structure:

Given a (Hausdorff, second-countable) topological space \(M\), we say \(\mathcal{A}=\{(U_\alpha,f_\alpha)\}\) is a differentiable structure on \(M\) or atlas if each \(U_\alpha\subset \mathbf{R}^n\) is open and each map \(f_\alpha:U_\alpha\rightarrow M\) is a homeomorphism and \(f_\alpha^{-1}\circ f_\beta:f^{-1}_\beta(W)\rightarrow\mathbf{R}^n\) where \(W=f_\alpha(U_\alpha)\cap f_\beta(U_\beta)\) is differentiable for each pair of \((\alpha,\beta)\) (this is automatically satisfied when \(f_\alpha(U_\alpha)\cap f_\beta(U_\beta)=\emptyset\)).

Again we can extend any differentiable structure into a maximal one.

Example 2
The simplest example of a differentiable structure consists of \(\mathbf{R}^n\) with an atlas \(\mathcal{A}\) of only one pair, \((\mathbf{R}^n,\operatorname{id})\). We can easily make the atlas bigger;We can adjoin \((U,f)\) if \(U\xrightarrow{f}V\) are homeomorphic with \(f,f^{-1}\) are differentiable. Indeed we can adjoin as many such \(f\)’s as we like (proof).


When \(n=1\), we consider the two structures on \(\mathbf{R}\): \((R,\mathcal{U})\) where \(\mathcal{U}\) is the maximal atlas containing \(\operatorname{id}\) and \((\mathbf{R},\mathcal{V})\) where \(\mathcal{V}\) is the maximal atlas containing the homeomorphism \(x\mapsto x^{3}\), which is not differentiable, together with all charts differentiable-related to it. Although \((R,\mathcal{U})\) and \((\mathbf{R},\mathcal{V})\) are not the same, there is a one-to-one and onto function \(f:\mathbf{R}\rightarrow \mathbf{R}\) such that \[
x\in\mathcal{U} \text{  if and only if  } f\circ x\in\mathcal{V}
\] namely, the obvious function \(f(x)=x^{3}\). Thus \((R,\mathcal{U})\) and \((\mathbf{R},\mathcal{V})\) are the sort of structures one would want to call ‘isomorphic’. The term actually used is diffeomorphic:

Definition 3: diffeomorphism
Two differentiable manifolds \((M,\mathcal{A})\) and \((N,\mathcal{B})\) are diffeomorphic if there is one to one and onto map \(f:M\rightarrow N\) such that \[
x\in \mathcal{A} \text{ if and only if } f\circ x \in \mathcal{B}
\] The map \(f\) is called a diffeomorphism and clearly \(f^{-1}\) is a diffeomorphism also.


The another definition of diffeomorphism based on the definition of differentiable map between manifolds is given in the next section.
Less trivial examples are the following ones.

Example 4: The real projective plane \(P^2(\mathbf{R})\)
We will denote by \(P^2(\mathbf{R})\) the all lines in \(\mathbf{R}^3\) that pass through the origin \((0,0,0)\) of \(\mathbf{R}^3\), i.e., \(P^2(\mathbf{R})\) is the set of all ‘directions’ in \(\mathbf{R}^3\).
We want to introduce a differentiable structure in \(P^2(\mathbf{R})\). For that, let \((x,y,z)\in \mathbf{R}^3\), and notice that \(P^2(\mathbf{R})\) is the quotient space of \(\mathbf{R}^3-\{(0,0,0)\}\) by the equivalence relation \(\sim\): \[
(x,y,z)\sim(\lambda x,\lambda y,\lambda z),\qquad \lambda\in\mathbf{R},\quad \lambda\neq0
\] The points of \(P^2(\mathbf{R})\) will be denoted by \([x,y,z]\).
We now define sets \(V_1,V_2,V_3\) in \(P^2(\mathbf{R})\) by: \[
\begin{aligned}
&V_1=\{[x,y,z]:x\neq0\}\\
&V_2=\{[x,y,z]:y\neq0\}\\
&V_3=\{[x,y,z]:z\neq0\}
\end{aligned}
\] and maps \(f_i:\mathbf{R}^2\rightarrow V_i,\,i=1,2,3\) by \[
f_1(u,v)=[1,u,v],\quad
f_2(u,v)=[u,1,v],\quad
f_3(u,v)=[u,v,1]
\] where \((u,v)\in \mathbf{R}^2\).
Geometrically \(V_2\), for instance, is the set of all lines that pass through origin and do not belong to the plane \(xOz\). We claim that the family \(\{(\mathbf{R}^2,f_i)\}\) is a differentiable structure for \(P^2(\mathbf{R})\).
Actually we need only show that \(f_i^{-1}(V_i\cap V_i)\) is open in \(\mathbf{R}^2\) and \(f_j^{-1}\circ f_i\) is differentiable. Let us consider the case \(i=1,j=2\); the other cases are entirely analogous.
The points of \(f_1^{-1}(V_1\cap V_2)\) are of the form \((u,v)\) with \(u\neq0\); thus the set \(f_1^{-1}(V_1\cap V_2)\) is open in \(\mathbf{R}^2\) and \[
f_2^{-1}\circ f_1(u,v)=f_2^{-1}([1,u,v])=f_2^{-1}([1/u,1,v/u])=(1/u,v/u)
\] is differentiable, as we claimed.






Example 5: The Klein bottle
The Klein bottle is the subset of \(\mathbf{R}^4\) defined as follows (its projection in \(\mathbf{R}^3\) is given in the video above); let \(Ox,Oy,Oz,Ow\) be the four coordinate axis in \(\mathbf{R}^4\). Let \(S\) be a circ with radius \(r\), contained in the plane \(xOz\), with center \(C\) in the axix \(Ox\) so that \(C\) is at a distance \(a>r\) from 0. The Klein bottle is generated by rotating this circ around \(Oz\) in such a way that when the center \(C\) has described a rotation of an angle \(u\) in the plane \(xOz\), the plane of \(S\) has described a rotation of an angle \(u\) around \(Oc\) in the \(3\)-space \(OCOzOw\) (this is possible because we are in \(\mathbf{R}^4\) but the projection of the moving circle in \(\mathbf{R}^3\) is twisted into a line where the intersection happens when \(u=\pi\)).
Let \(u\) and \(v\) be as in video, then we can describe the surface as: \[
\begin{aligned}
&F(u,v)=(x,y,z,w)\qquad 0\leq u<2\pi ,0\leq v<2\pi \\
&x(u,v)=(r\cos v+a)\cos u \\
&y(u,v)=(r\cos v+a)\sin u \\
&z(u,v)=r\sin v \cos \frac{u}{2}\\
&w(u,v)=r\sin v\sin \frac{u}{2}
\end{aligned}
\] via simple calculus we know that circ \(S\) keeps its shape of a circle in \(\mathbf{R}^4\);however, when projected into \(\mathbf{R}^3\), the shape is broken and the surface even has self-intersection; to see that we notice that when \(u=\pi\) , \(\operatorname{proj}\circ F(\pi,2\pi-v)=\operatorname{proj}\circ F(\pi,v)=(-(r\cos v+a),0,0)\) and circle is twisted into the line \([-a-r,-a+r]\).


Let’s show that the Klein bottle is indeed a differentiable manifold.

Proof. Let \(U_1=\{(u,v)\in\mathbf{R}^2:0<u<2\pi,0<v<2\pi\}\) and define a map \(f_1=U_1 \rightarrow \mathbf{R}^4\) by \[
f_1(u,v)=
\begin{cases}
&x= (r\cos v+a)\cos u \\
&y=(r\cos v+a)\sin u \\
&z=r\sin v \cos \frac{u}{2}\\
&w=r\sin v\sin \frac{u}{2}
\end{cases}
\] It’s clear that \(f_1(U_1)\) contains the points of the Klein bottle that are not on the circs \(u=0\) and \(v=0\). We claim that \(f_1\) is injective.
To this end, let us first assume that \(z\neq 0\). Then both \(\sin v\) and \(\cos \frac{u}{2}\) are nonzero. Since \(0<u/2<\pi\), the expression \(\frac{w}{z}=\tan \frac{u}{2}\) determines \(u\). By knowing \(u\), we can use that \[
\sin v=\frac{w}{r\sin \frac{u}{2}},\quad \cos v=\frac{\frac{y}{\sin u}-a}{r}
\] to determine \(v\). If \(z=0\), then \(v=\pi\) or \(u=\pi\), and the injectivity is easily checked.
It can be shown that if we we change the origin of \(u\) and the origin of \(v\), we can cover the whole Klein bottle by the images of maps similar to the above. For instance, if we define a map \(f_2:U_2\rightarrow \mathbf{R}^4\) given by \[
f_2=
\begin{cases}
&x=-(r\cos v^\prime+a)\sin u^\prime \\
&y=(r\cos v^\prime+a)\cos u^\prime \\
&z=r\sin v^\prime \cos (\frac{u^\prime}{2}+\frac{\pi}{4})\\
&w=r\sin v^\prime\sin (\frac{u^\prime}{2}+\frac{\pi}{4})\\
\end{cases}
\qquad 0<u^\prime,v^\prime<2\pi
\] Geometrically this means that we measure \(u^\prime\) from \(Oy\); we see that \(f_2(U_2)\) induces the points of the Klein bottle with \(u=0\) and that \(f_2\) is injective. Notice that \(f_1(U_1)\cap f_2(U_2)=W\) is not connected but has two connected components: \[
W_1=\{f_1(u,v):\frac{\pi}{2}<u<2\pi,0<v<2\pi\},\, W_2=\{f_1(u,v):0<u<\frac{\pi}{2},0<v<2\pi\}
\] The change of coordinates is given by: \[
\begin{aligned}
&f_2^{-1}\circ f_1\,(u,v)=
\begin{cases}
&u^\prime=u-\frac{\pi}{2}\\
&v^\prime=v
\end{cases}\qquad \text{in } f^{-1}(W_1) \\
&f_2^{-1}\circ f_1(u,v)=
\begin{cases}
&u^\prime=u+\frac{3\pi}{2} \\
&v^\prime=2\pi-v
\end{cases}\qquad \text{in } f^{-1}(W_2)
\end{aligned}
\] which is clearly differentiable;
In a similar way, we can find an injective map \(f_3:U_3\rightarrow \mathbf{R}^4\) which induces the points with \(v=0\); for instance: \[
f_3=
\begin{cases}
&x=(-r\sin v^{\prime\prime}+a)\cos u^{\prime\prime} \\
&y=(-r\sin v^{\prime\prime}+a)\sin u^{\prime\prime} \\
&z=r\cos v^{\prime\prime} \cos \frac{u^{\prime\prime}}{2}\\
&w=r\cos v^{\prime\prime} \sin \frac{u^{\prime\prime}}{2}\\
\end{cases}
\qquad 0<u^{\prime\prime},v^{\prime\prime}<2\pi
\].
It is also not difficult to check that the changes of coordinates are differentiable and this shows that \(\{(U_i,f_i)\}\) is a differentiable structure on the Klein bottle.





Remark. The Klein bottle (projected in \(\mathbf{R}^3\)) can be thought of as a twisted torus in the following sense (like the video above): The torus is obtained from a rectangle by identifying the opposite sides. In the Klein bottle, one of the sides is reflected across its center before performing the identification. Indeed the model in this case is another projection of Klein bottle (after a differentiable homeomorphism) which looks more like a real bottle. And it’s not a regular surface in \(\mathbf{R}^3\) for it has obvious self-intersections on this model.

Next we show a non-example which is even not a topological manifold.

Example 6: Double-cone
We consider \(M:=\{(y^1,y^2,y^3)\in\mathbf{R}^3:(y^1)^2=(y^2)^2+(y^3)^2\}\), the double cone.
Since \(M\subset \mathbf{R}^3\), it’s clearly Hausdorff and has a countable basis.
But \(M\) is not a \(2\)-dimensional manifold. If it were, then there would exist an open subset \(U\subset M\) with \(0\in U\), an open subset \(V\subset \mathbf{R}^2\) and a homeomorphism \(x:U\rightarrow V\) with \(x(0)=0\).
Wlog, assume that \(V=B_r(x(0))\) with \(r>0\). Choose \(q_1,q_2\in U\) with \(q_1^1>0\) and \(q_2^1<0\). Furthermore choose a continuous path \(c:[0,1]\rightarrow V\) with \[
c(0)=x(q_1),c(1)=x(q_2) \text{ and } c(t)\neq x(0) \text{ for all } t\in[0,1]
\]
Define the continuos path \(\tilde{c}:=x^{-1}\circ c:[0,1]\rightarrow U\). Then \[
\tilde{c}(0)=q_1,\tilde{c}(1)=q_2
\] that is, we have \(\tilde{c}^1(0)>0\) while \(\tilde{c}^1(1)<0\). Applying the mean value theorem we find, that there exists a \(t\in (0,1)\) with \(\tilde{c}^1(t)=0\). Then by the definition of \(M\), \(\tilde{c}(t)=(0,0,0)\) and consequently \(c(t)=x(\tilde{c}(t))=x(0)\), which contradicts the choice of \(c\). Hence, \(M\) is not a \(2\)-dimensional topological manifold.

title: Tangent vector as an equivelence class of curves
text:
Here we introduce an alternative definition of tangent vectors to differentiable manifold, which differs from the one in the textbook.

Definition 1
Let \(M\) be a differentiable manifold and \(p\in M\).
A tangent vector on \(M\) at the point \(p\) is an equivalence class of differentiable curves \(c:(-\epsilon,+\epsilon)\rightarrow M\) with \(\epsilon > 0\) and \(c(0)=p\), where two such curves \(c_1\) and \(c_2\) are called equivalent, if for a chart \(x:U\rightarrow V\) where \(p\) is coordinate neighborhood of \(p\) we have \[
\frac{d}{dt} (x^{-1}\circ c_1)\restriction_{t=0}=\frac{d}{dt}(x^{-1}\circ c_2)\restriction_{t=0}
\]



Remark. This definition does not depend on the choice of the chart \(x:U\rightarrow V\). Namely, if \(y:\tilde{U}\rightarrow\tilde{V}\) is another coordinate map of \(p\) then we get by the chain rule: \[
\frac{d}{dt}(y^{-1}\circ c)\restriction_{t=0}=\frac{d}{dt}\big((y^{-1}\circ x)\circ (x^{-1}\circ c)\big)\restriction_{t=0}=\big(d(y^{-1}\circ x)\big)_{x^{-1}(p)}\circ (\frac{d}{dt}(x^{-1}\circ c)\restriction_{t=0})\, .
\] Therefore the condition \[
\frac{d}{dt}(x^{-1}\circ c_1)\restriction_{t=0}=\frac{d}{dt}(x^{-1}\circ c_2)\restriction_{t=0}
\] is equivalent to the condition \[
\frac{d}{dt}(y^{-1}\circ c_1)\restriction_{t=0}=\frac{d}{dt}(y^{-1}\circ c_2)\restriction_{t=0}\, .
\]


Notation 1
We denote the equivalence class of \(c\) by \(\dot c(0)\).



Definition 2
The set \[
T_pM:=\{\dot c(0)\vert \, c:(-\epsilon,+\epsilon)\rightarrow M \text{ differentiable with } c(0)=p\}
\] is called the tangent space of \(M\) at the point \(p\).



Lemma 1
Let \(M\) be an \(n\)-dimensional differentiable manifold, let \(p\in M\) and let \(x:U\rightarrow V\) be a chart of \(M\) with \(p\in V\). Then the map \[
(dx)_p:T_pM\rightarrow \mathbf{R}^n,\qquad \dot c(0)\mapsto \frac{d}{dt}(x^{-1}\circ c)\restriction_{t=0}
\] is well-defined and bijective.



Proof. The well-definedness and injectivity are straightforward by the definition of \(\dot c(0)\); To show surjectivity let \(\mathbf{v}\in\mathbf{R}^n\) and set \(c(t):=x(x^{-1}(p)+t\mathbf{v})\). Choose \(\epsilon>0\)so small that \(x^{-1}(p)+t\mathbf{v} \in U\) whenever \(\vert t \vert<\epsilon\). Then we have \[
(dx)_p(\dot c (0))=\frac{d}{dt}(x^{-1}\circ c)\restriction_{t=0}=\frac{d}{dt}(x^{-1}\circ x\big(x^{-1}(p)+t\mathbf{v}\big))\restriction_{t=0}=\frac{d}{dt}(x^{-1}(p)+t\mathbf{v})\restriction_{t=0}=\mathbf{v}.
\]


Definition 3
We equip \(T_pM\) with the unique vector space structure for which \((dx)_p\) becomes a linear isomorphism. In other words, for \(a,b\in\mathbf{R}\) and \(c_1:(-\epsilon,+\epsilon)\rightarrow M\), \(c_2:(-\epsilon,+\epsilon)\rightarrow M\) we set: \[
a\cdot \dot c_1(0)+b\cdot \dot c_2(0):=(dx)_p^{-1}\big(a\cdot (dx)_p(\dot c_1(0))+b\cdot (dx)_p(\dot c_2(0))\big)\,.
\]



Lemma 2
The vector space structure on \(T_pM\) does not depend on the choice of chart \(x:U\rightarrow V\).

title: Integration on Manifolds
text:
\(\newcommand{\R}{\mathbf{R}}\) \(\newcommand{\w}{\omega}\) \(\newcommand{\d}{\operatorname{d}\!}\) \(\newcommand{\a}{\mathbf{a}}\) \(\newcommand{\x}{\mathbf{x}}\) \(\newcommand{\y}{\mathbf{y}}\)
In this section we will define the integral of a differential \(n\)-form on an \(n\)-dimensional differentiable manifold. We will start with the case of \(\R^n\).
Let \(\w\) be a differential form defined in an open set \(U\subset M^n\). The support \(K\) of \(\w\) is the closure of the set \[
A=\{p\in M^n:\w(p)\neq 0\}.
\]

Example 1
Let \(\w\) be a \(n\)-form and \(M^n=\R^n\). Then \[
\w=a(x_1,\cdots,x_n)\d x_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge \d x_n=a(\x)\d x_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge \d x_n.
\] Assume that the support \(K\) of \(\w\) is compact and contained in \(U\). We define \[
\int _{U}\w =\int _{\R^n} a(\x) \d\x
\] where the right hand is the usual multiple integral of a function with compact support in \(\R^n\) as defined in here.


We will now proceed to the definition of the integral of an \(n\)-form on \(M^n\). To avoid convergence problems, it is convenient to assume that \(M\) is compact; then the support \(K\) of \(\w\), being a closed set in a compact space, is also compact. As we will see in a while, it is also necessary to assume that \(M\) is orientable, i.e., that \(M\) is covered by a family of coordinate neighborhoods \(\{V_\alpha\}\) such that the coordinate changes have positive Jacobians.
Let us assume initially that \(K\) is contained in some coordinate neighborhood \(V_{\alpha}=f_\alpha(U_\alpha)\). Then, if the local representation \(\w_{\alpha}\) of \(\w\) in \(U_\alpha\) is \[
\w=a_{\alpha}(x_1,\dots,x_n)\d x_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \d x_n,
\] we define \[
\int _{M} \w :\,= \int _{V_\alpha} \w_{\alpha} =\int _{U_{\alpha}} a_\alpha \d\x,
\] where the right hand side is an integral in \(\R^n\).
It may happen that \(K\) is contained in another coordinate neighborhood \(V_\beta=f_\beta(U_\beta)\) of the same family, and must show that the above definition is independent of the choice of the coordinate neighborhood.
For that, we can assume, by contracting \(U_\alpha\) and \(U_\beta\) if necessary, that \(V_\alpha=V_\beta\). Let the change of coordinates \[
f=f_\alpha^{-1}\circ f_\beta: U_\beta \rightarrow U_\alpha
\] be given by \[
\begin{aligned}
& x_i=f_i(y_1,\cdots,y_n),\quad i=1,\dots,n, \\
& (x_1,\dots,x_n)\in U_\alpha, \quad (y_1,\dots,y_n)\in U_\beta
\end{aligned}
\] Since \(\w_{\beta}=f^*(\w_\alpha)\), we obtain that \[
\w_\beta=\det(\d f)a_\beta\, \d y_1\wedge\cdots \wedge \d y_n
\] where \[
a_\beta=a_\alpha(f_1(y_1,\dots,y_n),\dots,f_n(y_1,\dots,y_n))\,.
\] By definition and change of variables, we have \[
\begin{aligned}
\int_{V_\beta}\w_\beta & =\int_{U_\beta}\det(\d f)a_\alpha(f(\y)) \d \y \\
& =\int_{U_\beta}|\det(\d f)|a_\alpha (f(\y))\d \y \\
& = \int_{U_\alpha}a_\alpha \d\x =\int _{V_\alpha}\w_\alpha.
\end{aligned}
\]
Notice that without the hypothesis of orientability for \(M\), the sign of the integral of \(\w\) is not well defined. The choice of an orientation for \(M\) fixes a sign for the integral of \(\w\) which changes with the change of orientation.
Let us now consider the case in which the support \(K\) of \(\w\) is contained in no coordinate neighborhood. For that, we need some preliminaries, and before going into details, we will present a sketch of what we intend to do.
Given a covering \(\{V_\alpha\}\) of a compact differentiable manifold \(M\), we will construct a finite family of differentiable functions \(\varphi_1,\dots,\varphi_m\) such that:

\(\sum _{i=1}^{m}\varphi_i=1\),
\(0\leq \varphi_i\leq 1\), and the support of \(\varphi_i\) is contained in some \(V_{\alpha_i}=V_i\).

The family \(\{\varphi_i\}\) is called a differentiable partition of unity subordinate to the covering \(\{V_\alpha\}\). (When \(M\) is orientable, we choose \(\{V_\alpha\}\) compatible with the orientation.)
Let us assume, for the time being, the existence of such a family. Assume furthermore that \(M\) is orientable. We will define the integral of an \(n\)-form \(\w\) on \(M^n\) as follows.
The support of the form \(\varphi_i\w\) is contained in \(V_i\). By a previous definition, it makes sense to write \[
\int_{M} \w =\sum_{i=1}^{m} \int _M\varphi_i \w \,,
\] the only question being whether this definition is independent of the choices made.
Consider another covering \(\{W_\beta\}\) of \(M\) which determines on \(M\) the same orientation as \(\{V_\alpha\}\), and let \(\{\psi_j\},j=1,\dots,s\) be a partition of unity subordinate to \(\{W_\beta\}\). Then \(\{V_\alpha\cap W_\beta\}\) will be a covering for \(M\) and the family \(\varphi_i\psi_j\) will be a partition of unity subordinate to \(\{V_\alpha \cap W_\beta\}\). Thus \[
\sum_{i=1}^{m}\int _M \varphi_i \w =\sum_{i=1}^{m} \int _M \varphi_i \Big( \sum_{j=1} ^{s} \psi_j \Big)\w =\sum_{ij} \int_M \varphi_i \psi_j \w\,,
\] where in the last equality it was used that, for each \(i\), the functions \(\varphi_i \psi_j\) are defined in \(V_i\). Similarly, \[
\sum_{j=1}^s \int _M \psi_j \w=\sum _{j=1}^s \int_M \Big(\sum_{i=1}^m \varphi_i\Big)\psi_j \w=\sum_{ij}\int_M \varphi_i\psi_j\w
\] which proves the required independence.

Remark. What we have done was essentially the following. We observed that the integral of a differential form whose domain is contained in a coordinate neighborhood reduces to a multiple integral. To integrate differential forms in more complicated domains we can proceed in either of the two following ways; We divide the complicated domain in simpler domains, and add up the results, or we decompose the form into forms that are zero outside simple domains and add up the results. Since it is easier to work with functions than with domains, the second alternative is usually preferred, and it was the one used here.

title: Differential of Functions
text:
This note is mainly from Multidimensional Real Analysis I by J.J.DUISTERMAAT and J.A.C.KOLK and Zorich’s Analysis I,II.
The reformulation of differential without \(\epsilon,\delta\) is due to Hadamard.

Definition 1: differentiable mapping and its differential at a point
Let \(U\subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\) be an open set, let \(a \in U\) and \(f:U \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^m\). Then \(f\) is said to be a differentiable mapping at \(a\) if there exists \((df)_a\in \operatorname{Lin}(\mathbb{R}^n,\mathbb{R}^m)\) such that \[
\operatorname{lim}_{x \to a}\frac{\| f(x)-f(a)-(df)_a(x-a)\Vert }{\|x-a \Vert }=0
\] \((df)_a\) is calledd the total derivative of \(f\) at \(a\) (or differential at \(a\)).



Definition 2: Version 2
A function \(f:E \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^m\) defined on a set \(E\subset \mathbb{R}^n\) is differentiable at the point \(a\in E\) which is a interior point (or weaker, limit point) of \(E\), if \[
f(a+h)-f(a)=L(a)h+\alpha(a;h)
\] where \(f(a+h)-f(a)=F(a)(h)\) may be seen as a function of variable \(h\in \{h\in \mathbb{R}^n:a+h \in E\}\equiv S_{a}\); \(L(a):\mathbb{R}^n \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^m\) is a linear map defined on the space \(\mathbb{R}^n\); \(\alpha(a;h)\) is defined to be a function \(S_a \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^m\) such that \(\alpha(a;h)=o (h)\)



Proposition 1: Uniqueness of differential at a point
If a function \(f:E \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^m\) defined on a subset \(E \subset \mathbb{R}^n\) is differentiable at an interior point \(a\in E\) of that set, then the function has a partial derivative at that point with respect to each variable, and the differential of the function is uniquely determined by \(a\) and admits the form: \[
(df)_a(h)=\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1}\vert _{a} h^1+\dots+\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_n}\vert _{a} h^n, \qquad h\in \mathbb{R}^n
\] Thus we know that if \(F(a)(h)\) admits of the form of version 2, it’s uniquely written in this form.



Example 3: Differential of coordinate function
The coordinate functions \(x_i\)’s on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) are the functions which map \((a_1,\dots,a_n)\) to \(a_i\); clearly coordinate functions are differentiable at each point; thus we can define their differentials at each point, denoted by \(({dx_i})_{p}, p \in \mathbb{R}^n\); keep in mind that \(({dx_i})_p\) are just the linear mappings from \(\mathbb{R}^n\) to \(\mathbb{R}\).



Theorem 2: Chain rule of differentiation for products of differentiable functions
Let \(D\subset \mathbf{R}^n\) and \(f:D\rightarrow \mathbf{R}^m\); Suppose that \(g:\mathbf{R}^m\supset\!\rightarrow \mathbf{R}^k\) is differentiable on an open set containing \(f(D)\). Then \(g\circ f\) is differentiable on \(D\), and if \(p\in D\) and \(q=f(p)\), then \[
\big(d(g\circ f)\big)_p=(dg)_q\circ (df)_p\,.
\]

title: Change of variables
text:
\(
ewcommand{\G}{\mathbf{G}}\) \(
ewcommand{\aa}{\mathbf{a}}\) \(
ewcommand{\d}{\operatorname{d}\!}\) \(

title: Change of variables
text:
Integration

Definition 1
Suppose that \(I^k\) is a \(k\)-cell in \(\R^k\) consisting of all \[
\x=(x_1,\cdots,x_k)
\] such that \[
a_i \leq x_i \leq b_i \qquad i=1,\ldots,k
\] \(I^j\) is the \(j\)-cell in \(\R^j\) defined by the first \(j\) inequalities, and \(f\) is a real continuous function on \(I^k\).
Put \(f=f_k\) and define \(f_{k-1}\) on \(I^{k-1}\) by \[
f_{k-1}(x_1,\cdots,x_{k-1})=\int _{a_k} ^{b_k} f_k(x_1,\cdots,x_{k-1},x_k)\d x_k
\] The uniform continuity of \(f_k\) on \(I^k\) shows that \(f_{k-1}\) is continuous on \(I^{k-1}\). Hence we can repeat this process and obtain functions \(f_j\), contiunous on \(I^j\), such that \(f_{j-1}\) is the integral of \(f_j\) with respect to \(x_j\) over \([a_j,b_j]\). After \(k\) steps we arrive at a number \(f_0\), which we call the integral of \(f\) over \(I^k\); we write it in the form \[
\int_{I^k} f(\x)\d\x \,.
\]


A priori, this definition of the integral depends on the order in which the \(k\) integrations are carried out. To prove thiss, let us introduce the temporary notation \(L(f)\) for the integral and \(L^\prime(f)\) for the result obtained by carring out the \(k\) integrations in some other order.

Lemma 2
For every \(f\in C(I^k)\), \(L(f)=L^\prime(f)\).



Proof. If \(h(\x)=h_1(x_1)\cdots h_k(x_k)\), where \(h_j\in C[a_j,b_j]\), then \[
L(h)=\prod_{i=1}^k \int _{a_i}^{b_i}h_i(x_i)\d x_i=L^{\prime}(h).
\] If \(\mathscr{A}\) is the set of all finite sums of such functions \(h\), it follows that \(L(g)=L^\prime(g)\) for all \(g\in\mathscr{A}\). Also, \(\mathscr{A}\) is an algebra of functions on \(I^k\) to which the Stone-Weierstrass Theorem applies.
Put \(V=\prod_{i=1}^k(b_i-a_i)\). If \(f\in C(I^k)\) and \(\epsilon >0\), there exists \(g\in \mathscr{A}\) such that \(\Vert f-g\Vert < \epsilon/V\), where \(\Vert f \Vert\) is defined as \(\max \vert f(\x) \vert\,(\x \in I^k)\). Then \(\vert L(f-g)\vert<\epsilon\), \(\vert L^\prime(f-g)\vert < \epsilon\), and since \[
L(f)-L^\prime(f)=L(f-g)+L^\prime(g-f)
\] we conclude that \(\vert L(f)-L^\prime (f) \vert <2\epsilon\).


Definition 2
The support of a (real or complex) function \(f\) on \(\R^k\) is the closure of the set of all points \(\x \in \R^k\) at which \(f(\x)\neq 0\). If \(f\) is a continuous function with compact support, let \(I^k\) be any \(k\)-cell which contains the support of \(f\) and define \[
\int _{\R^k}f:=\int_{I^k}f\,.
\] The integral so defined is evidently independent of the choice of \(I^k\), provided only that \(I^k\) ccontains the support of \(f\).

title: Change of variables
text:
Primitive mappings

Definition 3
If \(\mathbf{G}\) maps an open set \(E\subset \mathbf{R}^n\) into \(\mathbf{R}^n\), and if there is an integer \(m\) and a real function \(g\) with domain \(E\) such that \[
\begin{equation}
\mathbf{G}(\x)=\sum_{i\neq m} x_i \mathbf{e}_i+g(\x)\mathbf{e}_m , \qquad x\in E
\end{equation}
\tag{1}\] then we call \(\mathbf{G}\) primitive.


A primitive mapping is thus one that changes at most one coordinate; If \(g\) is differentiable at some point \(\aa\in E\), so is \(\G\). The matrix \([\alpha_{ij}]\) of the operator \((\d\G)_{\aa}\) has \[
[(\frac{\partial g}{\partial x_1})_{\aa},\cdots,(\frac{\partial g}{\partial x_m})_{\aa},\cdots,(\frac{\partial g}{\partial x_n})_{\aa}]
\] as its \(m\)’th row. For \(j\neq m\), we have \(\alpha_{jj}=1\) and \(\alpha_{ji}=0\) if \(i\neq j\). The Jacobian of \(\G\) at \(\aa\) is thus given by \[
J_G(\aa)=\det[(\d \G)_{\aa}]=(\frac{\partial g}{\partial x_m})_{\aa}\,.
\] Clearly \((\d\G)_{\aa}\) is invertible if and only if \((\frac{\partial g}{\partial x_m})_{\aa}\neq 0\).

Notation 1

A linear operator \(B\) on \(\R^n\) that interchanges some pair members of the standard basis and leaves the others fixed is called a flip.
By \(P_m,0\leq m\leq n\) we mean the projections in \(\R^n\): \(P_0 \x=0\) and \[
P_m \x=x_1\mathbf{e}_1+\cdots+x_m\mathbf{e}_m,\qquad x\in\R^n\,.
\]




Theorem 3: Theorem of local representation
Suppose \(\mathbf{F}\) is a \(C^1\)-mapping of an open set \(E\subset \R^n\) into \(\R^n\), \(\mathbf{0}\in E\), \(\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{0})=\mathbf{0}\), and \((\d\mathbf{F})_{\mathbf{0}}\) is invertible. Then there is a neighbourhood of \(\mathbf{0}\) in \(\R^n\) in which a representation \[
\begin{equation}
\mathbf{F}(\x)=B_1\circ\cdots\circ B_{n-1}\circ \G_n \circ \cdots \circ \mathbf{G}_1(\x)
\end{equation}
\tag{2}\] is valid.
In Equation 2, each \(\G_i\) is a primitive \(C^1\)-mapping in some neighborhood of \(\mathbf{0}\); \(\G_i(\mathbf{0})=\mathbf{0}\), \((\d\G_i)_0\) is invertible, and each \(B_i\) is either a flip or the identity operator.
Briefly, Equation 2 represents \(\mathbf{F}\) locally as a composition of primitive mappings and flips.



Proof. Assume that for each \(1\leq m\leq n-1\) there exists a neighborhood \(V_m\) of \(\0\) and a \(C^1\)-mapping \(\F_m\) on it, with \(\F_m(\0)=\0\) and \((\d\F_m)_0\) invertible, for which the following holds: \[
P_{m-1}\F_m(\x)=P_{m-1}\x\qquad (\x\in V_m).
\tag{3}\]
By Equation 3, we have \[
\F_m(\x)=P_{m-1}\x+\sum_{i=m}^{n}\alpha_i(\x)\mathbf{e}_i,
\] where \(\alpha_m,\dots,\alpha_n\) are real \(C^1\)-functions in \(V_m\). Hence \[
(\d\F_m)_\0\, \mathbf{e}_m=\sum_{i=m}^{n}(\frac{\partial \alpha_i}{\partial x_m})_\0\, \mathbf{e}_i
\tag{4}\] Since \((\d\F_m)_\0\) is invertible, the left side of Equation 4 is not \(\0\), and therefore there is a \(k\) such that \(m\leq k \leq n\) and \((\frac{\partial \alpha_k}{\partial x_m})_\0\neq 0\).
Let \(B_m\) be the flip that interchanges this \(m\) and this \(k\) (if \(k=m\), \(B_m\) is the identity) and define \[
\G_m(\x)=\x+[\alpha_k(\x)-x_m]\mathbf{e}_m \qquad \x\in V_m\,.
\] Then \(\G_m\in C^1(V_m)\), \(\G_m\) is primitive and \((\d\G_m)_\0\) is invertible.
The inverse function theorem shows therefore that there is an open set \(U_m\) with \(\0\in U_m\subset V_m\) such that \(\G_m\) is a 1-1 mapping of \(U_m\) onto a neighborhood \(V_{m+1}\) of \(\0\), in which \(\G^{-1}_m\) is continuously differentiable. Define \(\F_{m+1}\) by \[
\F_{m+1}(\y)=B_m\circ \F_m \circ \G_m^{-1} (\y),\qquad \y\in V_{m+1}\,.
\tag{5}\] Then \(\F_{m+1}\in C^1(V_{m+1}),\F_{m+1}(\0)=\0\) and \((\d\F_{m+1})_\0\) is invertible by the chain rule. Also, for \(\x\in U_m\), \[
\begin{aligned}
P_m\F_{m+1}(\G_m(\x)) & = P_m B_m \circ \F_m(\x) \\
& = P_m[P_{m+1}\x+\alpha_k(\x)\mathbf{e}_m+\cdots] \\
& =P_{m-1}\x+\alpha_k(\x)\mathbf{e}_m \\
&=P_m \G_m (\x)
\end{aligned}
\] so that \[
P_m\F_{m+1}(\y)=P_m\y, \qquad  \y \in V_{m+1}\,.
\] Take \(\F_1=\F\); it follows from the argument above that Equation 3 also holds for \(m=n\). Moreover, since \(B_m\circ B_m=I\), Equation 5, with \(\y=\G_m(\x)\), is equivalent to \[
\F_m(\x)=B_m\circ \F_{m+1} (\G_m(\x)), \qquad \x\in U_m\,.
\] If we apply this with \(m=1,\ldots,n-1\), we successively obtain \[
\begin{aligned}
\F=\F_1 & =B_1\circ \F_2 \circ \G_1 \\
&=B_1\circ B_2 \circ \F_3 \circ \G_2 \circ \G_1 = \cdots \\
&=B_1\circ \cdots \circ B_{n-1} \circ \F_n \circ \G_{n-1} \circ \cdots \circ \G_1
\end{aligned}
\] in some neighborhood of \(\0\). By Equation 3, \(\F_n\) is primitive. This completes the proof.

title: Change of variables
text:
Partitions of Unity

Theorem 4
Suppose that \(K\) is a compact subset of \(\mathbf{R}^n\) and \(\{V_\alpha\}\) is an open cover of \(K\). Then there exist functions \(\psi_1,\dots, \psi_s\in C(\R^n)\) such that

\(0\leq \psi_i \leq 1\) for \(1\leq i\leq s\);
each \(\psi_i\) has its support in some \(V_\alpha\), and
\(\psi_1(\x)+\dots+\psi_s(\x)=1\) for every \(\x \in K\).

\(\{\psi_i\}\) is called a partition of unity, and (b) is sometimes expressed by saying that \(\{\psi_i\}\) is subordinate to the cover \(\{V_\alpha\}\).



Corollary 5
If \(f\in C(\R^n)\) and the support of \(f\) lies in \(K\), then \[
f=\sum_{i=1}^s \psi_i f\,.
\] Each \(\psi_if\) has its support in some \(V_\alpha\).

title: Change of variables
section: Change of variables in multiple integrals
text:
Change of variables in multiple integrals

Theorem 6
Suppose \(T\) is a one-to-one \(C^1\)-mapping of an open set \(E\subset \R^k\) into \(\R^k\) such that \(J_T(\x)\neq 0\) for all \(\x \in E\). If \(f\) is a continuous function on \(\R^k\) whose support is compact and lies in \(T(E)\), then \[
\int_{\R^k} f(\y) \d\y = \int_{\R^k} f(T(\x)) \, |J_T(\x)| \d\x.
\tag{6}\]



Proof. \(\textbf{step 1}\): If \(T\) is a primitive mapping, then \(T\) only changes one coordinate, say \(T(\x)=(x_1,\dots,\hat{x_t},\dots,x_k)\) where \(\hat{x_t}=g(\x)\). It follows from the change of variable in integral of one variable that \[
\begin{aligned}
\int _{\R^k}f(T(\x)) \, \vert J_T(\x)\vert \d\x & =\int_{\R^k}f(x_1,\dots,\hat{x_t},\dots,x_k)\,\big\vert \frac{\partial g}{\partial x_t}\big\vert\d\x \\
& = \int _{\R^{k-1}}\d\x\int _{\R}f(x_1,\dots,\hat{x_t},\dots,x_k)\big\vert\frac{\partial g}{\partial x_t}\big\vert \d \x_t \\
& = \int _{\R^{k-1}} \d\x \int_{\R} f(x_1,\dots,x_t,\dots,x_n)\d\x_t \\
& = \int _{\R^k} f(\x) \d\x\,.
\end{aligned}
\] Thus Equation 6 holds for primitive mappings.
\(\textbf{step 2}\): If \(T\) is a flip which interchanges two coordinates, say \(x_m\) and \(x_n\), then Equation 6 also holds, for Lemma 2 and \[
\int_{\R^k} f(T(\x)) \, \vert J_T(\x) \vert \d\x = \int _{\R^k} f(T\x)\d\x\,.
\]
\(\textbf{step 3}\): If Equation 6 holds for \(T\) and \(Q\), then it also holds for \(S=T\circ Q\). Because: \[
J_{T\circ Q}(\x)=J_T(\x) \cdot J_Q(\x).
\]
\(\textbf{step 4}\): Each point \(\mathbf{a} \in E\) has a neighborhood \(U\subset E\) in which \[
T(\x)=T(\mathbf{a})+B_1\cdots B_{k-1}\G_k \circ \G_{k-1}\circ \cdots \circ \G_1 (\x -\mathbf{a}),
\] where \(\G_i\) and \(B_i\) are as in Equation 2. Setting \(V=T(U)\), it follows that Equation 6 holds if the support of \(f\) lies in \(V\). Thus:
Each point \(\y\in T(E)\) lies in an open set \(V_{\y}\subset T(E)\) such that Equation 6 holds for all continuous functions whose support lies in \(V_{\y}\).
\(\textbf{step 5}\): Now let \(f\) be a continuous function with compact support \(K\subset T(E)\). Since \(\{V_{\y}\}\) covers \(K\), the Corollary of partition of unity shows that \(f=\sum \psi_i f\), where each \(\psi_i\) is continuous and each \(\psi_i\) has its support in some \(V_{\y}\). Thus Equation 6 holds for each \(\psi_i f\), and hence also for their sum \(f\).

title: Faisceaux
text:
Definition of sheaves (faisceaux)

Definition 1
Suppose that \(X\) is a topological space. A sheave of abelian groups (faisceau de groupes abéliens) over \(X\) (we may simply call it sheaf) consists of:

A function \(X\rightarrow \operatorname{Ab};\qquad x\mapsto \mathfrak{F}_x\) which assigns every \(x\in X\) an abelian group \(\mathfrak{F}_x\).
A topological structure on the set \(\mathfrak{F}\) which is the direct sum of \(\mathfrak{F}_x\).

Suppose that \(f\) is an element of \(\mathfrak{F}_x\), we set \(\pi(f)=x\); The mapping \(\pi\) is called the projection of \(\mathfrak{F}\) over \(X\); the subset \(\{(f,g):\pi(f)=\pi(g)\}\) of \(\mathfrak{F}\times\mathfrak{F}\) is denoted by \(\mathfrak{F}+\mathfrak{F}\).
Moreover, we need to impose two additional axioms:

for any \(f\in\mathfrak{F}\), there exists a neighbourhood \(V\) of \(f\) and a neighbourhood \(U\) of \(\pi(f)\) such that the map \(\pi\restriction_{V}\) is a homeomorphism from \(V\) to \(U\).
The map \(f\rightarrow -f\) is a continuous map from \(\mathfrak{F}\) to \(\mathfrak{F}\); the map \((f,g)\rightarrow f+g\) is a continuous map from \(\mathfrak{F}\times\mathfrak{F}\rightarrow \mathfrak{F}\).

title: Wonderings of Lee
text:
Example 1
There is a contravariant functor \(C\) from the category of compact Hausdorff spaces and continuous maps to the category of normed rings over \(\mathbb{R}\) and continuous homomorphisms which assigns to \(X\) its normed ring of continuous real-valued functions.



Remark. The norm is defined to be \(\Vert f \Vert = \sup _{x\in X} \vert f(x) \vert\) where \(f\in C(X)=C(X;\mathbb{R})\).


Example 2
There is a covariant functor \(H_0\) from the category of topological spaces and continuous maps to the category of abelian groups and homomorphisms such that \(H_0(X)\) is the free abelian group generated by the set of components of \(X\),and if \(f{:}X\to Y\),then \(H_0(f){:}H_0({X})\to H_0(Y)\) is the homomorphism such that if \(C\) is a component of \(X\) and \(C^\prime\) is the component of \(Y\) containing \(f(C)\), then \(H_0(f) C= C^\prime\).


Any functor from the category of topological spaces and continuous maps to an algebraic category (such as the category of abelian groups and homomorphisms) is a representation of the topological category by an algebraic one. Algebraic topology is the study of such functors; we show that simple remarks about functors can be used to obtain necessary conditions for the solvability of topological problems.

Theorem 1
Let \(T\) be a functor from a category \(\mathcal{C}\) to a category \(\mathcal{D}\). Then \(T\) maps isomorphism in \(\mathcal{C}\) to isomorphism in \(\mathcal{D}\).


In particular, if \(T\) is an algebraic functor on the category of topological spaces and continuous maps, a necessary condition that \(X\) be homeomorphic to \(Y\) is that \(T(X)\cong T(Y)\).

Example 3
The real line \(\mathbb{R}\) and the real plane \(\mathbb{R}^2\) are not homeomorphic.
If they were homeomorphic, then \(\mathbb{R}-0\) would be homeomorphic to \(\mathbb{R}^2-p\) for some \(p\in\mathbb{R}^2\), but \(H_0(\mathbb{R}-0)\) is a free abelian group on two generators, while \(H_0({\mathbb{R}}^2-p)\) is a free abelian group on one generator.


In applications of algebraic functors to topological problems the algebra will frequently play an essential role. For example, let \(T_0(X)\) be the functor obtained by composing the functor \(H_0\) with the forgetful functor, which assigns to every abelian group its underlying set. The functor \(T_0\) contains less information than the functor \(H_0\) and does not give as strong a necessary condition for homeomorphism, for example, \(T_0( \mathbb{R} - 0)\) and \(T_0(\mathbb{R}^2-p)\) are both countably infı nite sets and are equivalent in the category of sets and functions. For this reason it is important to provide functors with as much algebraic structure as possible. Later we shall consider functors which depend on a chosen topological space. These functors take values in the category of sets and functions, but sonne of them, depending on properties of the particular spaces which define them, are functors to the category of groups and homomorphisms. The added algebraic structure in such cases will prove useful.
To show how functors can be applied to another problem, let \(A\) be a subspace of a topological space \(X\) and let \(f:A\rightarrow Y\) be continuous. The extension problem is to determine whether \(f\) has a continuous extension to \(X\)一that is, whether the dotted arrow in the triangle.



corresponds to a continuous map making the diagram commutative.

Theorem 2
Let \(T\) be a covariant functor (or contravariant functor) from the category of topological spaces and continuous maps to a category \(\mathcal{C}\). A necessary condition that a map \(f: A \to Y\) be extendable to \(X\) (where \(i: A \subset X\)) is that there exists a morphism \(\varphi: T(X) \to T(Y)\) [or \(\varphi: T(Y) \to T(X)\)] such that \[
\varphi \circ T(i) = T(f) \quad [\text{or } T(f) = T(i) \circ \varphi].
\]



Proof. Assume that \(f': X \to Y\) is an extension of \(f\). Then \(f'\circ i = f\). Therefore
\[
T(f') \circ T(i) = T(f) \quad [\text{or } T(f) = T(i) \circ T(f')],
\]
and \(T(f')\) can be taken as the morphism \(\varphi\).


Example 4
The above result can be applied to prove that the identity map of \(\dot{I}\) cannot be extended to a continuous map \(I \to \dot{I}\). We use the functor \(H_0\) and obtain the necessary condition that there must exist a homomorphism \(\varphi: H_0(I) \to H_0(\dot{I})\) such that \(\varphi \circ H_0(i) = H_0(1_{\dot{I}})\) (where \(i: \dot{I} \subset I\)). Because \(H_0(\dot{I})\) is a free abelian group on two generators and \(H_0(I)\) is a free abelian group on one generator, there is no such homomorphism \(\varphi\). Again, this is a trivial example, but it illustrates the method, and the general homology functors \(H_q\) defined later can be used in the same way to show that there is no continuous map \(E^{n+1} \to S^n\) that is the identity map on \(S^n\).



Remark. Here \(I=[0,1]\) and \(\dot{I}=\{0,1\}=S^0\).

Thus we see that a functor yields necessary conditions for the solvability of topological problems. There are situations in which these necessary conditions are also sufficient. For example, the functor \(C\) of example 1 gives a necessary and sufficient condition for homeomorphism—that is, two compact Hausdorff spaces \(X\) and \(Y\) are homeomorphic if and only if \(C(X)\) and \(C(Y)\) are isomorphic. This is not a particularly useful result, however, because it seems to be no easier to determine whether or not two normed rings are isomorphic than it is to determine whether or not two compact Hausdorff spaces are homeomorphic. We seek functors to categories that are somewhat simpler than the category of topological spaces, so that the algebraic problems that arise in these categories can be effectively solved. One big problem of algebraic topology is to find, and compute, sufficiently many such functors that the solvability of a particular topological problem is equivalent to the solvability of the corresponding (and simpler) algebraic problems.
